## Evidence separation and source volume

Area existence, boundaries and legacy-group synthesis rely on area-level task/skill/activity evidence and area sources only. Role-level sources can justify an individual role's route into a defined area; they cannot create or define an area.

No fixed 15-sources-per-category quota. Completeness is measured by layer x task x item-category x maturity x source-family coverage, claim-specific independent corroboration for material claims, exact locators, counter-evidence, and a documented saturation point.

### Credibility checks for grey sources

Grey sources are included when relevant and assessed individually, not dismissed by category. Record publisher/accountability, named author or accountable organization, date/version, transparent method or source trail, scope and conflicts/access, inspectable claim-level content, and independent corroboration. Use grey literature for documented practice, employer tasks, practitioner methods, implementation examples and discovery; do not let self-description, marketing, forum votes, vendor claims, a single posting, or community curation alone establish truth, prevalence, universal requirements, area boundaries or graph dependencies. State the level at which each claim is credible and retain limitations.

## Area search stopping point

**Closed:** 11/11 areas. All canonical areas are closed within their recorded, bounded search scopes: Quantitative Pricing and Financial Engineering; Quantitative Financial Risk Modeling; Systematic Investment and Quantitative Trading; Vehicle Sensing and Sensor Calibration; Perception and Scene Understanding; High-Definition Mapping and Map Data; Localization and Vehicle State Estimation; Automated Driving Planning; Vehicle Control and Dynamics; Vehicle Interface and System Integration; ADS Safety, Verification and Validation. This is not a global source-saturation claim or a source-count quota.

Close an area only when each applicable item-family × maturity × source-family cell has evidence, a reasoned not-applicable state, or an explicit bounded search disposition; material claims and counterevidence have locators and limits; and prerequisites, alternatives, complements, outputs, and downstream task links are mapped. Then run the dated gap/counter-search. If it finds a material gap, update and recheck only the affected cells. Source-count quotas do not close an area.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Derivative pricing foundations connect contract payoffs and cash flows to no-arbitrage valuation; fixed-income valuation additionally uses discount factors and arbitrage-free term-structure models. Probability, stochastic models and numerical methods become necessary as payoffs or dynamics prevent a closed-form solution. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Level II Derivatives and Arbitrage-Free Valuation Framework readings; QuantLib official documentation's pricing-engine and instrument abstractions. **Sources:** D011-CFA-CONTINGENT-CLAIMS-2026, D011-CFA-ARBITRAGE-FREE-FIXED-INCOME-2026, D011-QUANTLIB-DOCS **Area context:** This is the prerequisite layer for pricing options, fixed-income instruments and engineered contracts: identify instrument/payoff and market inputs before selecting a pricing model or numerical engine. **Limit:** Curriculum and library documentation establish an instructional/software framing, not an exhaustive theorem-level foundation. Instrument conventions, collateral, funding, market data and jurisdiction-specific valuation policies add context; not every product requires stochastic simulation. **Relationship:** Payoff and contract terms plus market conventions feed model choice; no-arbitrage assumptions constrain calibration; stochastic dynamics and numerical analysis support model/engine selection; calibration and price/Greeks outputs then support hedging and downstream risk analysis.
- **Claim:** One current mathematical/computational-finance MSc makes its preparation structure explicit: introductory probability, statistics, PDEs, Python and financial-markets/instruments; a compulsory core then covers stochastic calculus, derivatives, numerical methods, financial data analysis, fixed income/credit, stochastic control, quantitative risk and deep learning; selected electives, C++ practicals and a dissertation add specialization and assessed implementation outputs. **Locator:** University of Oxford Mathematical Institute, MSc Mathematical and Computational Finance 2026–2027 course regulations, sections 4–5; companion programme page for admissions background and course structure. **Sources:** D011-OXFORD-MCF-CURRICULUM-2026-27 **Area context:** This is a concrete curriculum example for quantitative pricing and financial engineering: it connects mathematical and financial foundations to pricing, numerical implementation, model/risk topics and assessed computational work. It helps distinguish broad preparation from later product/topic electives. **Limit:** A single degree's course status and ordering do not establish universal industry prerequisites, nor do co-taught/core topics automatically create item-to-item dependencies. Oxford labels the introductory courses non-assessed; exact prerequisite edges require item-level technical evidence and independent curriculum/employer corroboration. **Relationship:** Probability/PDE/statistics and financial-instrument concepts prepare learners for stochastic calculus and derivative valuation in this curriculum; numerical methods and C++ practicals support implementation; product/risk topics and electives branch by specialization. Treat these as the programme's stated teaching structure, not a universal blocker chain.
- **Claim:** The mathematical prerequisite chain depends on the pricing method. Probability supports discrete risk-neutral valuation; continuous-time derivative models add Brownian motion, stochastic integration/Itô calculus, martingales and measure change (including Girsanov), with Feynman–Kac linking selected SDE expectations to PDEs. A PDE numerical solver then adds consistency, stability, convergence and error analysis. An Oxford derivative course explicitly makes Probability a prerequisite, marks Measure and Martingales as good background and integration/Fourier as useful but not required; its binomial-tree material does not make the full continuous-time chain a prerequisite for every option model. **Locator:** Princeton ORF 527 Spring 2026 course synopsis (opened 2026-10-28); Oxford B8.3 Mathematical Models of Financial Derivatives 2026–27 general prerequisites and synopsis (opened 2026-10-28); MIT OCW 18.336 numerical-PDE syllabus (opened 2026-10-28); Oxford MCF 2026–27 course regulations. **Sources:** D011-PRINCETON-ORF527-STOCHASTIC-CALCULUS-2026, D011-OXFORD-B8-3-FINANCIAL-DERIVATIVES-2026-27, D011-MIT-OCW-18336-PDE-NUMERICAL-ERROR-2009, D011-OXFORD-MCF-CURRICULUM-2026-27, D011-ELSEVIER-CRR-1979 **Area context:** These are method-specific foundations for pricing: probability/no-arbitrage can introduce discrete models; continuous-time valuation requires additional stochastic-process and measure tools; PDE-based computation adds numerical-analysis concepts. This avoids converting one graduate course's sequence into compulsory prerequisites for all product families and engines. **Limit:** Course synopses establish each institution's teaching scope and explicit prerequisite wording, not a universal qualification standard. The numerical-PDE course is general mathematics; its depth is needed only for relevant PDE solvers, not every pricing task. CRR and analytical methods provide complementary lower-mathematics entry points. **Relationship:** Contract payoff and probability/no-arbitrage concepts -> discrete tree or analytic model where applicable; continuous-time route adds stochastic process, Ito/martingale/measure-change reasoning and may connect to PDE via Feynman–Kac; numerical PDE route adds discretization stability/convergence/error checks. These are alternative method branches, not a single compulsory ladder.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Research on learned pricing and hedging builds on stochastic-process/PDE or SDE modeling, numerical approximation and computational optimization; neural methods add statistical learning, differentiability, generalization and model-validation competencies. **Locator:** PNAS deep-learning PDE paper (2018); Ludkovski's statistical ML for quantitative finance review (2023); Fan and Sirignano's derivatives-pricing review (2026); Buehler et al. Deep Hedging (2019). **Sources:** D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-LUDKOVSKI-STAT-ML-QUANT-FINANCE-2023, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019 **Area context:** These are advanced foundations for pricing/hedging research, following instrument/payoff, probability, stochastic models and classical numerical baselines; not prerequisites for every quant-finance learner. **Limit:** Methods differ in target and evidence; sources do not prove that neural pricing replaces calibration, PDE, trees or Monte Carlo, or that ML is needed in every pricing role. **Relationship:** Classical dynamics/payoff define the task; numerical methods create the baseline; learning methods approximate a solution or hedge policy; validation under new states/regimes and model-risk review determine safe downstream use.
- **Claim:** The emerging Heston PINN branch assumes stochastic-volatility and PDE/Feynman–Kac foundations: the Heston pricing equation, terminal payoff and boundary conditions are encoded in a neural solver objective. This is a specific research formulation rather than a prerequisite for ordinary derivatives pricing. **Locator:** Hainaut and Casas (2024), Annals of Finance 20(3), 353–376; model/PDE formulation in the open full text; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HAINAUT-CASAS-PINN-HESTON-2024, D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018 **Area context:** Optional computational-finance competency for learners extending classical stochastic-volatility/PDE pricing into physics-informed learning; it builds on, rather than bypasses, the model and PDE setup. **Limit:** One Heston European-option paper; it does not establish a universal curriculum requirement, market-calibration expertise or production deployment. **Relationship:** Stochastic-process/PDE knowledge -> formulate the model-specific pricing PDE and conditions -> define PINN residual/data losses -> train and validate against a classical solution. Ordinary pricing routes remain available without neural methods.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Future**
- **Claim:** Frontier neural SDE/PDE pricing and proposed quantum PDE pricing sit on top of established derivatives and quantitative foundations. The neural-model branch calls for stochastic-process/PDE understanding, numerical discretization and error analysis, statistical learning and out-of-sample validation; the quantum branch additionally depends on quantum information, algorithm/resource reasoning and classical benchmark design. These are specialist foundations for optional research routes, not prerequisites for every pricing learner. **Locator:** Fan and Sirignano, Quantitative Finance 26(6) (2026), publisher abstract describing neural SDE/PDE coefficient models compared with Black–Scholes, Dupire and Heston on option pricing and hedging; Ludkovski, Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application 10 (2023), abstract/review scope; arXiv:2605.26610 (2026) abstract on quantum PDE pricing under local-volatility and Heston models with resource analysis; ESMA TRV Risk Analysis, 13 May 2026, pp. 3–4 on early-stage maturity and hardware limits. **Sources:** D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026, D011-LUDKOVSKI-STAT-ML-QUANT-FINANCE-2023, D011-QUANTUM-PDE-MULTIASSET-PRICING-2026, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026 **Area context:** This cell describes prerequisites for advanced pricing research rather than a new general pricing foundation: learners first need product/payoff, no-arbitrage, stochastic-model and numerical-method foundations, then select neural approximation or quantum algorithm study according to the chosen research route. **Limit:** The neural-pricing article is represented here at publisher-abstract level; the review is a literature map, not proof of prevalence; the quantum PDE work is an unreviewed preprint with theoretical resource analysis; ESMA is a maturity context source rather than a technical benchmark. These sources do not establish universal prerequisites, broad performance advantage or production readiness. **Relationship:** Classical derivative, probability/stochastic-process, PDE and numerical-analysis foundations feed both advanced routes. Statistical learning and leakage-aware validation extend the neural branch. Quantum information and resource/error accounting are additional prerequisites only for the quantum branch; any claimed benefit must be tested against a matched classical pricing baseline before price or hedge outputs are interpreted.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Classical derivative valuation includes a continuous-time no-arbitrage theoretical formula and a discrete-time arbitrage lattice. The Black-Scholes publisher abstract establishes a theoretical option valuation; Cox-Ross-Rubinstein presents a discrete-time model with the Black-Scholes model as a limiting case and a numerical procedure for options where early exercise may be optimal. **Locator:** Black and Scholes (1973), Journal of Political Economy 81(3), publisher abstract; Cox, Ross and Rubinstein (1979), Journal of Financial Economics 7(3), publisher abstract. **Sources:** D011-UCHICAGO-BLACK-SCHOLES-1973, D011-ELSEVIER-CRR-1979, D011-CFA-CONTINGENT-CLAIMS-MODELS-2026 **Area context:** These are established option-pricing methods. The contract payoff and model assumptions determine whether a closed-form theoretical model or a discrete lattice is relevant; early exercise creates a distinct computational need for the lattice example. **Limit:** Primary-paper full texts were not accessible in this pass; claims are limited to publisher abstracts and current curriculum corroboration. This is not a complete pricing-method inventory, and neither method is suitable for every payoff, market convention or model risk question. **Relationship:** Payoff and no-arbitrage assumptions precede method choice. The lattice provides a discrete-time route and early-exercise computation; the continuous-time formula provides a theoretical benchmark under its model assumptions. Calibration, numerical error checks, sensitivities and hedge use follow valuation and are not established by the abstracts alone.
- **Claim:** Interest-rate and counterparty-credit valuation branch by contract and output. A Hull–White one-factor short-rate model can provide bond/bond-option formulas and a lattice/tree representation; PDE finite differences are a numerical alternative for selected nonstandard or multi-factor claims, while market-quoted Black-style swaption engines are not the same model. Even within a library, support is contract/engine-specific: QuantLib warns that many engines approximate OIS-underlying swaptions as vanilla swaps and identifies a narrower set of OIS-capable engines. For counterparty adjustments, exposure paths, market-implied PD/credit spread, LGD, collateral and wrong-way dependence inform CVA valuation; sensitivities can feed regulatory SA-CVA capital, while BA-CVA is another capital approach. Trade-level conditional expected-exposure allocation is a portfolio-to-trade attribution output. The Federal Reserve's 2026 stress-test CVA model instead produces supervisory stressed-loss estimates and uses a fallback for incomplete submitted exposure data. These measures consume related pricing/exposure outputs but are not interchangeable. **Locator:** QuantLib Hull–White model source and Swaption instrument header (opened 2026-10-28); Hu and Wang (2020) publisher-indexed abstract; Basel Framework MAR50 §§50.2–50.3, 50.9–50.11, 50.31–50.36; Federal Reserve 2026 Supervisory Stress Test Documentation, CVA Model pp. 239–264; Pykhtin and Rosen (2010) official abstract. **Sources:** D011-QUANTLIB-HULL-WHITE-CURRENT-SOURCE, D011-QUANTLIB-SWAPTION-ENGINE-SUPPORT, D011-MATH-HULL-WHITE-FD-IRD-2020, D011-BIS-CVA-CREDIT-VALUATION-FRAMEWORK, D011-FED-2026-STRESS-TEST-CVA-MODEL, D011-FED-CVA-TRADE-LEVEL-ALLOCATIONS-2010 **Area context:** This extends pricing coverage beyond equity options into rates and counterparty credit. Rate model and numerical engine choices should follow the payoff, exercise, curve/settlement conventions and target output. Exposure modelling and CVA calculations reuse derivative values over future risk-factor paths, then produce adjustment, sensitivity, capital or stress-loss outputs under different definitions and purposes. **Limit:** The QuantLib pages establish implementation-specific equations and support boundaries, not relative accuracy or a market-wide model ranking. The numerical PDE paper was inspected only at publisher-abstract level. Basel MAR50 concerns regulatory CVA capital and is jurisdiction/adoption-specific; the 2026 Federal Reserve document is a supervisory stress-test model with assumed upstream input quality; neither is a universal accounting-CVA procedure. The 2010 trade-allocation paper's closed forms rely on stated distribution assumptions. **Relationship:** Contract cash flows and curve conventions -> selected rate model / quote model -> analytic, lattice, PDE or simulation engine -> price and sensitivities. For counterparty risk, derivative revaluation on risk-factor paths -> expected exposure with netting/collateral and credit inputs -> valuation CVA and sensitivities; those sensitivities may feed SA-CVA capital, while BA-CVA supplies a distinct standardized capital calculation. A separate supervisory stress model transforms submitted CVA/exposure data into stressed-loss estimates. Trade attribution decomposes portfolio CVA/exposure into trade contributions. Each arrow is purpose/output dependent, not a universal prerequisite sequence.
- **Claim:** Representative established pricing-model families now span: diffusion/contingent-claim equity pricing (Black–Scholes) and discrete arbitrage lattices (CRR); stochastic short-rate models (Vasicek, CIR and Hull–White); forward-rate models (HJM and the tenor-specific BGM/LMM market model); stochastic-volatility/smile models (Heston and SABR); and structural versus reduced-form credit pricing (Merton versus Duffie–Singleton). Their inputs and outputs differ: spot/forward curves and model factors support bond/cap/swaption values; spot/volatility/correlation/smile inputs support option prices and Greeks; firm-value/payoff assumptions or hazard/recovery inputs support defaultable-bond and credit-claim values. The model is a contract/market representation; tree, PDE, transform/Fourier and Monte Carlo techniques are numerical routes used to solve selected claims under it. **Locator:** Original/publisher papers and abstracts inspected 2026-10-28: Vasicek (1977); CIR (1985); HJM (1992); Brace–Gatarek–Musiela (1997); Heston (1993); Hagan et al. SABR practitioner paper; Merton (1974); Duffie–Singleton (1999). Current MathWorks R2026b BGM documentation confirms model volatility/correlation inputs and instrument-to-Monte-Carlo workflow; QuantLib swaption support and Hull–White records already indexed. **Sources:** D011-VASICEK-TERM-STRUCTURE-1977-2026, D011-CIR-TERM-STRUCTURE-1985-2026, D011-HJM-FORWARD-RATE-VALUATION-1992-2026, D011-BGM-MARKET-MODEL-1997-2026, D011-OUP-HESTON-STOCHASTIC-VOL-1993, D011-SABR-MANAGING-SMILE-RISK-2002-2026, D011-MERTON-STRUCTURAL-CORPORATE-DEBT-1974-2026, D011-DUFFIE-SINGLETON-REDUCED-FORM-DEFAULT-1999-2026, D011-MATHWORKS-BGM-2026-DOCS, D011-QUANTLIB-HULL-WHITE-CURRENT-SOURCE, D011-QUANTLIB-SWAPTION-ENGINE-SUPPORT **Area context:** This supports selecting a model family after identifying instrument, payoff, market inputs and required outputs. A short-rate model, forward-rate market model, stochastic-volatility smile model and credit-default model address different state variables and contract risks; learners should see these as product/method branches, not as a universal linear ladder. **Limit:** The sources establish model definitions, assumptions and representative products, not common-sample accuracy, calibration stability, market adoption or a universal winner. HJM is represented at publisher-indexed abstract scope; Vasicek and Duffie–Singleton have access/text-extraction limits; SABR performance statements are author-reported. The list is a representative family map rather than every model or hybrid product. **Relationship:** Instrument/payoff and market conventions -> model family and state/input choice -> calibrated parameters/curves/surfaces -> product-compatible numerical pricer -> price and model-specific sensitivities/default outputs -> independent market, numerical and risk validation. Short-rate/forward-rate alternatives share term-structure inputs but differ in modeled state and calibration; Heston/SABR connect stochastic volatility to smile/Greek outputs; structural and intensity credit branches encode default differently. Numerical algorithms complement model choices.
- **Claim:** Reusable numerical benchmarks now cover distinct pricing branches with common contracts, parameter sets, reference outputs and accuracy/time measures: BENCHOP defines one-factor European/American/barrier/dividend, local-volatility, Heston, Merton-jump and two-asset spread cases; BENCHOP–SLV compares SDE Monte Carlo, Fourier and PDE methods for selected SABR, Heston/QLSV and Heston–Hull–White products; a lower-weight two-asset study compares binomial, variance-reduced Monte Carlo and finite-element PDE methods under changing correlation/volatility. Their findings explain conditional tradeoffs, not universal winners. Reference construction, optimization, confidence intervals, hardware, dimensionality and payoff coverage limit comparisons. **Locator:** BENCHOP version 2.0 specification and reference-value appendix (2015), problems 1–6; von Sydow et al., International Journal of Computer Mathematics (2018), sections 2–5 and Appendix 1; Niklasson and Tivedal, Chalmers master's thesis (2018), chapters 3–6 and appendices D–F. **Sources:** D011-BENCHOP-OPTION-PRICING-BENCHMARK-SUITE-2015, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018, D011-CHALMERS-MULTI-ASSET-OPTION-NUMERICAL-COMPARISON-2018 **Area context:** After identifying payoff/model family, benchmark problems make the next numerical choice concrete: select the method representation that can solve that contract under the model, then compare converged price/error and compute output. These are examples for tree/PDE/PIDE/Fourier/simulation branches; they do not establish which items a student must select or a mandatory sequence. **Limit:** The suites are finite stylized cases. BENCHOP–SLV reports code and runtime limitations and lacks confidence intervals for one Monte Carlo experiment; numerical references can carry error. The 2018 two-asset source is a master's thesis and assumes correlated constant-parameter GBM. Results should not be generalized to untested products, calibrated market inputs, second-order Greeks or production hardware. **Relationship:** Contract/payoff, exercise and market inputs -> model representation (Black–Scholes/local/stochastic volatility/jump/rates/multi-asset) -> compatible numerical route (analytic/tree/PDE or PIDE/Fourier/Monte Carlo) -> reference price and error/convergence estimate -> runtime/cost and statistical uncertainty -> compare only within matching assumptions, outputs and implementations. Model families and numerical routes are separate choices; a benchmark links them for one stated task.
- **Claim:** Early-exercise and hybrid pricing methods must be matched to the contract and state dimension. A full-text Heston study combines a tree for the CIR-type variance state with finite differences for a transformed asset state, and compares selected European/American and barrier cases with pure-tree, Longstaff–Schwartz Monte Carlo and reference values. A current spread-option example shows why European closed-form approximations do not automatically extend to American exercise, where FD grids or LSMC are used and produce distinct price/Greek estimates. **Locator:** Briani, Caramellino and Zanette, full manuscript Sections 2 and 4, pp.18–20; MathWorks R2026b example sections 'Overview of the Pricing Methods' and 'Pricing an American Spread Option', including reported prices/Delta/Gamma; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-BRIANI-CARAMELLINO-ZANETTE-HESTON-AMERICAN-HYBRID-TREE-FD-2013, D011-MATHWORKS-SPREAD-OPTION-METHOD-COMPARISON-R2026B, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018 **Area context:** These are optional specialist branches after model/payoff definition: early exercise introduces an optimal-stopping boundary; multi-state stochastic volatility/rates can motivate hybrid or grid methods, while simulation supports higher-dimensional state spaces. Energy spread examples connect joint price/correlation inputs to prices and two-asset Greeks. **Limit:** Distinct studies use different contracts, parameters and reference methods; MathWorks is vendor documentation and the Heston paper tests a narrow model family. Do not combine their timings/prices into a common ranking or imply one method is best across products. **Relationship:** Contract payoff/exercise + calibrated model state -> choose an analytic approximation only when its assumptions fit; otherwise tree/PDE/LSMC or a documented hybrid -> compare price and Greeks to a suitable reference and test grid/path convergence -> downstream valuation/hedge analysis. A hybrid combines numerical components; it does not make those components universally required.

- **Claim:** For Bermudan early-exercise derivatives whose downstream analytics need sensitivities along future scenarios, Rolling Adjoints extends the regress-later SGBM pricing scheme: it differentiates the fitted regression coefficients and propagates sensitivities backward across monitoring dates to obtain pathwise state/model-parameter Greeks. It does not show a general method suitable for all products, replace independent sensitivity validation, or prove that SIMM/MVA calculations are compliant merely because pathwise Greeks are available. **Relationship:** Bermudan payoff + risk-neutral state model + monitoring schedule -> SGBM regress-later continuation approximation -> regression-coefficient derivatives plus adjoint propagation -> pathwise state/model Greeks and time-zero checks -> exposure/initial-margin/MVA consumer. **Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Neural numerical methods form a distinct research branch for high-dimensional pricing/control PDEs, while deep hedging uses learned policies to optimize a stated risk objective under trading frictions; these solve different downstream problems and should not be presented as interchangeable ‘AI pricing’ methods. **Locator:** PNAS 115(34), 8505–8510 (2018), article record/abstract for deep-learning approximation of BSDE/PDE solutions and nonlinear Black–Scholes/HJB examples; Bühler et al., Quantitative Finance 19(8), 1271–1291 (2019), open manuscript for hedge-policy optimization with costs, market impact, liquidity and risk constraints; Fan & Sirignano (2026) publisher abstract for neural SDE/PDE pricing comparisons with Black–Scholes, Dupire and Heston. **Sources:** D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026, D011-LUDKOVSKI-STAT-ML-QUANT-FINANCE-2023 **Area context:** This emerging computational branch belongs downstream of stochastic calculus, derivative valuation and numerical methods; it supports high-dimensional approximation or friction-aware hedge control where the research objective requires it. **Limit:** Evidence ranges from a bounded numerical paper, an open peer-reviewed hedging paper and an abstract-level 2026 pricing comparison. It does not show production adoption, universal superiority or replacement of model risk, calibration, benchmark and out-of-sample evaluation. **Relationship:** Deep BSDE methods build on stochastic differential/PDE formulations and simulation; learned pricing models must be compared with structural baselines under matched instruments/data. Deep hedging consumes scenarios, transaction-cost/liquidity assumptions and an explicit risk measure and outputs a policy; it complements price/Greek hedging rather than producing a fair value by itself.
- **Claim:** Recent pricing research branches by product and output rather than a single neural replacement for classical pricing. Deep reflected BSDE/neural regression Monte Carlo has been applied to high-dimensional multi-asset Bermudan portfolios and produces prices, Delta/Gamma and hedge-rebalancing decisions; a neural jump-SDE embeds learned parameter estimation within a conventional jump-diffusion; learned calibration has been studied for a characteristic-function Wishart/jump commodity model. These research designs complement model-specific analytic, tree/PDE, transform and Monte Carlo engines only where their model, product and output match. **Locator:** Negyesi and Oosterlee (2026), SIAM J. Financial Mathematics 17(3), publisher abstract; Zheng (2026), Journal of Futures Markets abstract; 2025 Results in Applied Mathematics article 100661 publisher abstract; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-SIAM-DEEP-BSDE-BERMUDAN-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-WILEY-NEURAL-JUMPS-OPTION-PRICING-2026, D011-ELSEVIER-WISHART-NEURAL-COMMODITY-OPTION-CALIBRATION-2025, D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026 **Area context:** This is an optional emerging branch after the learner understands risk-neutral pricing, product payoff, model dynamics, numerical error and calibration objectives. Choose the output first: price, calibrated parameters, Greeks, hedge policy or large-portfolio valuation. A price surrogate does not automatically yield reliable Greeks or a hedging strategy; deep BSDE with Gamma/hedging is a distinct design from learning prices or sensitivities alone. **Limit:** Recent evidence is largely publisher-abstract level and author-reported experiments. No independent reproduction, standardized hardware/runtime comparison or production adoption is established. The 2026 deep-BSDE study is specific to multi-asset Bermudan portfolios and up to 100 risk factors; neural-jump and learned-calibration claims are confined to their named option data/models. Do not generalize benchmark gains across payoff families or products. **Relationship:** Product/payoff + stochastic model/market conventions + calibration data -> selected pricing engine or learned solver -> distinct outputs (price; calibrated parameters; Delta/Gamma; hedge action) -> matched numerical, market-quote and sensitivity validation. If a learned output is a price only, additional Greek estimation is required; if it emits price and Greeks, validate each separately; hedge actions feed hedging execution only under an independently specified risk/transaction-cost objective.
- **Claim:** A constrained Gaussian-process regression (CGPR) solver has been proposed for American-option optimal stopping: transform the variational pricing PDE into an iterative penalized Feynman-Kac problem, constrain the regression to payoff boundary and interior equation samples, and estimate the value surface. This differs from LSM/Monte Carlo, where regression estimates continuation values along simulated paths, and from GP-plus-control-variate designs that reduce simulation estimator variance. The CGPR paper's tested examples are American puts under Heston and two-factor Hull-White; the authors report comparisons with LSMC, but identify kernel tuning, regularization bias and high-dimensional matrix inversion as limitations. **Locator:** Hainaut, Applied Mathematics and Computation 512 (2026), article 129747, publisher abstract; full UCLouvain ISBA-LIDAM author manuscript (2024), Sections 2–6 and Tables 3–14; Mu et al., Foundations of Computing and Decision Sciences 43(3) (2018), publisher abstract; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HINAUT-CGPR-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2026, D011-HINAUT-UCL-CGPR-AMERICAN-MANUSCRIPT-2024, D011-MU-GODINA-KRIGING-CV-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2018, D011-FU-LAPRISE-MADAN-AMERICAN-MC-COMPARISON-2001, D011-CCSE-AMERICAN-OPTION-VALUATION-COMPARISON-2018 **Area context:** This is an optional advanced branch after the learner understands American exercise/optimal stopping, risk-neutral model dynamics, PDE/Feynman-Kac or simulation regression, and numerical error. The next method depends on the target: explicit exercise-boundary/value function (tree/PDE/CGPR), flexible pathwise state dimension (LSM/primal-dual simulation), or lower variance for a Monte Carlo estimate (control variates, possibly GP-assisted). **Limit:** The studies use different models, products, algorithms and implementations; they are not a matched benchmark. The full CGPR author manuscript is a 2024 version and its final 2026 journal article was inspected at abstract level. The 2001 Monte Carlo comparison is publisher-abstract only. Reported speed/accuracy results are study-specific and no production adoption or cross-product superiority is established. **Relationship:** American payoff and exercise rights + stochastic state model + market inputs -> choose a solution design: lattice/PDE for tractable state spaces; LSM/primal-dual simulation for path/state flexibility; PDE-constrained CGPR to approximate the value surface under the equation/boundary; or GP/Kriging within simulation for continuation regression, optionally paired with a known control variate -> validate price, exercise boundary/policy and numerical uncertainty separately -> pass only the validated output needed by valuation/risk/hedging. CGPR, LSM and control variates are not alternatives at one undifferentiated layer: CGPR versus LSM are candidate solvers for the value/continuation problem, while a control variate modifies a simulation estimator and can combine with a regression method.
- **Claim:** A 2024 conference abstract proposes Hybrid Least Squares Monte Carlo (HLSM) for American-option continuation-value estimation by combining standard LSM and Positive LSM exercise values; the abstract reports PLSM alone can lower overall prices and fail to provide efficient adaptive exercise timing. This is a candidate variant to assess, not an established improvement. **Locator:** Zhang and Zhang (2024), ACM conference paper record/abstract at HKU Scholars Hub, especially abstract; full text may require subscription, inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HKU-HYBRID-LEAST-SQUARES-MONTE-CARLO-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2024, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-FABOZZI-PALETTA-TUNARU-WLSMC-2017 **Area context:** Optional early-exercise estimator research after canonical Longstaff–Schwartz regression and exercise-policy validation; the source record identifies a proposed variation but does not establish its scope across products. **Limit:** Abstract only: exact contracts, model settings, uncertainty, numerical comparisons, code and independent replication are unavailable from the inspected record. Do not claim HLSM outperforms LSM or make it a required/selectable tool based on this source alone. **Relationship:** American payoff and simulated paths -> estimate continuation/exercise values with LSM; HLSM changes the regression target by combining LSM/PLSM values -> compare price and exercise-policy behavior against canonical LSM and suitable references before any performance or adoption claim.
- **Claim:** A physics-informed neural network can encode the Heston/Feynman–Kac pricing PDE and approximate selected European option values across specified parameters as a learned alternative to direct numerical pricing. It remains a research branch after stochastic-volatility/PDE foundations, not a universal replacement for analytic, transform, tree, finite-difference or Monte Carlo methods. **Locator:** Hainaut and Casas (2024), Annals of Finance 20(3), 353–376; UCLouvain open repository record and PDF, model formulation and numerical results; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HAINAUT-CASAS-PINN-HESTON-2024, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018, D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018 **Area context:** Optional emerging method for selected European Heston pricing after stochastic-volatility models, PDE/Feynman–Kac and numerical solution foundations.
