**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Future**
- **Claim:** Quantum amplitude-estimation and related quantum-circuit methods are a plausible future research branch for derivative expectation pricing: peer-reviewed work combines QAE with SDE discretization for Heston Asian/barrier options and estimates logical resources, while current supervisory analysis says the field remains early-stage and hardware-limited; therefore this is frontier literacy, not an established pricing prerequisite or proven commercial accelerator. **Locator:** Wang & Kan, Quantum 8, 1504 (2024), abstract and resource-cost description for Heston Asian/barrier options; ESMA TRV Risk Analysis dated 13 May 2026, pp. 3–4 and quantum-finance use-case discussion; IEEE NQComp 2026 DOI record/abstract for representation error in a low-qubit Qiskit vanilla-option implementation (full IEEE page returned HTTP 418).; an additional 2026 arXiv preprint proposes PDE-based local/Heston multi-asset pricing with explicit resource accounting; Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 lists educational implementations for option/fixed-income pricing and credit risk. **Sources:** D011-QUANTUM-HESTON-OPTION-PRICING-2024, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026, D011-IEEE-QUANTUM-OPTION-REPRESENTATION-ERROR-2026, D011-QUANTUM-PDE-MULTIASSET-PRICING-2026, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-PRICING-TUTORIALS-0401 **Area context:** In quantitative pricing, the proposed composition is a classical stochastic asset/volatility model and numerical discretization plus quantum amplitude estimation of discounted payoffs or risk expectations; it depends on encoding the probability distribution and payoff into a circuit and interpreting circuit-resource/error costs. **Limit:** Peer-reviewed algorithm/resource studies are not hardware demonstrations or evidence of end-to-end quantum advantage on real market workloads. ESMA is an official but high-level supervisory outlook; the 2026 IEEE counterexample is abstract-only. No student should infer that quantum methods currently outperform validated classical Monte Carlo, PDE, tree or Fourier methods in production. A PDE-based 2026 preprint adds a proposal, not empirical quantum advantage; Qiskit examples are versioned learning artifacts and their presence does not imply active maintenance or deployment. **Relationship:** The learning dependency runs from stochastic calculus/model assumptions and classical SDE/Monte Carlo pricing to quantum information, amplitude estimation and state/payoff encoding, followed by error/resource benchmarking against the same classical problem. Encoding overhead, fault tolerance and accuracy may erase theoretical query-complexity gains; the branch is optional future specialization, not a blocker for classical pricing competence.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Traditional**
- **Claim:** For a fixed option example, QuantLib implements analytic, finite-difference, binomial-tree and Monte Carlo pricing engines, demonstrating distinct computational alternatives that can return prices and Greeks. **Locator:** QuantLib maintainer repository `Examples/EquityOption/EquityOption.cpp`; the example compares European, Bermudan and American exercise cases by replacing the pricing engine and reports price/Greeks. **Sources:** D011-QUANTLIB-OPTION-ENGINE-COMPARISON, D011-CFA-CONTINGENT-CLAIMS-MODELS-2026 **Area context:** The technique choice is part of derivative valuation implementation and depends on payoff, exercise, model and required output; it is not a choice of software alone. **Limit:** One library example establishes implementation availability, not numerical convergence, independent validation, universal accuracy or market-wide prevalence. The CFA reading supplies method context but is not a comparative benchmark. **Relationship:** Instrument/payoff and model assumptions determine the admissible engine; calibration supplies parameters, the engine produces valuation and sensitivities, and convergence/benchmark tests validate numerical results. Analytic, lattice, PDE and simulation methods are alternatives only where their assumptions and product scope overlap.
- **Claim:** Established pricing families include stochastic-volatility models with characteristic-function valuation, explicit finite-difference discretization for bond and bond-option PDE problems, and least-squares Monte Carlo estimating continuation value for American options. These are distinct model and numerical-method choices, not interchangeable tools: stochastic volatility changes the dynamics, while finite differences and simulation approximate valuation under chosen dynamics and exercise rules. **Locator:** Heston (1993), Oxford Academic abstract; Hull and White (1990), Cambridge Core abstract; Longstaff and Schwartz (2001), Oxford Academic abstract. **Sources:** D011-OUP-HESTON-STOCHASTIC-VOL-1993, D011-CUP-HULL-WHITE-EXPLICIT-FD-1990, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001 **Area context:** These sources extend the traditional methods map across stochastic-volatility dynamics, PDE discretization and simulation-based early-exercise valuation. They make clear that product structure and model assumptions drive the choice. **Limit:** Publisher abstracts only; exact scheme stability, regression design, convergence, model calibration and comparative error/cost must be checked in full studies and common-product benchmarks. No source here establishes universal superiority or market-wide prevalence. **Relationship:** Observed smile/skew motivates considering richer volatility dynamics; a selected model then requires an implementation method. PDE finite differences discretize a valuation equation; least-squares Monte Carlo estimates continuation and exercise decisions for path-dependent or multifactor cases. Compare with analytic/lattice approaches when assumptions and product allow, and validate calibration, numerical error and exercise policy before downstream hedge or risk use.
- **Claim:** For American-style and path-dependent claims, Longstaff-Schwartz simulation estimates continuation values by regression and uses those estimates to approximate exercise decisions, making it applicable to selected multifactor problems where conventional trees or finite-difference grids become impractical. A weighted-least-squares extension addresses heteroscedastic continuation-regression errors and reports lower bias in its tested settings. **Locator:** Longstaff and Schwartz (2001), Review of Financial Studies 14(1), publisher abstract; Fabozzi, Paletta and Tunaru (2017), EJOR 263(2), Kent accepted-manuscript record and abstract. **Sources:** D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-FABOZZI-PALETTA-TUNARU-WLSMC-2017 **Area context:** This links optimal-stopping regression and its weighted-regression refinement to the American/Bermudan pricing branch. It is a numerical method choice after defining dynamics, payoff, exercise schedule and path state; it complements rather than replaces the contract/model specification. **Limit:** Longstaff-Schwartz and WLSMC sources support specific formulations and tested cases, not universal accuracy or a universal advantage of WLS over OLS. Basis choice, heteroscedasticity, path count, exercise-date discretization and out-of-sample exercise-policy validation remain material. **Relationship:** Risk-neutral path simulation produces state/payoff observations; regression estimates continuation value and compares it with immediate exercise; that policy yields an approximate price and exercise boundary. Weighted regression modifies continuation estimation when its assumptions fit. Compare against trees/PDE on tractable cases and use independent benchmarks/error analysis before downstream Greeks or hedge decisions.
- **Claim:** QMC path constructions are a numerical-integration design around a chosen stochastic model, not an alternative pricing model. Earlier option experiments found Sobol/Faure QMC and principal-component path construction often reduced error relative to tested ordinary-MC/bridge variants, while a peer-reviewed counterexample found Brownian-bridge construction worse than standard discretization for a digital option. A later study reports that aligning payoff discontinuities with coordinates can improve QMC pricing and Greek estimation in selected cases. **Locator:** Acworth, Broadie and Glasserman (1998), Columbia/Springer chapter abstract; Papageorgiou (2002), Journal of Complexity publisher abstract; Wang and Tan (2013), Management Science full publisher abstract. **Sources:** D011-ACWORTH-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MCQMC-OPTIONS-1998, D011-PAPAGEORGIOU-QMC-BROWNIAN-BRIDGE-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2002, D011-WANG-TAN-QMC-DISCONTINUITY-ALIGNMENT-2013 **Area context:** Shows a practical alternatives branch after Monte Carlo foundations: pseudo-random MC, antithetic variance reduction, low-discrepancy QMC, and path construction choices such as Brownian bridge or PCA. A payoff-aware path-generation method can be complementary to QMC; it is not a universal dependency or always-better tool. **Limit:** The papers use different payoffs, dimensions and constructions; two cited results are abstract-level. Neither the early positive comparison nor a digital-option counterexample establishes an invariant ranking. Randomized-QMC error estimates, convergence, effective dimension and payoff discontinuity require task-specific benchmarking. **Relationship:** Model and payoff define the stochastic integral; sampling/path construction approximates it; variance reduction changes estimator dispersion, while randomized replication/error analysis supports uncertainty estimates. Prices and Greeks can have different numerical behavior, so validate them separately.
- **Claim:** Established Monte Carlo Greek estimators include pathwise differentiation and likelihood-ratio score weighting; they derive sensitivities from simulated paths without a separate bump for every parameter, but apply under different payoff/model regularity conditions. Malliavin integration-by-parts supplies another weighted-expectation representation for selected multidimensional diffusion and discontinuous path-dependent payoffs. These are distinct estimators, not labels for the same formula. **Locator:** Broadie and Glasserman (1996), Management Science publisher abstract and author manuscript; Fournié et al. (1999), Finance and Stochastics indexed abstract. **Sources:** D011-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MC-GREEKS-1996, D011-FOURNIE-MALLIAVIN-MC-GREEKS-1999 **Area context:** This supplies the foundation for a Greek-estimation branch after Monte Carlo expectation pricing. The derivative target (price with respect to spot, volatility, rates or model inputs) and payoff smoothness determine whether pathwise, density-score or Malliavin weights apply. **Limit:** Fournié is abstract-only; pathwise differentiation needs interchange/regularity conditions, and likelihood-ratio/Malliavin estimators can have high variance or density/weight constraints. Neither is a universal replacement for finite differences or analytic derivatives. **Relationship:** A pricing model and simulated payoff define an expectation; the pathwise estimator differentiates the payoff/path, whereas likelihood-ratio or Malliavin methods shift the derivative to a probability-density weight. Finite differences instead bump an input and reprice. All yield Greek estimates with distinct bias/variance/compute tradeoffs that must be tested against analytic or trusted benchmark cases.
- **Claim:** Numerical pricing techniques combine a product/model with a numerical representation and produce outputs whose accuracy conditions differ. Fourier-cosine pricing can combine a characteristic function with barrier monitoring and a truncation interval; a GARCH-plus-double-exponential-jump study compares that method with Monte Carlo only for its discrete barrier cases. For American exercise, least-squares Monte Carlo estimates continuation values/regression-based exercise policies over simulated paths; basis and path count affect convergence, and a study of weighted LSMC shows improved regression accuracy away from the exercise boundary need not improve exercise decisions or option prices. Conditional randomized QMC can improve theoretical error rates for selected discontinuous option/Greek integrands under stated conditions. Pricing a claim accurately does not guarantee its Delta/Gamma is accurate: full-text experiments show Carr–Madan, COS and Lewis can yield poor sensitivities for selected digital-payoff/model parameters, with finite-difference estimates as a proposed alternative in those cases. **Locator:** Huang and Guo (2020), full text §§2–4; Yu and Liu (2014), full text and convergence/empirical sections; Finance Research Letters (2024) publisher abstract/highlights; He (2019) SIAM abstract; Behrens, Junike and Schoutens (2025), full text and Tables 1–2; COS truncation paper (2022) publisher abstract. **Sources:** D011-WILEY-COS-BARRIER-GARCH-JUMP-2020, D011-WILEY-CANONICAL-LSMC-AMERICAN-2014, D011-FRL-WLSMC-CRITICAL-ANALYSIS-2024, D011-SIAM-CONDITIONAL-RQMC-DISCONTINUOUS-2019, D011-BEHRENS-JUNIKE-SCHOUTENS-FOURIER-GREEKS-2025, D011-ELSEVIER-COS-TRUNCATION-ERROR-2022 **Area context:** This is numerical technique selection for options: payoff/exercise/monitoring and stochastic model determine whether closed-form, tree/PDE, transform or simulation methods apply; a separate estimator or numerical treatment may be needed for sensitivities and errors. Reproducible error/convergence checks and output-specific validation are part of using the algorithm. **Limit:** These results concern selected models/payoffs and methods. The 2024 WLSMC and 2022 COS-range publisher pages were accessible only at abstract/highlights level; the 2014 CLM benchmark is not a matched-input universal comparison. Conditional-QMC rates require theorem assumptions. The 2025 Fourier-Greek counterexample does not show that Fourier methods generally fail or that finite differences are always superior. No source in this packet ranks these methods across products, hardware or data regimes. **Relationship:** Payoff/exercise/monitoring + stochastic model -> analytic/tree/PDE/transform/simulation price procedure; simulation paths -> regression continuation estimate -> American exercise policy; a characteristic function + controlled Fourier truncation -> COS price; optional conditional smoothing + randomized QMC -> selected integration estimates; price representation -> Greek estimator, whose regularity/stability must be checked separately. Complementary estimators should be linked only where the numerical result or sensitivity output is actually consumed downstream.
- **Claim:** For American exercise, published comparisons cover binomial/trinomial lattices, explicit/implicit/Crank–Nicolson finite differences, approximations and simulation methods; one open study compares canonical LSM against a binomial tree and finite differences on OEX/IBM puts, varying regression basis/path counts and reporting standard errors and moneyness-specific error. A separate LSM+RQMC experiment evaluates exercise policies on independent paths and reports variance/bias changes for its tested examples. For European/Asian contracts, another publisher-indexed study compares RQMC accuracy against analytic solutions while measuring computing-time trade-offs. These are bounded examples, not a common benchmark: American price evaluation and exercise-policy quality must be assessed separately, and RQMC changes path sampling rather than the pricing model or stopping-rule design. **Locator:** Zhao, American Option Valuation Methods (2018), journal abstract/full-text link; Yu and Liu, Canonical Least-Squares Monte Carlo Valuation of American Options (2014), full text sections 3–5; Dion and L'Ecuyer, American Option Pricing with RQMC Simulations (2010), full text; L'Ecuyer and Lemieux, Randomized quasi-Monte Carlo Methods in Pricing Securities, publisher record (abstract only); QuantLib American-option regression tests; all checked 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-CCSE-AMERICAN-OPTION-VALUATION-COMPARISON-2018, D011-WILEY-CANONICAL-LSMC-AMERICAN-2014, D011-WSC-AMERICAN-RQMC-LSM-2010, D011-ELSEVIER-RQMC-SECURITIES-COMPARISON-2004, D011-QUANTLIB-AMERICAN-ENGINE-TESTS-2026, D011-FRL-WLSMC-CRITICAL-ANALYSIS-2024, D011-SIAM-CONDITIONAL-RQMC-DISCONTINUOUS-2019, D011-ACWORTH-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MCQMC-OPTIONS-1998 **Area context:** These comparison sources help a learner understand when numerical routes are being compared on identical contract/model inputs and when the comparison actually changes data, probability measure, sampling, basis, or exercise policy. They show why an American-option learner should inspect boundary/exercise behavior and out-of-sample policy value, and why QMC should be evaluated by payoff and effective dimension rather than as a universal faster Monte Carlo. **Limit:** Study rankings are not transferable across product classes, underlying models, dimensions, calibration inputs, implementation and hardware. The CLM market study has data/moneyness-specific outcomes; the RQMC conference paper uses selected models and does not compare every variance-reduction method; the 2004 QMC article was only accessible as an abstract. QuantLib tests do not establish external accuracy. **Relationship:** Contract payoff/exercise and stochastic model -> choose tree/finite-difference/dynamic-programming/LSM representation -> choose ordinary or randomized low-discrepancy path sampling within a simulation design -> estimate price and exercise policy -> independent out-of-sample policy evaluation, bias/variance/error and runtime checks. QMC is a complement to a selected simulation estimator; tree/PDE/LSM are alternatives for the stopping problem under stated state/model conditions.
- **Claim:** Calibration diagnostics answer distinct questions and should be read in layers: quote repricing/residuals test fit to selected instruments; scaling errors by bid-ask and inspecting parameter stability/Jacobian conditioning probe practical fit and identifiability; analytic identities and independent tree/PDE/Monte Carlo or implementation comparisons test internal/numerical consistency; Greek reconciliation, dynamic/hedge tests, benchmarking and suitable out-of-sample outcomes test downstream behavior. Calibration uncertainty can also be propagated through parameter sensitivities into a distribution of derivative values. A good calibration fit alone does not establish correct dynamics, unique parameters or reliable exotic valuation. **Locator:** Feng et al., Journal of Economic Surveys (first published 2026-09-09), sections 6.10–6.11; OSFI CAR 2026 Chapter 9 paragraphs 106 and 283; Cummins et al. (2022), sections 2–5; Federal Reserve interagency CCR guidance sections V.3 and Appendix B; BIS Working Paper record on modelling versus calibration errors. **Sources:** D011-WILEY-INTEREST-RATE-MODELS-CURVE-TO-SWAPTION-CUBE-2026, D011-OSFI-CAR-2026-MARKET-RISK-MODEL-VALIDATION, D011-CUMMINS-DISTRIBUTIONAL-CALIBRATION-PARAMETER-RISK-2022, D011-FED-INTERAGENCY-CCR-GUIDANCE-2011, D011-BIS-CREDIT-MODEL-CALIBRATION-ERRORS, D011-FED-SR26-2-2026 **Area context:** This is a validation branch after learning a product/model's calibration inputs and objective. It directs learners from fitted parameters to diagnostic evidence, then to independent pricing, risk and outcomes checks. It supports model developers and validators when the task requires calibration or model review; the checks are not universal prerequisites for every pricing method or learner. **Limit:** Diagnostic layers are synthesized from a review, applied studies and jurisdiction-specific guidance; they are not one harmonized standard or fixed pass/fail threshold. The gas-storage parameter-risk method and prudential requirements are context-specific. Quote fit and market calibration are not equivalent to independent validation, hedge performance or future-regime robustness. **Relationship:** Instrument/payoff and market data -> specify model and calibration objective -> fit parameters to selected liquid instruments -> inspect quote residuals, parameter stability and identifiability -> check identities and independent numerical implementation -> reconcile sensitivities and assess dynamic/out-of-sample performance where the target permits -> benchmark or quantify parameter/model risk. Calibration is an input-estimation step; validation methods assess separate failure modes and downstream valuation consequences.
- **Claim:** Greek estimators form conditional alternatives and complements. Bump-and-revalue finite differences are broadly usable but repeat valuation and depend on bump size; pathwise differentiation is efficient for sufficiently regular payoffs; likelihood-ratio/Malliavin methods differentiate the density and can handle payoff discontinuities under suitable conditions; vibrato combines pathwise propagation with conditional likelihood-ratio evaluation; AAD propagates many derivatives through a differentiable pricing program and can be layered onto regression Monte Carlo; Fourier differentiation is available for transform methods but can fail for some model/parameter/payoff settings even when prices look accurate. Therefore a price benchmark does not validate Delta/Gamma, and estimator choice depends on payoff regularity, model transition, Greek order, dimension, regression/exercise structure and implementation cost. **Locator:** Broadie and Glasserman, Management Science 42(2), 1996 (publisher abstract/full author manuscript); Giles, Vibrato Monte Carlo Sensitivities, MCQMC 2008/Springer 2009 (full text); Capriotti, Jiang and Macrina, Algorithmic Finance 6 (2017), sections 3–5 (full text); Lyuu et al., Quantitative Finance 19(7), 2019 (publisher abstract); Behrens, Junike and Schoutens, Frontiers of Mathematical Finance 4 (2025), full text/table examples; Chan and Joshi, Mathematical Finance 23(3), 2013 (publisher abstract). **Sources:** D011-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MC-GREEKS-1996, D011-GILES-VIBRATO-MC-GREEKS-2009, D011-CAPRIOTTI-JIANG-MACRINA-AAD-LSMC-XVA-GREEKS-2017, D011-LYUU-TENG-TSENG-WANG-GREEKS-DISCONTINUOUS-2019, D011-BEHRENS-JUNIKE-SCHOUTENS-FOURIER-GREEKS-2025, D011-CHAN-JOSHI-DISCONTINUOUS-GREEKS-2013, D011-CAPRIOTTI-GILES-AAD-REVIEW-2024, D011-FOURNIE-MALLIAVIN-MC-GREEKS-1999 **Area context:** After selecting a model, contract and price engine, learners may need sensitivities for hedging, risk or calibration. The estimator branch explains when to differentiate simulated paths, likelihood weights, conditional expectations, program execution or Fourier representations. Each branch must be checked against the actual payoff/model and Greek output; it is not a compulsory sequence for every pricing learner. **Limit:** Evidence spans different products, models, payoff regularity, discretizations, Greek orders and implementations. AAD speed claims are author-reported for stated workloads; the Lyuu paper is abstract-only; the Fourier failure is a bounded empirical counterexample. No universal efficiency or accuracy ranking is supported. **Relationship:** Contract payoff and requested Greek -> inspect smoothness/discontinuity, stochastic transition and regression/exercise structure -> choose eligible estimator (bump, pathwise, likelihood-ratio/Malliavin, vibrato, AAD or Fourier derivative) -> test estimator bias/variance and convergence against analytic, independent numerical or controlled finite-difference references -> propagate sensitivities to hedge/risk/calibration use. AAD may complement pathwise/likelihood or LSM computation; Fourier is coupled to transform pricing; methods are alternatives only under the same target and assumptions.
- **Claim:** Reusable numerical benchmarks now cover distinct pricing branches with common contracts, parameter sets, reference outputs and accuracy/time measures: BENCHOP defines one-factor European/American/barrier/dividend, local-volatility, Heston, Merton-jump and two-asset spread cases; BENCHOP–SLV compares SDE Monte Carlo, Fourier and PDE methods for selected SABR, Heston/QLSV and Heston–Hull–White products; a lower-weight two-asset study compares binomial, variance-reduced Monte Carlo and finite-element PDE methods under changing correlation/volatility. Their findings explain conditional tradeoffs, not universal winners. Reference construction, optimization, confidence intervals, hardware, dimensionality and payoff coverage limit comparisons. **Locator:** BENCHOP version 2.0 specification and reference-value appendix (2015), problems 1–6; von Sydow et al., International Journal of Computer Mathematics (2018), sections 2–5 and Appendix 1; Niklasson and Tivedal, Chalmers master's thesis (2018), chapters 3–6 and appendices D–F. **Sources:** D011-BENCHOP-OPTION-PRICING-BENCHMARK-SUITE-2015, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018, D011-CHALMERS-MULTI-ASSET-OPTION-NUMERICAL-COMPARISON-2018 **Area context:** After identifying payoff/model family, benchmark problems make the next numerical choice concrete: select the method representation that can solve that contract under the model, then compare converged price/error and compute output. These are examples for tree/PDE/PIDE/Fourier/simulation branches; they do not establish which items a student must select or a mandatory sequence. **Limit:** The suites are finite stylized cases. BENCHOP–SLV reports code and runtime limitations and lacks confidence intervals for one Monte Carlo experiment; numerical references can carry error. The 2018 two-asset source is a master's thesis and assumes correlated constant-parameter GBM. Results should not be generalized to untested products, calibrated market inputs, second-order Greeks or production hardware. **Relationship:** Contract/payoff, exercise and market inputs -> model representation (Black–Scholes/local/stochastic volatility/jump/rates/multi-asset) -> compatible numerical route (analytic/tree/PDE or PIDE/Fourier/Monte Carlo) -> reference price and error/convergence estimate -> runtime/cost and statistical uncertainty -> compare only within matching assumptions, outputs and implementations. Model families and numerical routes are separate choices; a benchmark links them for one stated task.
- **Claim:** Pathwise/IPA and likelihood-ratio estimators differentiate different parts of the expectation (payoff/path versus density/measure) and have different regularity conditions. A peer-reviewed paper reports that pathwise generally has lower variance when both estimators apply but requires a Lipschitz-continuous payoff; its proposed importance-sampling formulation is intended to handle a broader payoff class and is illustrated on selected multi-asset and path-dependent options. **Locator:** Lyuu and Teng (2011), Finance and Stochastics 15(1), pp.141–181; NYCU Academic Hub abstract inspected 2026-10-28; publisher full text not reviewed. **Sources:** D011-LYUU-TENG-UNBIASED-EFFICIENT-GREEKS-2011, D011-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MC-GREEKS-1996 **Area context:** This comparison helps learners choose an estimator based on payoff regularity and available model-density/path derivatives. It complements finite-difference and Malliavin examples but does not rank all estimators or imply that importance sampling is needed for every option. **Limit:** One article's abstract-level statements; derivations and detailed experiments were not inspected. Claims are restricted to the authors' stated conditions and examples. **Relationship:** Payoff/model regularity and desired Greek -> determine whether pathwise differentiation can pass through payoff, whether score/density derivatives are available for LR, or whether a weighting/importance-sampling construction is justified -> measure bias and variance under the chosen setup. These are conditional method choices; they are not interchangeable prerequisites.
- **Claim:** Ordinary MC, randomized QMC, conditional-expectation smoothing and path dimension reduction are distinct, composable choices. One peer-reviewed comparison covers selected European/Asian pricing; another first smooths discontinuities through conditional expectations, then applies gradient-informed PCA before QMC for selected discontinuous price/hedge problems. **Locator:** Ökten and Eastman (2004), publisher abstract/indexed sections; Weng, Wang and He (2018), publisher abstract/indexed binary Asian/barrier sections; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-OKTEN-EASTMAN-RQMC-PRICING-SECURITIES-2004, D011-WENG-WANG-HE-CONDITIONAL-QMC-DISCONTINUOUS-2018, D011-ACWORTH-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MCQMC-OPTIONS-1998, D011-PAPAGEORGIOU-QMC-BROWNIAN-BRIDGE-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2002 **Area context:** Optional numerical branch after Monte Carlo integration and payoff/path modeling. For discontinuous contracts, test whether a tractable conditional expectation can smooth the payoff, then consider path transformation/dimension reduction; RQMC adds replicate-based error estimation. **Limit:** Separate studies use different products, models, methods and budgets. No pooled performance ranking or universal QMC advantage is inferred. **Relationship:** Contract/model/output -> choose pseudorandom MC or low-discrepancy sampling; if a discontinuity and tractable conditioning variable exist, smooth by conditional expectation -> select path transform/dimension reduction -> for RQMC estimate uncertainty with independent randomizations -> validate against a reference under the same contract, discretization and compute budget. None is universally required or beneficial.
- **Claim:** Early-exercise and hybrid pricing methods must be matched to the contract and state dimension. A full-text Heston study combines a tree for the CIR-type variance state with finite differences for a transformed asset state, and compares selected European/American and barrier cases with pure-tree, Longstaff–Schwartz Monte Carlo and reference values. A current spread-option example shows why European closed-form approximations do not automatically extend to American exercise, where FD grids or LSMC are used and produce distinct price/Greek estimates. **Locator:** Briani, Caramellino and Zanette, full manuscript Sections 2 and 4, pp.18–20; MathWorks R2026b example sections 'Overview of the Pricing Methods' and 'Pricing an American Spread Option', including reported prices/Delta/Gamma; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-BRIANI-CARAMELLINO-ZANETTE-HESTON-AMERICAN-HYBRID-TREE-FD-2013, D011-MATHWORKS-SPREAD-OPTION-METHOD-COMPARISON-R2026B, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018 **Area context:** These are optional specialist branches after model/payoff definition: early exercise introduces an optimal-stopping boundary; multi-state stochastic volatility/rates can motivate hybrid or grid methods, while simulation supports higher-dimensional state spaces. Energy spread examples connect joint price/correlation inputs to prices and two-asset Greeks. **Limit:** Distinct studies use different contracts, parameters and reference methods; MathWorks is vendor documentation and the Heston paper tests a narrow model family. Do not combine their timings/prices into a common ranking or imply one method is best across products. **Relationship:** Contract payoff/exercise + calibrated model state -> choose an analytic approximation only when its assumptions fit; otherwise tree/PDE/LSMC or a documented hybrid -> compare price and Greeks to a suitable reference and test grid/path convergence -> downstream valuation/hedge analysis. A hybrid combines numerical components; it does not make those components universally required.
- **Claim:** Early-exercise and hybrid pricing methods must be matched to the contract and state dimension. A full-text Heston study combines a tree for the CIR-type variance state with finite differences for a transformed asset state, and compares selected European/American and barrier cases with pure-tree, Longstaff–Schwartz Monte Carlo and reference values. A current spread-option example shows why European closed-form approximations do not automatically extend to American exercise, where FD grids or LSMC are used and produce distinct price/Greek estimates. **Locator:** Briani, Caramellino and Zanette, full manuscript Sections 2 and 4, pp.18–20; MathWorks R2026b example sections 'Overview of the Pricing Methods' and 'Pricing an American Spread Option', including reported prices/Delta/Gamma; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-BRIANI-CARAMELLINO-ZANETTE-HESTON-AMERICAN-HYBRID-TREE-FD-2013, D011-MATHWORKS-SPREAD-OPTION-METHOD-COMPARISON-R2026B, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018 **Area context:** These are optional specialist branches after model/payoff definition: early exercise introduces an optimal-stopping boundary; multi-state stochastic volatility/rates can motivate hybrid or grid methods, while simulation supports higher-dimensional state spaces. Energy spread examples connect joint price/correlation inputs to prices and two-asset Greeks. **Limit:** Distinct studies use different contracts, parameters and reference methods; MathWorks is vendor documentation and the Heston paper tests a narrow model family. Do not combine their timings/prices into a common ranking or imply one method is best across products. **Relationship:** Contract payoff/exercise + calibrated model state -> choose an analytic approximation only when its assumptions fit; otherwise tree/PDE/LSMC or a documented hybrid -> compare price and Greeks to a suitable reference and test grid/path convergence -> downstream valuation/hedge analysis. A hybrid combines numerical components; it does not make those components universally required.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Current**
- **Claim:** Deep BSDE methods use neural-network approximations to solve selected high-dimensional semilinear PDEs, while deep hedging learns a trading/hedging policy against a specified risk objective; these techniques solve different problems and should be compared with numerical PDE/Monte Carlo and conventional hedging baselines. **Locator:** Han, Jentzen and E (PNAS 2018) high-dimensional PDE method; Buehler et al. Deep Hedging (2019); 2026 review of ML methods for financial derivative pricing. **Sources:** D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026, D011-QUANTLIB-OPTION-ENGINE-COMPARISON **Area context:** Current research techniques for high-dimensional pricing or hedging; selection follows the exact target (PDE value versus hedge policy), model, market constraints and compute budget. **Limit:** Research formulations and reviewed papers do not establish universal production suitability or superior accuracy. The 2026 review is secondary; PNAS results concern a defined PDE class; Deep Hedging is a specified framework. **Relationship:** Instrument/payoff and stochastic dynamics feed the target equation or hedging objective; discretization/data and risk constraints shape training; pricing or policy outputs require out-of-sample, benchmark, transaction-cost and model-risk checks.
- **Claim:** Multilevel Monte Carlo estimates an SDE payoff expectation by coupling coarse and fine time-step paths and summing level corrections; its cost advantage depends on payoff regularity, weak/strong discretization error, correction variance and coupling. Giles's financial examples include GBM, Heston and a multi-asset basket; these establish an academic implementation path, not a production engine. **Locator:** Giles (2008), Operations Research publisher record; Oxford Mathematical Institute author software page and examples inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-GILES-MLMC-OPTION-PRICING-2008, D011-GILES-MLMC-REFERENCE-CODE-2026 **Area context:** MLMC is a variance/cost-reduction estimator layered on a discretized stochastic pricing model. It is a candidate when many path simulations are needed and level coupling is valid; it is not a payoff model, calibration method or automatic improvement for Greeks and discontinuous payoffs. **Limit:** The theoretical complexity result uses stated assumptions and does not generalize to every financial payoff/model. The code is research reference code without production support. Bias, confidence intervals, coupling and Greek-specific behavior must be checked on matched products. **Relationship:** A selected SDE and payoff create coupled coarse/fine simulations; differences between adjacent levels estimate corrections; aggregation yields an expected payoff estimate. This complements the underlying model and can be compared with single-level MC/QMC under common error and cost budgets.
- **Claim:** Adjoint/reverse-mode algorithmic differentiation propagates sensitivities backward through a pricing computation and can be efficient when a small number of outputs depends on many market/model inputs. It is an implementation of derivatives for a computation graph, not a distinct pricing model; pathwise AAD still inherits discontinuous-payoff limitations. For calibrated instruments, implicit differentiation can propagate through the calibration map without differentiating the root solver itself. A study also finds QMC plus finite differences can match AAD accuracy for a small Greek set in tested cases, illustrating a conditional implementation tradeoff. **Locator:** Giles and Glasserman Oxford author manuscript (2005/2006); Capriotti and Giles (2024) full review; Henrard OpenGamma technical note; Scoleri et al. (2021) Wiley abstract. **Sources:** D011-GILES-GLASSERMAN-SMOKING-ADJOINTS-2005, D011-CAPRIOTTI-GILES-AAD-REVIEW-2024, D011-OPENGAMMA-AAD-CALIBRATION-IFT, D011-SCOLERI-BIANCHETTI-KUCHERENKO-QMC-AAD-2021 **Area context:** Current sensitivity-computation techniques can support pricing, calibration and portfolio risk calculations. Choose by the number of outputs/inputs, price-engine architecture, calibration mapping, payoff regularity and implementation cost rather than treating AAD as an automatic next item for every pricing learner. **Limit:** AAD speed claims depend on computational graph and input/output dimensions. The OpenGamma note is specialist technical guidance; the QMC-FD/AAD comparison is abstract-level and study-specific. AAD does not make an inaccurate model or discontinuous derivative valid, and second-order sensitivities may have different costs/conditions. **Relationship:** Price engine and calibration produce a scalar valuation; forward or reverse differentiation propagates input sensitivities; calibrated sensitivities require chain-rule/implicit-function treatment; validated Greeks feed hedging and portfolio-risk tasks. For few sensitivities, bump-and-revalue or QMC-FD may be adequate; for many inputs and few outputs, adjoints may reduce repeated computation.
- **Claim:** For discontinuous trigger payoffs, research offers methods that repair or redesign Greek estimation rather than applying naive pathwise AAD: importance sampling near a payoff-boundary hypersurface, path discretizations with a one-dimensional proxy constraint, and hybrid pathwise/likelihood-ratio ideas. These methods target different boundary structures and model conditions; none is a generic universal fix. **Locator:** Tong and Liu (2016), INFORMS Journal on Computing abstract; Chan and Joshi (2013), Mathematical Finance publisher abstract; Giles' Oxford MCQMC conference paper on vibrato sensitivities. **Sources:** D011-TONG-LIU-IMPORTANCE-SAMPLING-GREEKS-2016, D011-CHAN-JOSHI-DISCONTINUOUS-GREEKS-2013, D011-GILES-VIBRATO-MC-GREEKS-2009 **Area context:** A specialist branch for digitals, barriers, autocallables or trigger payoffs after students recognize that a discontinuity can invalidate ordinary pathwise differentiation. Selection follows the payoff boundary, simulation scheme and available conditional distribution. **Limit:** Publisher abstracts and a method-specific LIBOR market model study; full assumptions and empirical comparisons are not uniform. Tail/boundary variance and discretization bias require independent benchmarking. **Relationship:** Discontinuous payoff identifies the failed regularity step; boundary-focused sampling or a tailored discretization estimates the missing boundary contribution; estimates should be compared with bump-and-revalue using common random numbers, analytic cases or trusted numerical references.
- **Claim:** Rolling Adjoints is a conditional pathwise sensitivity technique for Bermudan options implemented with regress-later SGBM: combine sensitivity of fitted continuation coefficients with adjoint propagation between monitoring dates to produce scenario-wise state and model-parameter Greeks. It complements SGBM pricing and supports sensitivity-dependent exposure/MVA use; generic bump-and-revalue LSM Greeks are a comparator, with instability near the exercise boundary reported in the paper's specific tests. **Locator:** Jain, Leitao and Oosterlee (2019), full author manuscript Sections 4–6 and numerical Tables 1–10; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-JAIN-LEITAO-OOSTERLEE-ROLLING-ADJOINTS-2019 **Area context:** Teach only after Monte Carlo paths, Bermudan exercise, SGBM/regress-later, and basic pathwise/adjoint differentiation; select when downstream work needs sensitivities at future scenario dates, not just current price/Greeks. **Limit:** Single SGBM-specific study and selected tests; speed/accuracy does not generalize to all hardware, path dimensions or products. Validate state and parameter Greeks separately, including exercise-boundary behavior. **Relationship:** Path simulation and exercise policy -> fitted continuation representation -> differentiated coefficients + adjoint propagation -> pathwise Delta/Vega/model sensitivities -> exposure and margin analytics. This is a technique hybrid, not a required dependency of all pricing methods.
- **Claim:** American-option Greek estimation can combine a generalized IPA sensitivity estimator, LSM exercise-policy estimation and randomized quasi-Monte Carlo sampling. Brownian bridge and PCA act as path-dimension reduction strategies within the sampler. In a peer-reviewed study, this composition was tested for single/multi-asset options under Black–Scholes and Variance Gamma, with authors reporting variance reduction versus MC. The estimator, stopping-policy method, sampling sequence and path transform occupy separate layers and each affects the result. **Locator:** Xiang and Wang (2022), Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics 413, 114268, DOI 10.1016/j.cam.2022.114268; publisher abstract and indexed sections inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-XIANG-WANG-RQMC-AMERICAN-OPTION-SENSITIVITIES-2022 **Area context:** This is an optional advanced route after Monte Carlo estimators, American/Bermudan optimal stopping and basic Greek definitions. It is relevant when estimating sensitivities under an exercise policy and when effective path dimension limits ordinary MC; compare with pathwise/LR/vibrato estimators and SGBM Rolling Adjoints only for matching product/model/output. **Limit:** Publisher-abstract scope only; no tables, error bars, speed data or independent replication were reviewed. Findings are restricted to the named model families and study design; QMC does not guarantee lower variance for every payoff or parameterization. **Relationship:** Risk-neutral paths + payoff and monitoring schedule -> LSM exercise policy + generalized IPA Greek estimator -> scrambled-Sobol RQMC path sampling -> optional Brownian-bridge/PCA transform -> price/sensitivity estimates with randomized-replicate uncertainty -> validate price, exercise policy and each Greek against suitable references. Change one layer at a time for fair comparison.
- **Claim:** A full-text exponential-Lévy study compares Malliavin Monte Carlo Greek weights with Richardson-extrapolated finite differences and a hybrid estimator. In the tested continuous Asian-payoff jump-diffusion case, finite differences perform better for first-order Greeks and a Malliavin first-order estimate followed by finite differences performs best for the reported second-order estimate. For a discontinuous digital Asian payoff, Malliavin Monte Carlo is substantially more stable than finite differences even when the latter uses many more paths. This directly shows that payoff regularity and Greek order affect estimator choice. **Locator:** Hudde and Rüschendorf (2023), Sections 3–5; full open-access Springer text inspected 2026-10-28, especially Section 4.1 (continuous Asian payoff), Section 4.2 (digital Asian payoff), and summary. **Sources:** D011-HUDDE-RUESCHENDORF-LEVY-EUROPEAN-ASIAN-GREEKS-2023, D011-FOURNIE-MALLIAVIN-MC-GREEKS-1999, D011-BROADIE-GLASSERMAN-MC-GREEKS-1996 **Area context:** Use as a worked comparison after learners understand pathwise/finite-difference sensitivities, Monte Carlo uncertainty and payoff smoothness. It explains why an estimator route may change between continuous versus discontinuous contracts and between first- and second-order Greeks; it does not supply a universal method ordering. **Limit:** Selected Asian products under a specified exponential-Lévy jump-diffusion and simulation setup; not a common matched benchmark spanning all model families, estimators, discretizations, hardware or implementation costs. The article does not prove a general preference across products. **Relationship:** Model and payoff regularity + requested Greek order -> choose a differentiable pathwise/FD or Malliavin-weight route as assumptions allow -> for selected second-order outputs, test a hybrid first-order estimate plus FD -> compare bias/stability/variance against a product-appropriate reference. For discontinuous payoffs, Malliavin weighting may avoid unstable payoff bumps; validate the weight's assumptions and variance.
- **Claim:** Adjoint algorithmic differentiation can be composed with regression-based Longstaff–Schwartz/Bermudan Monte Carlo to estimate price sensitivities for early-exercise and XVA problems. The regression-function contribution must be differentiated to avoid omitting terms in the Greek estimate. **Locator:** Capriotti, Jiang and Macrina, Algorithmic Finance 6(1–2) (2017), publisher full text and practical examples; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-AAD-LEAST-SQUARES-MONTE-CARLO-BERMUDAN-XVA-2017, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-SCOLERI-BIANCHETTI-KUCHERENKO-QMC-AAD-2021 **Area context:** A current specialist technique branch after simulation, early-exercise regression and sensitivity foundations; useful for Bermudan and XVA sensitivity workloads where regression-based pricing is already used. **Limit:** One article and selected practical examples; it does not establish universal speed or accuracy against every finite-difference, pathwise, likelihood-ratio or Malliavin estimator. **Relationship:** Simulated paths and exercise-date regression -> LSM/Bermudan value estimate -> differentiate both the simulated valuation and regression contribution with AAD -> price Greeks for XVA/hedging analysis -> validate against finite differences or suitable references on the same model and payoff.
- **Claim:** A regime-switching Heston–Hull–White European-option study combines stochastic volatility, stochastic rates and a switching regime, derives a semi-analytical model pricer, uses a learned local residual surrogate to assist parameter search, and recomputes final prices with the original formula. This is a complementary calibration design: learning accelerates/localizes the search while the financial model remains the final valuation authority. **Locator:** Li, Scientific Reports 16, article 29332 (2026), full open-access article, especially model, calibration workflow, SSE 50 ETF experiment and diagnostics; DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-67726-0; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-LI-REGIME-SWITCHING-HESTON-HULL-WHITE-DL-CALIBRATION-2026, D011-HAINAUT-CASAS-PINN-HESTON-2024, D011-ZHANG-AMICI-MORANDOTTI-DEEP-DIFFERENTIAL-HESTON-CALIBRATION-2024, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018 **Area context:** Current mixed-model pricing/calibration branch for European options when stochastic volatility, stochastic rates and regime switching are jointly in scope. It links model choice and numerical pricing to data calibration; it is not a universal requirement for a basic pricing pathway. **Limit:** One peer-reviewed paper with one named ETF-option data context and selected comparators. Its reported fit improvement does not establish generalization across markets, products, or regimes, nor does it establish production deployment or universal optimizer superiority. **Relationship:** Market quotes + joint Heston/Hull–White/regime model -> semi-analytical model pricer -> learned local residual surrogate guides parameter search -> recompute candidate prices in original model -> compare held-out fit and calibration diagnostics -> pass calibrated parameters and prices to model validation/valuation consumers. The surrogate assists calibration; it is not a replacement pricer. This differs from PINN pricing, which directly approximates a PDE solution, and from a deep differential network, which learns price/parameter sensitivities for calibration.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Neural SDE/PDE solvers, learned pricing surrogates and differentiable/deep hedging methods are active research directions that may reduce repeated computation or handle high-dimensional problems; they remain conditional alternatives to established numerical methods, not a single combined method or automatic next step. **Locator:** Peer-reviewed PNAS deep-BSDE paper; 2019 Deep Hedging paper; 2023 statistical ML review; 2026 derivatives-pricing review. **Sources:** D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019, D011-LUDKOVSKI-STAT-ML-QUANT-FINANCE-2023, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026 **Area context:** Emerging computational techniques for specific pricing/hedging workloads; the student should first learn the target and classical baseline, then inspect the ML method's data, compute and validation requirements. **Limit:** Publication and review coverage are not proof of industry uptake, speedup or improved financial decisions. Training distribution, arbitrage consistency, calibration error, transaction costs and regime transfer remain material. **Relationship:** Classical model specification and numerical baselines frame the comparison; neural approximation consumes simulated/market states and produces prices, sensitivities or hedge actions; benchmark, stability, arbitrage and out-of-distribution tests are downstream gates.
- **Claim:** A 2021 research paper proposes neural-network automatic control variates for selected high-dimensional option-pricing integrals, alongside an effective-dimension-reduction approach. This is an ML-assisted variance-reduction extension to Monte Carlo/quadrature, not a new risk-neutral pricing model and not a replacement for classical control-variate baselines. **Locator:** El Filali Ech-Chafiq, Lelong and Reghai (2021), Monte Carlo Methods and Applications 27(2), RePEc/IDEAS indexed abstract; publisher full text is subscription restricted. **Sources:** D011-ELFILALI-LELONG-REGHAI-NEURAL-CONTROL-VARIATES-2021 **Area context:** An emerging/advanced technique to inspect after students understand expectation estimation and classical variance reduction. Its role depends on the target integral, available training/simulation data and whether a learnable approximation can be integrated or evaluated reliably. **Limit:** Abstract-only evidence; no implementation details or independent reproduction were inspected. No general speed, accuracy, robustness or industry-use claim is supported. **Relationship:** Classical MC or numerical integration supplies the target expectation; a trained network approximates a correlated control function whose expectation is tractable; the correction can reduce estimator variance if assumptions hold. It must be compared with ordinary MC, analytic controls, QMC and classical dimension reduction under matched error and compute accounting.
- **Claim:** A September 2026 preprint proposes an explicit boundary-correction term added to standard pathwise/AAD Monte Carlo sensitivities for piecewise-smooth discontinuous payoffs, with author-reported GBM, Heston and Hull-White benchmarks. It is a very recent research direction, not an established production technique. **Locator:** Lakshtanov (2026), arXiv:2609.06137, full preprint opened 2026-10-24; abstract, derivation and named-model benchmark sections. **Sources:** D011-LAKSHTANOV-DISCONTINUOUS-GREEKS-PREPRINT-2026 **Area context:** Potential advanced extension for digital, barrier and autocallable sensitivities where differentiating the payoff misses boundary terms. It follows stochastic simulation, AAD/pathwise Greeks and discontinuity analysis; it should remain presented as unreviewed research pending independent replication. **Limit:** Unreviewed single-author preprint and author-reported benchmark comparisons; formula relies on regularity and transversality/root assumptions. The AADC software dependency and automated detection claims are author-specific and do not establish an independently verified selectable tool. **Relationship:** Classical pathwise/AAD supplies the smooth interior derivative; the proposed method adds density-weighted payoff-boundary corrections; combined estimator is compared to analytic or bump-and-revalue references. Independent reproduction, stability near singular boundaries and comparison with established LR/Malliavin/vibrato methods are still needed.
- **Claim:** Emerging computational techniques include neural-network regression Monte Carlo for discretely reflected BSDEs with Malliavin/Gamma terms, differentiable jump-parameter estimation via Gumbel-Softmax, and ANN-assisted calibration of a Wishart stochastic-volatility/jump commodity model. Their computational role differs: approximate a high-dimensional price/sensitivity system, learn jump parameters, or accelerate calibration; none is merely a new payoff or interchangeable pricing formula. Separate product-level validation is required for price error, calibration fit/stability, Greek error and hedge performance. **Locator:** SIAM 2026 deep-BSDE article abstract; Wiley 2026 Neural Jumps abstract; Results in Applied Mathematics 2025 commodity-calibration abstract; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-SIAM-DEEP-BSDE-BERMUDAN-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-WILEY-NEURAL-JUMPS-OPTION-PRICING-2026, D011-ELSEVIER-WISHART-NEURAL-COMMODITY-OPTION-CALIBRATION-2025 **Area context:** Teach after classical model/numerical foundations as optional research techniques. The method's state, contract, model and required output determine whether it is applicable; compare with an engine solving the same product/model and a stated error/cost budget. A neural calibration map may still depend on a separately defined characteristic-function or Monte Carlo pricing model. **Limit:** Access is publisher-abstract level for the newer papers; code, data and implementation requirements were not verified. Published numerical results are study-specific and not independent evidence of production readiness, robust performance or compute requirements. **Relationship:** Product-specific market quotes and model -> (classical solver or learned solver/calibrator) -> price/calibration/Greek estimate -> independent repricing, residual and sensitivity diagnostics -> risk/hedging consumer. A neural estimator can complement the model/solver but does not remove payoff, measure, calibration or validation assumptions.
- **Claim:** For American-option pricing, constrained-GP regression, Kriging-based continuation-value regression and control variates play different computational roles. PDE-constrained CGPR approximates a value function subject to a penalized Feynman-Kac equation and terminal/payoff constraints; Monte Carlo Kriging learns continuation values from simulated states; a European-option control variate reduces variance when estimating the American value. These techniques can be paired only where their estimator design supports it; they are not interchangeable labels for one ML model. **Locator:** Hainaut (2024 full author manuscript; 2026 journal abstract); Mu et al. (2018) publisher abstract; Fu et al. (2001) publisher abstract; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HINAUT-CGPR-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2026, D011-HINAUT-UCL-CGPR-AMERICAN-MANUSCRIPT-2024, D011-MU-GODINA-KRIGING-CV-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2018, D011-FU-LAPRISE-MADAN-AMERICAN-MC-COMPARISON-2001 **Area context:** These are advanced optional techniques after American-option payoffs, stochastic dynamics and numerical/simulation foundations. Selection follows whether the learner needs a value-surface PDE solver, a continuation-value estimator under simulation, or variance reduction for a Monte Carlo estimate. **Limit:** Research examples are limited to stated American put models and study designs; there is no shared benchmark for accuracy, cost, Greek error or higher-dimensional scaling. No universal production fit or ranking is inferred. **Relationship:** Model/payoff/exercise definition -> solver or estimator choice -> price/value surface and, where explicitly measured, exercise/continuation estimates -> price and policy validation. A GP surrogate alone does not establish sensitivities or hedge quality; add and separately validate those outputs if the downstream task requires them.
- **Claim:** An emerging Malliavin/weak-derivative approach estimates sensitivities of diffusion losses conditional on rare or measure-zero path events. It first represents the conditional functional through Malliavin derivatives and a Skorohod-integral identity, then computes parameter gradients using a weak-derivative estimator. The authors' financial examples include barrier/digital-event Greeks, stressed xVA exposure and tail-risk conditioning. This is a specialized conditional-risk route rather than a general replacement for ordinary pathwise, likelihood-ratio, finite-difference, AAD or vibrato estimators. **Locator:** Krishnamurthy and Snow, arXiv:2602.02811v1, submitted 2026-02-02, full PDF inspected 2026-10-28: abstract; Sections 1–4; especially financial applications and estimator construction. Related earlier record: arXiv:2510.00297v1, abstract and full-text record inspected; not treated as independent replication. **Sources:** D011-KRISHNAMURTHY-SNOW-CONDITIONAL-GREEKS-2026, D011-KRISHNAMURTHY-SNOW-COUNTERFACTUAL-STOCHASTIC-OPT-2025 **Area context:** This is an optional research branch after diffusion/SDE modeling, Monte Carlo estimation, conditional expectation and basic Greek/sensitivity concepts. Consider it only when the requested output is conditional on a rare or singular event, such as barrier-hit behavior or a stressed exposure scenario; ordinary unconditional price Greeks do not require it. Learners must be prepared to reason about Malliavin derivatives, Skorohod integrals, regularity assumptions and estimator diagnostics. **Limit:** One unreviewed author preprint, with no independent replication or maintained implementation located in this pass. Its convergence/variance statements apply to the paper's assumptions and construction; no matched empirical benchmark against standard Greek estimators or production suitability is established. Related same-author preprints are not independent evidence. **Relationship:** Diffusion model + loss/payoff + explicit conditioning event -> conditional expectation representation using Malliavin/Skorohod machinery -> weak-derivative parameter gradient -> conditional sensitivity for the named stress/event -> validate assumptions, discretization bias, variance and event interpretation against a problem-specific reference. This complements rather than supersedes standard unconditional Greek estimators; the event-conditioned output is not interchangeable with an unconditional Greek.
- **Claim:** A 2024 conference abstract proposes Hybrid Least Squares Monte Carlo (HLSM) for American-option continuation-value estimation by combining standard LSM and Positive LSM exercise values; the abstract reports PLSM alone can lower overall prices and fail to provide efficient adaptive exercise timing. This is a candidate variant to assess, not an established improvement. **Locator:** Zhang and Zhang (2024), ACM conference paper record/abstract at HKU Scholars Hub, especially abstract; full text may require subscription, inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-HKU-HYBRID-LEAST-SQUARES-MONTE-CARLO-AMERICAN-OPTIONS-2024, D011-OUP-LONGSTAFF-SCHWARTZ-LSM-2001, D011-FABOZZI-PALETTA-TUNARU-WLSMC-2017 **Area context:** Optional early-exercise estimator research after canonical Longstaff–Schwartz regression and exercise-policy validation; the source record identifies a proposed variation but does not establish its scope across products. **Limit:** Abstract only: exact contracts, model settings, uncertainty, numerical comparisons, code and independent replication are unavailable from the inspected record. Do not claim HLSM outperforms LSM or make it a required/selectable tool based on this source alone. **Relationship:** American payoff and simulated paths -> estimate continuation/exercise values with LSM; HLSM changes the regression target by combining LSM/PLSM values -> compare price and exercise-policy behavior against canonical LSM and suitable references before any performance or adoption claim.
- **Claim:** A physics-informed neural network can encode the Heston/Feynman–Kac pricing PDE and approximate selected European option values across specified parameters as a learned alternative to direct numerical pricing. **Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Future**
- **Claim:** Quantum amplitude-estimation and quantum signal-processing approaches have been proposed for selected stochastic-volatility option-pricing problems, but their resource estimates and representation-error sensitivity keep them in a research-monitoring category rather than an established pricing technique. **Locator:** Wang and Kan, Quantum 8, 1504 (2024), for Heston Asian/barrier pricing and logical resource estimates; ESMA 2026 quantum-finance maturity report and IEEE NQComp 2026 abstract as maturity/error counter-sources. **Sources:** D011-QUANTUM-HESTON-OPTION-PRICING-2024, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026, D011-IEEE-QUANTUM-OPTION-REPRESENTATION-ERROR-2026 **Area context:** The proposed technique follows stochastic-process modeling, numerical SDE discretization, payoff representation, amplitude estimation and quantum resource/error analysis. Its current educational value is as an advanced research branch after classical pricing baselines. **Limit:** The Quantum paper is theoretical/resource-estimation work, ESMA describes immature market readiness, and IEEE full text was inaccessible (abstract only). No hardware advantage, production use or broad product coverage is established. **Relationship:** Classical pricing and Monte Carlo baselines define the target and comparison; discretization and payoff/state encoding precede quantum estimation; circuit resources and representation/discretization error constrain price accuracy. Quantum speedup claims must include the complete end-to-end encoding and fault-tolerant cost.

The software implements choices from the method layer rather than replacing method selection or validation.
