**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Current**
- **Claim:** QuantLib and OpenGamma Strata provide inspectable pricing implementations, but a production workflow still has to select the product/model/engine and calibrate to market quotes with defined conventions; software support is evidence of capability, not evidence that the model or data are suitable. **Locator:** QuantLib official documentation and equity-option engine example; OpenGamma Strata product/pricing-model coverage and RatesCurveCalibrator API, which describes curve-node reference trades, market-quote fitting by root finding and calibration-measure options. **Sources:** D011-QUANTLIB-DOCS, D011-QUANTLIB-OPTION-ENGINE-COMPARISON, D011-OPENGAMMA-STRATA-OVERVIEW-2026, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-PRODUCT-COVERAGE, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-RATES-CURVE-CALIBRATOR, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-CURVE-CALIBRATION **Area context:** These maintained libraries support model implementation, curve construction/calibration, instrument pricing and risk sensitivities across defined product coverage; their role is computational infrastructure inside the pricing workflow. **Limit:** First-party documentation describes project features and APIs, not independent model validation, market share, data quality, or suitability of conventions. Confirm release/version, licensing and product coverage for the target workflow. **Relationship:** Market quotes and instrument conventions feed curve calibration; calibrated curves/volatility and model parameters feed pricing engines; model outputs and sensitivities go to valuation, hedging and risk. Numerical and market-data validation remain separate controls.
- **Claim:** Current R2026b commercial documentation describes instrument pricing across fixed income and derivatives, curve bootstrapping, and multiple pricer families including closed-form, lattice, finite-difference, FFT and Monte Carlo methods, with price, implied-volatility and Greek outputs. **Locator:** MathWorks official R2026b ?Price Instruments Using Functions? documentation, opened 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-MATHWORKS-FINANCIAL-INSTRUMENTS-R2026B **Area context:** Provides a separate current software example of model/pricer selection and implementation across instrument families, complementing the open-source QuantLib and OpenGamma Strata records. **Limit:** Vendor-stated capabilities only; the documentation is not an independent performance comparison, and product coverage, licensing and model conventions must be checked for the intended workflow. **Relationship:** Instrument definition and market data feed curves/models, which are passed to a selected pricer; returned values and Greeks support analysis. The existence of several pricers makes method alternatives visible but does not select the right method automatically.
- **Claim:** Official QuantLib and OpenGamma Strata documentation describes two distinct open-source implementation ecosystems for quantitative pricing. QuantLib states its C++ framework has C#, Java, Python and R interfaces; Strata documents product models, market-data and curve/surface representations, pricing/risk measures, calculation and reporting components. Its rates calibrator prices and reprices node reference trades against selected market measures, producing calibrated curves from market and reference data. **Locator:** QuantLib official project page opened 2026-10-24; OpenGamma Strata reference documentation and RatesCurveCalibrator API opened 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-QUANTLIB-OFFICIAL-PROJECT-2026, D011-OPENGAMMA-STRATA-OVERVIEW-2026, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-RATES-CURVE-CALIBRATOR, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-PRODUCT-COVERAGE, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-CURVE-CALIBRATION **Area context:** These tools implement chosen product models and numerical methods. Market quotes, reference data, conventions and calibration definitions feed curve/surface construction; calibrated objects and product definitions then feed selected pricers and sensitivity calculations. Library choice does not replace understanding instrument payoffs, model assumptions or numerical methods. **Limit:** Maintainer documentation establishes stated implementation capability, not independent numerical validation or comparative performance. Check product coverage, version, bindings, licensing, calibration conventions and local market-data availability for the intended instrument and workflow. **Relationship:** Learners can compare software libraries after understanding the pricing task and method families. Calibration inputs precede calibrated curve outputs; those outputs become inputs to pricing and sensitivity calculations. A successful calibration is not itself evidence of correct model assumptions or independent valuation.
- **Claim:** Current pricing implementation options occupy different layers. QuantLib and OpenGamma Strata are open-source libraries embedded in a system a team builds; Strata supplies analytics, pricing, curve calibration, trade/market-data models and reporting but no database/server. ORE is an open-source workflow/application built on QuantLib with user guide, product catalogue, pricing-engine configuration, market-data/curve/convention inputs and methods for exposure simulation/XVA; its v17 roadmap documents current feature and curve-input changes. Commercial enterprise platforms bundle or connect pricing models with data, portfolio workflows and risk outputs: Bloomberg MARS couples its pricing library/market data with valuations, Greeks, XVA and collateral/API modules; Numerix Oneview connects trade/data capture, curve/surface construction, calibration, valuation, Greeks, model validation and Python/API integration; Murex MX.3 describes cross-asset trading/risk, curve calibration, GPU term-structure/volatility models, third-party data/models and model validation. These tools implement workflows and numerical methods; none is itself an alternative mathematical pricing method. **Locator:** OpenGamma Strata Overview (official documentation, opened 2026-10-28); ORE Documentation and Roadmap v17 (official project pages, opened 2026-10-28); Bloomberg MARS official product page; Numerix Oneview for Valuation official product page; Murex MX.3 Sales and Trading official product page (all opened 2026-10-28). **Sources:** D011-OPENGAMMA-STRATA-OVERVIEW-2026, D011-STRATA-MARKET-DATA-FACTORY-API-2026, D011-ORE-RISK-ANALYTICS-DOCS-2026, D011-ORE-MARKET-DATA-INPUTS-FAQ-2026, D011-ORE-ROADMAP-V17-2026, D011-BLOOMBERG-MARS-VALUATION-RISK-API-2026, D011-NUMERIX-ONEVIEW-VALUATION-2026, D011-MUREX-MX3-TRADING-PRICING-RISK-2026, D011-QUANTLIB-OFFICIAL-PROJECT-2026, D011-QUANTLIB-HULL-WHITE-CURRENT-SOURCE, D011-QUANTLIB-SWAPTION-ENGINE-SUPPORT **Area context:** These systems support different implementation contexts: a quant developer may embed a library, an analytics team may run a configurable open-source engine, and a trading/valuation/risk organization may integrate a licensed cross-asset platform. The documented dependency chain starts with provider/exchange observations and instrument conventions; quote inputs are transformed into par rates, curve groups, discount/index/FX rates or volatility surfaces, then model calibration and engine selection produce trade values/Greeks and downstream portfolio risk, XVA, validation and reporting. Data acquisition, entitlements, persistence and loader mapping are distinct integration steps; engine/version support and market conventions remain part of suitability. **Limit:** Commercial product features are vendor-declared and may depend on license, module and client configuration; no independent accuracy, cost, employer prevalence or superiority comparison is claimed. Open-source project docs are authoritative for their own declared versions and APIs but do not show that a given model is suitable or independently validated. This is a representative implementation map, not an exhaustive vendor directory. **Relationship:** Market and trade/reference data + conventions -> curves/surfaces and calibrated models -> chosen supported pricing engine/library -> values/Greeks/exposures -> portfolio risk, XVA, validation and reporting modules. An open-source library can be embedded in a custom application; ORE bundles a documented workflow; enterprise systems integrate pricing/data/risk but remain license/configuration dependent. These are software architecture choices; analytic/tree/PDE/Fourier/Monte Carlo remain methods executed within or alongside them.
- **Claim:** Quantra adds a distinct classical deployment option beside embedded pricing libraries: it runs isolated QuantLib workers behind Envoy and exposes the same product calculations through HTTP/JSON and gRPC/FlatBuffers. Its documented inputs include explicit trade conventions, curves, quotes and calibration requests; outputs include NPV, fair rates/spreads, cash flows, Greeks and other product-specific risk fields. It documents a functional request catalog checked against QuantLib, C++/Python clients, version-diff tooling and a BSD-3-Clause license. **Locator:** Quantra project website product/API pages and joseprupi/quantraserver README, tests, version instructions and license, inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-QUANTRA-OPEN-PRICING-SERVICE-2026, D011-QUANTRA-OPEN-PRICING-SERVICE-WEB-2026 **Area context:** This is useful when studying how a pricing library is deployed as a service across clients and concurrent valuation requests. It can complement QuantLib/Strata or ORE workflows; it does not replace the underlying model, payoff definition, market-data sourcing or product-specific model validation. **Limit:** The repository's parity suite compares against the same QuantLib implementation, so it can catch wrapper/serialization discrepancies but does not independently establish model correctness or market calibration quality. Performance figures are project-authored and workload/hardware specific; product and convention coverage must be checked against the actual trade. **Relationship:** Trade + explicit conventions + market quotes -> curves/surface/calibration -> QuantLib instrument and engine -> service request/response with prices, cash flows and risk -> caller's validation/risk workflow. The service architecture is complementary to pricing methods, while particular QuantLib engines remain product-specific implementation choices.
- **Claim:** The R2026b Financial Instruments Toolbox includes a runnable two-asset spread-option example with European closed-form approximations and American finite-difference/LSMC implementations, exposing price and Greeks alongside curve, volatility, correlation and grid/path inputs. **Locator:** MathWorks R2026b full example/code inspected 2026-10-28; sections 13–18, 29–32 and 142–232. **Sources:** D011-MATHWORKS-SPREAD-OPTION-METHOD-COMPARISON-R2026B, D011-BRIANI-CARAMELLINO-ZANETTE-HESTON-AMERICAN-HYBRID-TREE-FD-2013, D011-QUANTLIB-AMERICAN-ENGINE-TESTS-2026 **Area context:** Use as an implementation demonstration after two-asset payoffs, exercise policy, market inputs and numerical methods; it shows sensitivity outputs and practical convergence controls. **Limit:** Commercial vendor example with illustrative parameters; the FD/LSMC result difference is not independently adjudicated and is not a ranking. **Relationship:** Two underlying prices/volatilities/correlation + rate curve -> European approximation or American FD/LSMC -> price, Delta and Gamma -> check grid/path stability and compare with an independent reference before hedge use.
- **Claim:** The R2026b Financial Instruments Toolbox includes a runnable two-asset spread-option example with European closed-form approximations and American finite-difference/LSMC implementations, exposing price and Greeks alongside curve, volatility, correlation and grid/path inputs. **Locator:** MathWorks R2026b full example/code inspected 2026-10-28; sections 13–18, 29–32 and 142–232. **Sources:** D011-MATHWORKS-SPREAD-OPTION-METHOD-COMPARISON-R2026B, D011-BRIANI-CARAMELLINO-ZANETTE-HESTON-AMERICAN-HYBRID-TREE-FD-2013, D011-QUANTLIB-AMERICAN-ENGINE-TESTS-2026 **Area context:** Use as an implementation demonstration after two-asset payoffs, exercise policy, market inputs and numerical methods; it shows sensitivity outputs and practical convergence controls. **Limit:** Commercial vendor example with illustrative parameters; the FD/LSMC result difference is not independently adjudicated and is not a ranking. **Relationship:** Two underlying prices/volatilities/correlation + rate curve -> European approximation or American FD/LSMC -> price, Delta and Gamma -> check grid/path stability and compare with an independent reference before hedge use.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Emerging**
- **Claim:** The indexed implementation landscape contains maintained classical pricing libraries (QuantLib and Strata) with model/engine and curve-calibration components, alongside research papers on neural PDE/pricing and deep hedging; the latter papers do not themselves establish a maintained, student-ready software tool. **Locator:** QuantLib official docs and option-engine example; OpenGamma Strata product coverage/calibration docs; PNAS deep-BSDE and Deep Hedging research records. **Sources:** D011-QUANTLIB-DOCS, D011-QUANTLIB-OPTION-ENGINE-COMPARISON, D011-OPENGAMMA-STRATA-OVERVIEW-2026, D011-OPEN-GAMMA-CURVE-CALIBRATION, D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019 **Area context:** Distinguishes available implementation tools for established engines from ML research methods that still need a separately verified codebase, data, licensing and support before being presented as tools. **Limit:** Project documentation establishes documented capabilities only; paper publication is not a software release. Coverage and APIs are versioned and may not suit every product or market convention. **Relationship:** Curve and market data feed pricing libraries; engine selection and calibration produce values/sensitivities; ML papers motivate research experiments but require implementations, reproducibility and comparable baselines before tool-route inclusion.
- **Claim:** Verified implementation artifacts now distinguish three optional frontier tool types: (1) Deep Hedging's beta TensorFlow simulator learns a transaction-cost/risk-utility hedge policy from simulated market/hedge paths; (2) Qiskit Finance supplies quantum-finance tutorials and uncertainty components, but IBM support ended in 2023 and its latest listed release is 0.4.1 (2024); (3) Neutryx Core is a JAX/automatic-differentiation pricing-risk/XVA project whose production, speed and 500+ test claims remain self-reported, with no tagged release or independent validation located. Quantra is separately mapped as a classical QuantLib-based pricing service, not an ML or new pricing method. **Locator:** Deep Hedging repository README/code/license and dated update notes; Qiskit Finance repository README and release list; Neutryx Core README/repository metadata/license and public demo; Quantra server README/product/tests; all inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-DEEPHEDGING-REFERENCE-IMPLEMENTATION-2026, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-REPOSITORY-2026, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-RELEASES-2026, D011-NEUTRYX-CORE-DIFFERENTIABLE-FINANCE-2026 **Area context:** After classical pricing models, numerical engines and a clearly defined output target, learners can inspect these as optional implementation labs: learned hedging policy versus derivative price, differentiable risk/pricing prototype versus classical engine, and quantum-circuit experiment versus classical benchmark. Their different outputs and maturity must be shown before selection. **Limit:** The deep-hedging implementation is beta, GPL-3.0, based on simplified example worlds and explicitly not production-ready; Qiskit Finance is not IBM-supported and its last listed release is 2024; Neutryx's maturity/performance claims were not independently checked. None supplies evidence of cross-product performance superiority, employer adoption, safe deployment or practical quantum advantage. **Relationship:** Classical model/payoff + market or simulated path + objective -> numerical price/Greek or learned hedge action -> independent benchmark, calibration, stability, out-of-distribution and transaction-cost checks. Quantum tutorials add encoded distributions/circuits and must be compared to a classical reference. Quantra instead wraps conventional QuantLib valuation and data conventions behind service APIs. These are functional branches, not a compulsory combined stack.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Future**
- **Claim:** Qiskit Finance provides versioned example code for quantum amplitude-estimation option and fixed-income pricing, qGAN option pricing and credit-risk analysis. It is an inspectable educational/research artifact for exploring quantum circuit, distribution-loading and payoff-encoding workflows, not evidence of a production pricing platform. **Locator:** Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 official community tutorial index inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-PRICING-TUTORIALS-0401, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026 **Area context:** This tool record belongs to optional frontier exploration after classical pricing, stochastic/numerical methods and basic quantum-computing concepts; the learner can inspect implementation choices and resource/error tradeoffs. **Limit:** The tutorial version is old, and the index does not prove present maintenance, production readiness, reproducibility or advantage over classical methods. ESMA characterizes the field as early-stage; availability of a tutorial is not evidence of adoption. **Relationship:** Classical model/payoff formulation and discretization feed data and payoff encoding; quantum circuits estimate the encoded expectation; circuit output is decoded and benchmarked against matched classical pricing with full error and resource accounting.

**Mapped cell evidence — Standards, credentials and learning resources, Traditional**
- **Claim:** An established mathematical-finance learning route starts with calculus-based probability and stochastic processes, then develops stochastic calculus, martingales and risk-neutral pricing before continuous-time derivatives, exotic options and term-structure models. Shreve's textbook was developed from Carnegie Mellon's computational-finance master's program; MIT's later open-course syllabus similarly connects stochastic-calculus pricing to finance theory and computational assignments. **Locator:** Springer publisher record for Shreve, Stochastic Calculus for Finance II (2004); MIT OpenCourseWare 15.450 Analytics of Finance (Fall 2010) syllabus. **Sources:** D011-SPRINGER-SHREVE-STOCHASTIC-CALCULUS-2004, D011-MIT-OCW-ANALYTICS-FINANCE-2010 **Area context:** These resources substantiate a teachable prerequisite order within quantitative pricing: calculus/probability and finance theory lead into stochastic/martingale models, risk-neutral valuation, derivatives, numerical methods and implementation. **Limit:** The textbook is a publisher description and is not marked open access; MIT OCW is a specific historical course rather than a current degree requirement. Neither is a universal or exhaustive curriculum standard. **Relationship:** Core probability, stochastic processes and no-arbitrage ideas support later continuous-time pricing; computational exercises make the model executable. Advanced product methods should be chosen after those foundations and with the relevant payoff, data and numerical method in view.

**Mapped cell evidence — Standards, credentials and learning resources, Current**
- **Claim:** The CQF qualification currently sequences six modules and two electives with exams and a capstone; its modules include stochastic calculus and martingales, quantitative risk/return, Black-Scholes, data science and machine learning, and fixed income/credit. CFA Institute's current derivatives curriculum provides an additional professional learning reference. **Locator:** CQF official qualification curriculum, opened 2026-10-24; CFA Institute 2026 derivatives reading records already indexed. **Sources:** D011-CQF-QUALIFICATION-CURRICULUM-2026, D011-CFA-DERIVATIVES-2026-PDF, D011-CFA-CONTINGENT-CLAIMS-2026 **Area context:** This is evidence of a current formal learning pathway with selected pricing prerequisites and downstream topics; it can inform learning design without implying the qualification is mandatory for entry or practice. **Limit:** Provider curricula describe their own program, not a universal competency standard or complete academic/industry consensus; verify cohort version and distinguish credential requirements from learning references. **Relationship:** CQF's sequence connects mathematical/stochastic foundations to pricing, risk, ML and fixed income/credit; elective selection specializes later. The platform should treat it as one optional pathway alongside open textbooks, university materials and software tutorials.
- **Claim:** Current formal learning examples include a professional qualification pathway (CQF, six modules and two electives) and a Spring 2026 university course in stochastic calculus and advanced derivatives. The latter explicitly connects stochastic-calculus foundations to pricing/hedging exotic options, Greeks, interest-rate and credit derivatives, and risk management. **Locator:** CQF official qualification curriculum; Princeton ORF 515 / FIN 503 Spring 2026 course description. **Sources:** D011-CQF-QUALIFICATION-CURRICULUM-2026, D011-PRINCETON-ORFE515-SPRING2026 **Area context:** Provides separate professional and university examples of how pricing foundations lead into instrument-specific and advanced derivative learning; neither should be presented as compulsory for every learner. **Limit:** Provider and course descriptions are not labor-market requirements, full syllabi or consensus standards; verify current content and access before recommending resources. **Relationship:** Stochastic calculus precedes advanced derivatives pricing/hedging; elective or course choices specialize into products and models after the broad mathematical foundation. The sequence is an example supported by these curricula, not a universal dependency graph.
- **Claim:** A 2026 draft quantitative-development curriculum joins market/product foundations, Python and production engineering (low-latency systems, accelerated computing, MLOps), derivatives/fixed income and a capstone; Qiskit Finance supplies optional executable examples for quantum option, fixed-income and credit-risk algorithms. Together these illustrate separate career-preparation and frontier-lab choices, not compulsory prerequisites. **Locator:** University of Chicago Financial Mathematics/Data Science Institute, Quantitative Development Certificate draft dated 3 June 2026; Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 tutorials index inspected 2026-10-24; official CQF program overview. **Sources:** D011-UCHICAGO-QUANTDEV-CURRICULUM-2026, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-PRICING-TUTORIALS-0401, D011-CQF-QUALIFICATION-CURRICULUM-2026 **Area context:** The UChicago document is specifically a quantitative-development pathway, while Qiskit tutorials are optional research/teaching implementations for quantum algorithms. They serve different learners and maturity horizons, and should appear as distinct contextual resources. **Limit:** The UChicago curriculum is draft and institution-specific; CQF is a provider qualification, not a regulatory licence; Qiskit Finance documentation is version 0.4.1 and does not prove active maintenance or production use. No single curriculum defines a universal learning order. **Relationship:** Core probability, mathematics, derivatives and programming precede specialized computational pricing. Production engineering supports implementing and validating numerical workflows; quantum tutorial exercises sit downstream of classical pricing and numerical foundations plus quantum information, and remain optional exploratory work.
- **Claim:** Current Basel consolidated CAD30 guidance for banks expects independent validation of valuation models and material changes, including theoretical/mathematical integrity, assumptions against market practice and contract terms, sensitivity analysis, benchmarking to market prices or an independent model, backtesting, documented limitations, and explicit valuation-uncertainty assessment; it also connects valuation performance to P&L attribution and model-review triggers. **Locator:** Basel Committee consolidated guidelines CAD30, opened 2026-10-24; sections 30.14-30.16, 30.21-30.28 and 30.37-30.42. **Sources:** D011-BIS-VALUATION-GOVERNANCE-CAD30-2026 **Area context:** This is bank supervisory context for controls around quantitative pricing models. It explains why learners examine assumptions, independent prices/models, sensitivities, stress behavior and model limitations after learning how prices are produced. **Limit:** Guidance applies to banking valuation practices within Basel implementation and interacts with national law and accounting standards. It is not a universal legal requirement, a prescribed pricing technique, or a guarantee that a benchmark/model is independent or fit for purpose. **Relationship:** Valuation model inputs and assumptions produce prices and sensitivities; validation compares these with independent prices/models, sensitivity/stress results and later outcomes. Uncertainty and P&L attribution inform review or adjustment. This is a governance/control branch connected to pricing outputs, not an alternative pricing engine.
- **Claim:** For implementation learning, ORE exposes free, public documentation in distinct layers: its user guide teaches workflow, installation, examples and configuration of market data/curves/conventions; the product catalogue maps instrument payoffs to pricing methodologies and engine/trade XML; Methods documents exposure simulation, XVA and sensitivity analytics; and ORE Academy links instructional videos. This is a tool-specific learning resource, not a professional credential or a universal derivatives curriculum. **Locator:** Official ORE Documentation page (opened 2026-10-28), sections User Guide, Product Catalogue, Methods and ORE Academy; ORE v17 roadmap inspected for current release context. **Sources:** D011-ORE-RISK-ANALYTICS-DOCS-2026, D011-ORE-MARKET-DATA-INPUTS-FAQ-2026, D011-ORE-ROADMAP-V17-2026 **Area context:** Learners can use public implementation documentation to connect product payoff, market-data setup, curve conventions, pricing engine and risk outputs after relevant mathematical foundations. The learning material is optional, software-specific and hands-on; it does not prescribe use of ORE in every pricing path. **Limit:** The project page describes documentation and linked videos, not a formal assessment, credential, complete course sequence or guarantee that all content is beginner-level. Features/version requirements should follow the release documentation; this does not close the broader cross-university curriculum/resource comparison. **Relationship:** Derivative foundations and product definition -> ORE user guide/configuration -> product and pricing-engine catalogue -> runnable example -> price/sensitivity/XVA output; learning these docs can complement quantitative-method study but does not replace it.
- **Claim:** Current model-risk sources make calibration and validation relevant within specific institutional contexts: the Federal Reserve's 2026 revised model-risk guidance supersedes SR 11-7 for its stated banking scope; OSFI's 2026 market-risk guideline requires independent validation and tests of assumptions and distinguishes model-method risk from uncertainty in calibration parameters for complex products. These standards help explain why production pricing work may include documented calibration, benchmarking, backtesting and independent validation, while remaining jurisdiction- and institution-specific. **Locator:** Federal Reserve SR 26-2, issued 2026-04-17 and applicability note; OSFI CAR 2026 Chapter 9 paragraphs 106 and 283; Federal Reserve Interagency CCR Guidance, section V.3 and Appendix B (dated 2011). **Sources:** D011-FED-SR26-2-2026, D011-OSFI-CAR-2026-MARKET-RISK-MODEL-VALIDATION, D011-FED-INTERAGENCY-CCR-GUIDANCE-2011 **Area context:** These are standards and governance context for pricing/model validation tasks at applicable institutions. They can inform professional practice and role context; they do not imply that all jurisdictions use the same rules, or that a student must learn regulatory controls before choosing a pricing method. **Limit:** SR 26-2 and OSFI CAR apply to their respective regulated institutions and scopes. The CCR guidance is older and specific to counterparty credit risk. Do not treat these documents as universal law, an optimizer specification or a complete technical calibration curriculum. **Relationship:** Pricing model/calibration work in an institution -> identify jurisdiction and product scope -> apply relevant model-risk governance -> validate assumptions, components and outcomes -> document findings and remediation. Governance requirements frame professional use; they complement mathematical/numerical methods but do not substitute for them.
- **Claim:** Current university examples make different parts of the path explicit: ETH begins with no-arbitrage, martingales, stochastic calculus and Black–Scholes after measure-theoretic probability; Illinois' Spring 2026 numerical-methods course connects SDE/PDE foundations to FD, Monte Carlo, variance reduction, QMC, sensitivities and calibration; Copenhagen's 2026/27 course applies advanced models and Longstaff–Schwartz to options, hedging and simulation outputs. **Locator:** Official ETH Autumn 2026 page, content/prerequisites; University of Illinois IE525 last offered Spring 2026, course/syllabus description; University of Copenhagen NMAK26006U 2026/2027, content, learning outcomes and recommended qualifications. Inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-ETH-MATHEMATICAL-FOUNDATIONS-FINANCE-AUTUMN-2026, D011-ILLINOIS-IE525-NUMERICAL-METHODS-FINANCE-SPRING-2026, D011-COPENHAGEN-QUANTITATIVE-FINANCE-2026-27, D011-PRINCETON-ORFE515-SPRING2026 **Area context:** These sources help order the learning path from probability and stochastic calculus into numerical pricing, early exercise, calibration and hedge experiments; their distinct levels and access conditions should remain visible. **Limit:** Three institution-specific examples, not a global curriculum consensus; Illinois' page is an archived offering, ETH notes are enrollment-restricted, and each course's prerequisites apply to that course only. **Relationship:** Probability/measure foundations -> stochastic models and no-arbitrage -> numerical methods (PDE/FD, Monte Carlo/QMC, early-exercise methods) -> computed price/sensitivity/hedge experiment -> validation and model-risk interpretation. This is a supported illustrative pathway, not a mandatory sequence for every role.
- **Claim:** The current UCL MATH0088 specification sequences quantitative/computational finance from stated mathematics prerequisites through SDEs and derivatives, Black–Scholes/PDEs/Greeks/early exercise, finite differences and Monte Carlo, then volatility surfaces, fixed-income models/calibration and exotic options. Assessment is 90% exam and 10% coursework. **Locator:** UCL MATH0088 2026/27 full course specification, pp.1–2; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-UCL-MATH0088-QUANTITATIVE-COMPUTATIONAL-FINANCE-2026-27 **Area context:** This current course provides a concrete prerequisite-to-specialist sequence across derivative pricing and financial engineering; it supplements the other universities' differing level and resource access. **Limit:** One institution-specific course specification. It does not make its prerequisites or assessment pattern universal, and the PDF is a course outline rather than a complete open teaching resource. **Relationship:** Mathematics prerequisites -> SDE/product/payoff foundation -> PDE and numerical pricing -> Greeks/early exercise -> volatility/fixed-income calibration and exotics. It is an example sequence, not an all-student mandatory contract.

Deep Hedging; 2026 machine-learning derivatives-pricing review; named employer role records for derivatives quant analyst, quant researcher and quant technology developer. **Sources:** D011-PNAS-DEEP-BSDE-PRICING-2018, D011-BUEHLER-DEEP-HEDGING-2019, D011-FAN-SIRIGNANO-ML-PRICING-2026, D011-CITI-FX-OPTIONS-QUANT-ANALYST-2026, D011-CITI-EQUITY-DERIVATIVES-QUANT-2026, D011-CITI-QUANT-TECH-DEVELOPER-2026, D011-JS-QUANT-RESEARCHER-2026 **Area context:** Shows a possible research-to-role connection for frontier pricing: quantitative methods produce model outputs that may be implemented, tested or consumed by product/technology teams. Position/market risk and execution remain downstream consumers with separate responsibilities.
- **Claim:** A regime-switching Heston–Hull–White European-option study combines stochastic volatility, stochastic rates and a switching regime, derives a semi-analytical model pricer, uses a learned local residual surrogate to assist parameter search, and recomputes final prices with the original formula. This is a complementary calibration design: learning accelerates/localizes the search while the financial model remains the final valuation authority. **Locator:** Li, Scientific Reports 16, article 29332 (2026), full open-access article, especially model, calibration workflow, SSE 50 ETF experiment and diagnostics; DOI 10.1038/s41598-026-67726-0; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-LI-REGIME-SWITCHING-HESTON-HULL-WHITE-DL-CALIBRATION-2026, D011-HAINAUT-CASAS-PINN-HESTON-2024, D011-ZHANG-AMICI-MORANDOTTI-DEEP-DIFFERENTIAL-HESTON-CALIBRATION-2024, D011-BENCHOP-SLV-STOCHASTIC-LOCAL-VOL-BENCHMARK-2018 **Area context:** Current mixed-model pricing/calibration branch for European options when stochastic volatility, stochastic rates and regime switching are jointly in scope. It links model choice and numerical pricing to data calibration; it is not a universal requirement for a basic pricing pathway. **Limit:** One peer-reviewed paper with one named ETF-option data context and selected comparators. Its reported fit improvement does not establish generalization across markets, products, or regimes, nor does it establish production deployment or universal optimizer superiority. **Relationship:** Market quotes + joint Heston/Hull–White/regime model -> semi-analytical model pricer -> learned local residual surrogate guides parameter search -> recompute candidate prices in original model -> compare held-out fit and calibration diagnostics -> pass calibrated parameters and prices to model validation/valuation consumers. The surrogate assists calibration; it is not a replacement pricer. This differs from PINN pricing, which directly approximates a PDE solution, and from a deep differential network, which learns price/parameter sensitivities for calibration.

Error and cost checks are prerequisites to interpreting a claimed speedup.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Established risk foundations distinguish market loss distributions, credit default/loss components and realized high-frequency variation; time-series, probability, portfolio exposure and data-frequency/noise knowledge are needed before selecting a risk estimator. **Locator:** Basel CRE32 current IRB risk components; Zhang, Mykland and Aït-Sahalia two-scale realized volatility (2005); Barndorff-Nielsen et al. realized kernels (2008); Corsi HAR-RV (2009); 2026 ARCH volatility process docs. **Sources:** D011-BIS-CRE32-IRB-RISK-COMPONENTS-CURRENT, D011-ZHANG-MYKLAND-AITSAHALIA-TWO-SCALE-RV-2005, D011-BARNDORFF-HANSEN-LUNDE-SHEPHARD-REALIZED-KERNEL-2008, D011-CORSI-HAR-RV-2009, D011-ARCH-VOLATILITY-PROCESSES-2026 **Area context:** These foundations cover distinct foundational branches—credit parameters and market-volatility estimation—rather than one generic risk skill. They sit before model family selection and require identifying risk type, instrument, horizon and data granularity. **Limit:** The cited methods do not cover liquidity, operational, model or all portfolio-credit risk foundations. Realized-volatility methods use market-price/high-frequency data and should not be generalized to all risk types. **Relationship:** Data frequency and market microstructure affect realized-volatility inputs; borrower/facility information supports PD/LGD/EAD estimates; these model inputs feed later VaR/ES, credit-capital, stress and limit outputs under different assumptions.
- **Claim:** Market liquidity has several measurable dimensions: immediacy, breadth/depth, tightness (transaction cost/price impact) and resilience under stress. Market-liquidity loss therefore depends on position size, executable depth, trading horizon and own market impact; it differs from funding liquidity, which concerns the ability to obtain funds and meet cash/guarantee obligations. The dimensions can interact through margin calls, dealer capacity and forced liquidation. **Locator:** ECB Financial Stability Review special feature (May 2023), sections 1–2 and liquidity dimensions; Hisata and Yamai (2000), official BOJ abstract on L-VaR inputs and liquidation horizon. **Sources:** D011-ECB-MARKET-FUNDING-LIQUIDITY-2023, D011-BOJ-LIQUIDITY-ADJUSTED-VAR-2000 **Area context:** This foundation explains why a mark-to-market VaR based on a fixed close-out horizon may omit liquidation cost for a large or illiquid position. It supports understanding of liquidity-adjusted market risk and the separate bank funding-gap branch, without requiring every learner to use either model in every role. **Limit:** ECB material is euro-area financial-stability analysis, and L-VaR is a historical research framework. Neither establishes a single accepted universal liquidity metric or current supervisory requirement. A given task may require only one liquidity dimension or a different institution-specific measure. **Relationship:** Market depth, spreads, position size and horizon inform liquidation-cost/impact assumptions; funding cash flows, contingent liabilities and stress scenarios inform funding-gap analysis. Outputs interact under stress but should not be conflated.
- **Claim:** A current market-risk curriculum and task evidence corroborate the established foundations already mapped here: probability/loss-distribution reasoning, portfolio exposure, stress scenarios, and the distinction between market-liquidity loss and funding-liquidity need. Risk specialists use quantitative risk/scenario analysis; selected trading and investment-management tasks consume position, hedge and portfolio-risk outputs. Market-microstructure detail is included only to explain market depth, transaction cost and liquidation impact when that is the chosen liquidity question. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Measuring and Managing Market Risk public curriculum overview; BCBS Stress Testing Principles (2018); O*NET 2026 task profiles 13-2054, 41-3031 and 11-3031.03; ECB 2023 liquidity dimensions and BOJ/IMES L-VaR abstract. Exact task conditions and boundaries are recorded in the D011 risk role-area evidence records. **Sources:** D011-CFA-2026-MEASURING-MANAGING-MARKET-RISK, D011-BIS-STRESS-TESTING-PRINCIPLES-2018, D011-ONET-13-2054.00, D011-ONET-41-3031.00, D011-ONET-11-3031.03, D011-ECB-MARKET-FUNDING-LIQUIDITY-2023, D011-BOJ-LIQUIDITY-ADJUSTED-VAR-2000 **Area context:** These cross-checks corroborate concepts within the risk area's defined activities; occupational evidence illustrates downstream use but does not define the area. The curriculum overview cannot be used as proof that every listed topic is a universal prerequisite. **Limit:** CFA's full reading is access-controlled and only the public curriculum overview was inspected; Basel principles are high-level bank guidance, not a method or local law; O*NET is U.S. occupational evidence; ECB and BOJ sources have their stated regional/historical limits. This source set supports foundational distinctions, not exhaustive asset-class stress libraries or a universal liquidity metric. **Relationship:** Probability and portfolio exposure support loss-distribution estimates; stress scenarios test severe conditions; VaR/ES estimates and stress losses remain distinct outputs. Market depth and impact enter only the liquidation-cost branch, while funding gaps and contingency funding belong to bank funding-liquidity analysis.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Current**
- **Claim:** Risk modelling requires separating measurement of past variation from forecasting future conditional volatility and tail loss. High-frequency realized variation can be contaminated by microstructure noise and jumps, so noise-robust and jump-robust estimators answer different measurement questions; forecast methods such as HAR-RV then model the constructed series across daily, weekly and monthly components. **Locator:** Zhang, Mykland & Aït-Sahalia, JASA 100(472) (2005), two-time-scale estimator under microstructure noise; Barndorff-Nielsen et al. (2008), realized kernels; Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard (2004), bipower variation/jump decomposition; Corsi, JFE 7(2) (2009), HAR-RV heterogeneous horizon structure; current Federal Reserve FEDS 2025-061r1 (revised September 2026) compares econometric and ML realized-volatility forecasts across horizons. **Sources:** D011-ZHANG-MYKLAND-AITSAHALIA-TWO-SCALE-RV-2005, D011-BARNDORFF-HANSEN-LUNDE-SHEPHARD-REALIZED-KERNEL-2008, D011-BARNDORFF-SHEPHARD-BIPOWER-JUMPS-2004, D011-CORSI-HAR-RV-2009, D011-FED-REALIZED-VOL-ML-COMPARE-2025-REV2026 **Area context:** These are finance-specific quantitative foundations for risk measurement and forecasting: the data construction/estimator choice changes the series that downstream volatility models and risk forecasts consume. **Limit:** The foundational estimators have differing sampling assumptions and robustness properties; the FEDS paper is preliminary author research on US equity data and does not identify a universal winner. Realized variance is not itself a forward risk forecast, VaR/ES capital measure or a trading signal. **Relationship:** Timestamped high-frequency prices and sampling choices precede realized-variation construction; noise/jump handling determines the measurement target; HAR/ARCH or other forecast models consume that measure; forecast evaluation and VaR/ES/utility checks are downstream and horizon-specific.
- **Claim:** Current bank-risk foundations include liquidity as projected funding cash flows and contingent demands across horizons/currencies; operational risk as a separate non-market risk category; and model risk as uncertainty from model design, data, assumptions, use and performance. Liquidity projections require documented behavioral and asset-funding assumptions and stress conditions. These are related governance and exposure concepts, not interchangeable risk measures. **Locator:** BCBS consolidated LQY10 sections 10.26-10.34 and 10.54; Basel OPE25 version effective 2023-01-01; interagency SR 26-2 issued 2026-04-17. **Sources:** D011-BIS-LIQUIDITY-MANAGEMENT-CONSOLIDATED-2026, D011-BIS-OPERATIONAL-RISK-CAPITAL-SA-2023-CURRENT, D011-FED-SR26-2-2026 **Area context:** Complements the existing probability, time-series and market/credit-risk foundations with distinct bank-liquidity, operational-capital and model-governance contexts. Which branch matters depends on the institution, exposure and assigned work. **Limit:** Official banking guidance and prudential methods are jurisdiction/version scoped. OPE25 is a regulatory capital method rather than a full operational-risk management framework; SR 26-2 is non-prescriptive U.S. interagency guidance, most relevant to Federal Reserve-regulated organizations above $30bn. **Relationship:** Exposure and institution context select the relevant risk branch. Liquidity concepts precede cash-flow projection and stress/gap analysis; OPE25 inputs feed a capital output; model-risk concepts govern challenge and monitoring of whichever quantitative model is used. None automatically blocks learning another risk category.
- **Claim:** The IFRS 9 impairment framework separates accounting ECL stages: Stage 1 recognises 12-month ECL when credit risk has not significantly increased; Stage 2 recognises lifetime ECL after significant increase in credit risk; Stage 3 continues lifetime ECL for credit-impaired assets with interest calculated on amortised cost. Twelve-month ECL is the lifetime loss weighted by the chance of a default event in the next 12 months, not losses that would be paid only within that year. **Locator:** BIS FSI Executive Summary published 2017-12-13, 'Three stages of impairment' and 'Twelve-month versus lifetime expected credit losses' sections. **Sources:** D011-BIS-FSI-IFRS9-ECL-EXEC-SUMMARY-2017 **Area context:** This is accounting impairment and provisioning knowledge used for financial-statement ECL, distinct from Basel regulatory credit capital, market-risk VaR/ES and derivative counterparty exposure/CVA outputs. **Limit:** BIS supervisory summary rather than the IFRS 9 text; its simplified discussion focuses on loans. Detailed accounting rules, instruments, staging criteria, policy choices and local adoption require current IASB materials and applicable jurisdiction guidance. **Relationship:** Credit-risk change and default probability over an instrument's expected life inform staging; stage status determines 12-month versus lifetime ECL; PD, LGD, EAD, scenarios, cash-shortfall timing and discounting feed the accounting allowance. The allowance is not interchangeable with economic loss, regulatory capital or CVA.
- **Claim:** Core credit-risk inputs have distinct meanings and model uses: Basel IRB components include probability of default, loss given default, exposure at default and maturity; SA-CCR converts derivative replacement cost and potential future exposure into regulatory EAD, while IMM is a supervisory-approved alternative exposure method. These prudential components differ from IFRS 9 accounting ECL and from CVA fair-value adjustment, which uses exposure and counterparty credit quality. **Locator:** Basel CRE32 IRB risk components, CRE52 SA-CCR and CRE53 IMM current chapters; BIS FSI IFRS 9 executive summary (2017), staging sections; SR 11-10 CCR guidance, introduction and CVA section. **Sources:** D011-BIS-CRE32-IRB-RISK-COMPONENTS-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE52-SA-CCR-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE53-IMM-CURRENT, D011-BIS-FSI-IFRS9-ECL-EXEC-SUMMARY-2017, D011-FED-INTERAGENCY-CCR-GUIDANCE-2011 **Area context:** These are foundational credit/CCR concepts for interpreting banking risk models and outputs; applicability depends on exposure type and regulatory/accounting purpose. They complement market-risk probability/time-series foundations without becoming one interchangeable model family. **Limit:** Basel methods depend on national implementation and supervisory approval; BIS FSI is a dated accounting summary rather than the IFRS standard; SR 11-10 is dated U.S. supervisory guidance. Detailed firm implementation and local accounting requirements are not inferred. **Relationship:** Default risk and recovery concepts inform PD/LGD and credit loss; on-balance-sheet loans feed IRB/accounting ECL under distinct rules. Derivative trades and netting/collateral feed exposure profiles and regulatory EAD under SA-CCR or approved IMM; counterparty credit quality and future exposure jointly inform CVA and wrong-way-risk analysis.
- **Claim:** Current risk foundations are supported by both a structured market-risk curriculum and task evidence for the stored risk routes: financial-risk specialists quantify risk, develop or assess risk models and scenarios; selected traders monitor positions/markets and use hedge strategies; investment-fund managers monitor holdings against risk goals. Market microstructure concepts enter this foundation only when the task measures liquidity, executable depth, transaction costs or liquidation impact; they are not a universal prerequisite for credit ECL, operational risk or every portfolio-risk task. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Measuring and Managing Market Risk public curriculum overview; O*NET 2026 task profiles 13-2054 Financial Risk Specialists, 41-3031 Securities/Commodities/Financial Services Sales Agents and 11-3031.03 Investment Fund Managers; ECB 2023 market/funding-liquidity analysis; BOJ/IMES L-VaR abstract. Route-specific conditions remain recorded separately in conditional_role_area_task_evidence. **Sources:** D011-CFA-2026-MEASURING-MANAGING-MARKET-RISK, D011-ONET-13-2054.00, D011-ONET-41-3031.00, D011-ONET-11-3031.03, D011-ECB-MARKET-FUNDING-LIQUIDITY-2023, D011-BOJ-LIQUIDITY-ADJUSTED-VAR-2000 **Area context:** Curriculum and occupational tasks corroborate the use of market-risk, scenario and risk-output foundations without defining the area by role frequency. The area boundary remains grounded in risk measurement/modeling activities and their outputs. Liquidity/microstructure depth is selected by exposure, data and assigned task. **Limit:** The CFA page is a public curriculum overview, not the gated full reading; O*NET is U.S. occupational evidence and bundles varied roles; the ECB source is euro-area analysis and BOJ L-VaR is a historical research framework. These sources do not establish a universal syllabus, mandatory role prerequisite or single market-liquidity measure. **Relationship:** Probability, time-series and exposure concepts support risk measurement; stress design explores losses outside a single forecast; market depth, spreads and impact are added when a liquidity-adjusted liquidation estimate needs them. Role tasks corroborate selected uses of outputs, but do not make every foundation compulsory for every role.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Emerging risk-model competence includes comparing nonlinear, regime-aware and machine-learning volatility forecasts against long-memory econometric baselines, using multiple forecast horizons and statistical/economic risk diagnostics. **Locator:** Federal Reserve FEDS 2025-061r1 (September 2026 revision); peer-reviewed Journal of Empirical Finance 2024 cross-index comparison; Leushuis and Petkov 2026 review. **Sources:** D011-FED-REALIZED-VOL-ML-COMPARE-2025-REV2026, D011-JEF-REALIZED-VOL-ML-2024, D011-LEUSHUIS-PETKOV-REALIZED-VOL-FORECASTING-REVIEW-2026 **Area context:** This is advanced competence for a market-risk forecasting branch, extending econometrics with ML comparisons while preserving risk target, forecast horizon and validation as the organizing concepts. **Limit:** Findings vary by sample/horizon and the FEDS paper is preliminary author research; the peer-reviewed abstract is limited to ten global equity indices. No universal ML advantage is established. **Relationship:** Traditional time-series and realized-volatility foundations feed feature/target construction; ML adds nonlinear estimation; chronological validation and multiple metrics assess forecasts before any VaR/ES or limit use.
- **Claim:** Emerging risk competence extends beyond equity realized-volatility prediction. A fully inspected BIS study builds market-specific indicators from volatility, liquidity/microstructure and no-arbitrage dislocations in US Treasury, USD FX and money markets, then uses point-in-time rolling PCA and random-forest quantile forecasts to estimate future stress distributions; cross-market indicator values capture spillovers. Shapley values are used to inspect predictor contributions. For credit models, feature dependence is a separate explainability concern: the indexed 2024 study's abstract warns that independence assumptions in Kernel-SHAP can mislead explanations when predictors are dependent, but its full text was not available in this review. **Locator:** Aldasoro et al., BIS Working Paper 1250 (March 2025), full paper §§2–4 and especially §§2.1–2.2, 3.1–3.4 and 4; Do, Babaei and Pagnottoni (2024), Measurement 22(4), 315–340, publisher abstract and ERIC indexed record only. **Sources:** D011-BIS-ML-MARKET-STRESS-2025, D011-TF-DEPENDENT-SHAP-CREDIT-2024 **Area context:** This supports an optional advanced market-stress/systemic-risk branch involving market microstructure, funding/liquidity, cross-market dependence, distributional forecasting and explanation checks. It complements established probability, liquidity and time-series foundations; it does not make ML, Shapley values or high-frequency microstructure universal prerequisites for all credit, operational or portfolio-risk work. **Limit:** BIS findings are from one US Treasury/FX/money-market study at stated horizons and are not formal robustness tests across all structural breaks, asset classes or institutions; Shapley contributions are not causal effects. The credit explanation paper is abstract-only because the publisher returned 403; no detailed algorithm ranking is asserted. Independent replication across credit, commodities and other jurisdictions and formal regime-stability analysis remain open. **Relationship:** Market-risk inputs and market-condition construction precede distributional stress forecasts; point-in-time rolling estimation helps avoid look-ahead. Cross-market indicators supply dependence/spillover information, while Shapley values add a diagnostic explanation layer after prediction. Credit-feature dependence affects interpretation of attribution and needs its own validation; neither method replaces risk-model backtesting or independent validation.
- **Claim:** Interpretation of emerging credit-risk models requires recognizing correlated borrower and loan features. In a Lending Club P2P example, a peer-reviewed study evaluates dependence-aware Shapley explanations because an independence assumption can distort attribution. This is a foundation for reading model explanations and their assumptions, not evidence that Shapley values explain causes or establish model validity. **Locator:** Famà et al. (2024), publisher abstract and University of Bergamo repository record; related 2023 CLADAG conference-paper abstract. **Sources:** D011-UNIBG-DEPENDENT-KERNEL-SHAP-CREDIT-2024, D011-TF-DEPENDENT-SHAP-CREDIT-2024 **Area context:** This supports optional credit-ML interpretation competence after core credit modeling and feature-dependence concepts. It complements probability, model validation and credit-risk foundations; it is not a prerequisite for the other risk families. **Limit:** Detailed method and independent replication are not available in the inspected full text; results are limited to P2P Lending Club credit explanations. No causality, fairness or regulatory-compliance claim is inferred. **Relationship:** Understand the fitted model and feature dependence, then select an attribution approach and test its explanation behavior. Predictive performance, calibration, fairness and post-hoc explanation quality are separate review questions.
- **Claim:** Regime and stability diagnostics also apply within credit risk. Structural Merton/Heston models infer distance to default and PD from firm asset/debt dynamics; sequential tests can monitor drift and related parameter shifts so that an assumption of stable model parameters is checked as new returns arrive. A separate Bank of Canada early-warning design treats credit conditions as a threshold regime switch in a system financial-stress model. These are different targets: firm-level PD-model stability versus system-level stress probability. **Locator:** Andreou and Ghysels, full paper §§2–4 (University of Cyprus 2007-03; Journal of Econometrics 2008); Li and Xiao, Bank of Canada Staff Working Paper 2016-21, full paper abstract, non-technical summary and model specification §§2–3. **Sources:** D011-UCY-STRUCTURAL-CREDIT-MODEL-QUALITY-CONTROL-2008, D011-BANKCANADA-CREDIT-REGIME-STRESS-2016 **Area context:** This adds a credit-specific optional foundation for parameter stability, distance-to-default and threshold-regime interpretation. It complements credit PD/default foundations and the market-risk regime examples; it is not a prerequisite for every risk family or a universal current supervisory method. **Limit:** The structural-model paper's main stability procedures are theoretical/simulation evidence and assume model-specific asset dynamics; the Bank of Canada study is a historical Canadian system-stress application, not firm PD validation. Neither proves current deployment or global superiority. **Relationship:** Firm asset/debt assumptions generate distance-to-default and PD estimates; sequential stability monitoring checks whether parameters remain reliable. Separately, credit-aggregate conditions enter a threshold-regime model whose output is future system stress probability. Both produce diagnostics/forecasts, but serve different units and decisions.
- **Claim:** Financial risk forecasting must distinguish persistent high volatility, abrupt variance breaks and latent or observable regime transitions; these imply different diagnostics and model responses. In an inspectable 2025 comparison across eight international equity indices, the authors compare linear AR/HAR baselines with smooth and Markov regime-switching variants and evaluate VaR/ES applications. Relative gains vary by forecast horizon, so a detected regime or break is a model assumption to test rather than an automatic reason to replace a baseline. **Locator:** Ding, Kambouroudis and McMillan (2025), full paper §§1–5, especially model assumptions, eight-index sample, forecast tests and VaR/ES results; supporting structural-break VaR and BRICS forecast-combination studies are indexed at abstract/full-article scope as stated in the source cards. **Sources:** D011-STIRLING-REGIME-SWITCHING-RV-RISK-2025, D011-ELSEVIER-USD-STRUCTURAL-BREAK-VAR-2020, D011-MDPI-BRICS-STRUCTURAL-BREAK-VOLATILITY-2018 **Area context:** Optional advanced foundation for market-risk forecasting with regime or structural-change concerns. It complements time-series and volatility foundations and supports model comparison/backtesting; it is not a mandatory prerequisite for credit ECL, operational risk, liquidity gaps or every portfolio-risk task. **Limit:** Full detailed inspection is limited to the 2025 equity-index paper; USD and BRICS findings are at publisher abstract/full-page indexed scope as recorded. None establishes a universal regime detector or independent credit-risk validation. **Relationship:** First identify whether the target is volatility, a tail measure or market stress; then specify the break/regime representation and compare it with stable AR/HAR/GARCH baselines using chronological out-of-sample tests and risk metrics. Regime probabilities or break dates are inputs/diagnostics, not proof of a causal event or model fitness.
- **Scope limits:** Regime/break-aware evidence now covers equity volatility across eight markets and targeted USD exchange-rate/BRICS examples, but those do not establish stability or transfer for credit, counterparty or funding/liquidity risk. Run one bounded check for a directly relevant independent risk-family example; if none meets the source bar, record that scoped no-hit rather than reopen market-volatility evidence. Dependent-feature credit SHAP is established only at abstract/proceedings scope: detailed estimator equations, code, comparison tables and independent replication remain inaccessible. Reopen only if inspectable full text or reproducible comparison becomes available.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Future**
- **Claim:** A future quantum-computational risk research route adds quantum information and circuit-resource reasoning to classical financial-risk foundations. Learners still need probability/distribution modeling, portfolio loss construction, Monte Carlo, VaR/ES and numerical-error concepts; the additional quantum concepts are state preparation, circuit encoding, amplitude estimation, fault-tolerance/noise and end-to-end resource accounting. These are specialist research prerequisites, not general risk-role requirements. **Locator:** Matsakos and Nield, Quantum 8, 1306 (2024), full paper §§1–3 and resource analysis; Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 credit-risk tutorial and release metadata; ESMA TRV Risk Analysis (13 May 2026) and BIS Paper 149 (2024) for hardware and maturity limits. **Sources:** D011-QUANTUM-QMC-RISK-ANALYTICS-2024, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-CREDIT-RISK-TUTORIAL-2024, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-RELEASE-0-4-1, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026, D011-BIS-QUANTUM-FINANCE-OPPORTUNITIES-RISKS-2024 **Area context:** This foundation set applies only to optional quantum-risk research exploration after a student has learned the classical risk question and its simulation/validation baseline. Classical risk theory remains necessary to specify what the quantum circuit is estimating and how its output is checked. **Limit:** The quantum-risk literature is mainly theoretical or toy-scale. The 2024 QMC paper assumes fault-tolerant hardware, estimates very large circuits and ignores gate errors; the Qiskit tutorial has inconsistent VaR/CVaR toy outputs and is based on an older release. Supervisory outlooks describe early maturity, not an established occupational skill demand. **Relationship:** Classical risk measure, portfolio losses and baseline estimator precede quantum-specific state preparation and QAE. Resource/error analysis and matched classical comparison are needed before interpreting circuit estimates; no downstream regulatory or operational use is established.
- **Claim:** At the research frontier, a learner would need classical portfolio/risk-model literacy, probability and loss-distribution foundations, quantum-circuit and amplitude-estimation concepts, and resource/error analysis to evaluate quantum risk proposals. This is a prerequisite map for reading and reproducing research, not a current occupational requirement. **Locator:** BIS Paper 149 (2024); Matsakos and Nield, Quantum 8, 1306 (2024); Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 credit-risk tutorial and quantum-finance learning artifacts inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-BIS-QUANTUM-FINANCE-OPPORTUNITIES-RISKS-2024, D011-QUANTUM-QMC-RISK-ANALYTICS-2024, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-CREDIT-RISK-TUTORIAL-2024 **Area context:** Complements classical risk foundations with a clearly optional research branch; the same underlying risk model, loss definition and classical comparison baseline remain necessary to evaluate quantum proposals. **Limit:** Sources describe a theoretical resource study and a small tutorial, not a validated learning standard, role requirement, production workload or quantum advantage. The tutorial's toy VaR/CVaR outputs require diagnosis. **Relationship:** Classical risk measure, portfolio and loss function precede circuit encoding and quantum estimation; candidate estimates are compared against classical Monte Carlo or exact baselines with error, resource and noise accounting before any risk use.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Traditional market-risk analysis uses alternative distributional and historical approaches to estimate portfolio loss quantiles, while stress testing examines severe but plausible scenarios beyond a single VaR summary. Method choice depends on horizon, portfolio exposures, distributional assumptions and intended decision. **Locator:** BIS current Basel MAR32/MAR33 framework; 12 CFR Part 217 §217.203(6) recognizing variance-covariance, historical simulation and Monte Carlo for covered US institutions; Basel 2026 consolidated stress-testing chapter; 2013 VaR-methodology review as a comparative lead. **Sources:** D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT, D011-BIS-MAR33-EXPECTED-SHORTFALL-2026, D011-US-CFR-2026-217-203-MARKET-RISK-APPROACHES, D011-RISK-VAR-METHODOLOGY-REVIEW-2013 **Area context:** This maps core market-risk method families and their purpose: measure tail loss under a specified model and complement that measure with scenario-based stress analysis. It is a part of risk modeling, not the entirety of credit, liquidity, operational or model risk. **Limit:** The CFR methods are US regulatory options for covered entities; Basel rules are subject to local adoption; the 2013 review is an older secondary synthesis. The mapping does not rank methods or establish universal accuracy. **Relationship:** Portfolio positions, market data, risk-factor mapping and valuation feed loss distributions; VaR/ES metrics summarize selected tail properties; stress scenarios and backtesting/PLA probe different failure modes and are complementary rather than substitutes.
- **Claim:** VaR estimators are alternatives with different assumptions, not a single ladder: variance-covariance uses a specified distribution and estimated moments; historical simulation resamples observed risk-factor changes; Monte Carlo generates scenarios from a specified model; filtered historical simulation rescales historical residuals by current conditional volatility; EVT focuses on tail behavior. Current CFA curriculum compares the first three and states there is no single right method; RBA's full-text worked example demonstrates that distribution assumptions can change estimates; Bank of England research examines filtered-simulation conditionality and procyclicality. The evidence supports task- and portfolio-specific comparison, not a universal ranking. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Measuring and Managing Market Risk learning outcomes/summary; RBA RDP 9708 sections 2-3; Bank of England Working Paper 525 (2015); Abad and Benito, Mathematics and Computers in Simulation (2013) publisher record. **Sources:** D011-CFA-2026-MEASURING-MANAGING-MARKET-RISK, D011-RBA-VAR-METHODS-AND-BACKTESTING-1997, D011-BOE-FILTERED-HISTORICAL-SIMULATION-2015, D011-RISK-VAR-METHODOLOGY-REVIEW-2013 **Area context:** This is the core established market-risk estimation branch; it sits beside stress/scenario analysis and backtesting, and does not cover credit, liquidity, operational or model risk by itself. **Limit:** CFA is a current curriculum source, RBA is a historical Australian banking example, and the Bank of England and publisher records have paper-specific empirical scope. The source set explains assumptions and comparisons but does not rank methods for every instrument, nonlinear portfolio, horizon or data regime. **Relationship:** Portfolio positions and risk-factor data feed valuation and the selected loss-distribution method; the resulting VaR forecast is then compared with aligned realized P&L in backtesting. Stress/scenario analysis probes shocks beyond historical sampling, while ES requires tail-severity methods and tests beyond VaR exception counts. These branches complement each other; one method is not prerequisite to another.
- **Claim:** Bank stress testing is designed around material exposures and scenarios, not a universal asset-class checklist or one estimator. The CBN guideline names risk-specific and dynamic scenario testing, macroeconomic and asset-category shocks, simultaneous risk effects, reverse stress tests, and links between asset-market liquidity, funding liquidity and valuation under stress. Its Nigerian scope includes oil-price, FX, rates, equity/asset-value and bank-specific shocks. A CBN-hosted study gives one bounded application: SVAR-X scenarios for oil-price shocks and bank NPLs, while stating that data did not support a capital-adequacy extension. Market microstructure/liquidity-adjusted measures are therefore relevant when the task concerns liquidity, executable depth, liquidation or funding interaction; they are not general prerequisites for credit ECL, operational-risk capital or every risk scenario. **Locator:** CBN Guideline on Stress Testing for the Nigerian Banks (March 2019), §§3.1–3.3 and 3.8–3.10, paras. 10–23 and 37–45; Odu and Sanusi (2021), CBN Economic and Financial Review 59(2), abstract; existing BOJ L-VaR and ECB market/funding-liquidity evidence; BIS WP1250 full text §§2–4 for market-specific microstructure indicators. **Sources:** D011-CBN-STRESS-GUIDELINE-2019, D011-CBN-OIL-SHOCK-STRESS-SVAR-2021, D011-BOJ-LIQUIDITY-ADJUSTED-VAR-2000, D011-ECB-MARKET-FUNDING-LIQUIDITY-2023, D011-BIS-ML-MARKET-STRESS-2025 **Area context:** This closes the traditional stress-scope question for banking risk modeling: scenarios are selected from material institution/portfolio exposures and risk interactions. It adds Nigerian banking context without making that jurisdiction universal; specific market-liquidity measures remain a conditional branch inside risk modeling. **Limit:** The CBN guideline is dated March 2019; this source confirms its published text and scope, not whether it has been amended after issue. The CBN study is abstract-level evidence, has a 2007–2020 sample and states a data limitation for capital adequacy. The BOJ and ECB evidence has jurisdiction- and model-specific scope. None supplies an exhaustive catalogue of asset-class stress algorithms or makes microstructure measures mandatory for all risk work. **Relationship:** Exposure and risk identification determine scenario variables; scenarios feed valuation, credit-loss and liquidity projections; joint market/funding stresses reveal interactions. Market depth and liquidation measures enter when a market-liquidity or liquidation task requires them. Stress outcomes then inform capital/liquidity review and management actions; the scenario design complements VaR/ES rather than replacing its estimators or validation.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Current**
- **Claim:** Current financial risk modeling is a family of connected but purpose-specific designs: market-risk measurement and validation (VaR/ES, backtesting, P&L attribution), counterparty exposure (SA-CCR or approved IMM), credit capital (IRB components), accounting ECL, margin models and forward-looking stress testing produce distinct outputs under different scopes. **Locator:** Current Basel Framework MAR32/MAR33, CRE32/CRE52/CRE53 and MAR50; Basel ECL and CCR guidelines; EBA pro-forma initial-margin model validation; Basel stress-testing guidelines. **Sources:** D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT, D011-BIS-MAR33-EXPECTED-SHORTFALL-2026, D011-BIS-CRE32-IRB-RISK-COMPONENTS-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE52-SA-CCR-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE53-IMM-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CVA-CREDIT-VALUATION-FRAMEWORK, D011-BIS-ECL-MODEL-VALIDATION-GUIDELINES-2024, D011-EBA-CENTRAL-VALIDATION-ISDA-SIMM-2026 **Area context:** This shows why the learner needs to identify the risk question and regulated/accounting context before selecting a method. Similar inputs can be reused, but the designs are not one interchangeable risk model. **Limit:** Regulatory texts establish scoped frameworks, not every firm's internal design or the complete global law. Local implementation, applicable dates, product scope and entity eligibility need separate checks. **Relationship:** Instrument, portfolio, counterparty, market and accounting inputs feed different model branches; each branch creates a named output (market capital, exposure EAD, CVA capital, initial margin, accounting allowance or stress loss). Validation/governance and limit decisions consume these outputs but should not collapse them into one measure.
- **Claim:** Quantitative financial risk is not one estimator: current banking frameworks separately use a Liquidity Coverage Ratio stress measure for short-term liquidity resilience, a standardized operational-risk capital approach using defined business and loss-data inputs, climate scenario analysis that transmits physical/transition drivers into credit, market, operational and liquidity categories, and model validation methods that compare assumptions, alternatives and outcomes. **Locator:** Current Basel LCR and OPE standards; current BCBS 2022 climate-risk principles; full 2026 US interagency model-risk guidance. The OPE version effective in 2023 is current; a different OPE25 version is scheduled for 2027. **Sources:** D011-BIS-LCR-CURRENT-2019, D011-BIS-OPE-RWA-CURRENT-2023, D011-BIS-CLIMATE-RISK-PRINCIPLES-2022, D011-FED-REVISED-MRM-GUIDANCE-2026 **Area context:** These methods cover separate risk branches and downstream objectives: cash-flow/liquidity survival, operational-risk capital, climate scenario exposure, and model reliability/appropriate use. They broaden risk modeling beyond market VaR/ES, credit PD/LGD/EAD and counterparty exposure without collapsing them into one model family. **Limit:** Basel standards are globally agreed prudential standards but have local implementation; US model-risk guidance applies to US banking organizations and is non-prescriptive. Climate methods/data are evolving, and climate scenarios are not forecasts or standalone capital models. The scheduled 2027 operational-risk version is not current. **Relationship:** Risk classification, purpose, data and institution scope come before method selection. Liquidity inputs/scenarios produce LCR-related cash-flow measures; operational loss/business-indicator data feed a distinct capital calculation; climate pathways feed scenario analysis through traditional risk types; model validation evaluates conceptual soundness, alternatives, monitoring and outcomes after development and during use.
- **Claim:** Current backtesting separates two questions: VaR hit tests evaluate exceedance frequency and temporal independence, while ES tests assess tail-loss severity or cumulative tail violations and may require the forecast tail distribution. Method families include Kupiec unconditional coverage, Christoffersen conditional coverage/independence, McNeil-Frey exceedance-residual testing, Acerbi-Szekely conditional/unconditional/quantile or minimally biased tests, and Du-Escanciano cumulative-violation tests. **Locator:** CRAN rugarch VaRTest/ESTest reference manual; Acerbi-Szekely (2014) author paper; Du and Escanciano, Management Science (2017) publisher abstract; MathWorks R2026b ES backtesting overview; Basel MAR32/MAR33. **Sources:** D011-RUGARCH-CRAN-REFERENCE-AND-TESTS-2026, D011-ACERBI-SZEKELY-ES-BACKTESTS-2014, D011-DU-ESCANCIANO-ES-BACKTEST-2017, D011-MATHWORKS-ES-BACKTEST-TEST-FAMILIES-2026, D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT, D011-BIS-MAR33-EXPECTED-SHORTFALL-2026 **Area context:** These tests apply after risk-forecast generation and address distinct validation targets. Regulatory VaR backtesting and P&L attribution under Basel MAR32 do not make ES backtesting identical to VaR testing; ES capital under MAR33 is a separate risk-measure calculation. **Limit:** ES tests can be sensitive to VaR forecast error and may depend on full conditional-tail information, finite-sample critical values or distributional assumptions. The source set includes a publisher abstract for Du-Escanciano and vendor implementation guidance; verify full formulas and test power before making method rankings. Applicability of Basel requirements depends on local transposition and model scope. **Relationship:** A conditional risk forecast first produces VaR and ES; VaR hit indicators support frequency/independence tests; ES evaluation also uses tail-loss magnitude or tail-distribution information. A VaR test should not be presented as sufficient ES validation. Method comparison should use the same portfolio P&L, horizon, confidence level, forecast window and data availability.
- **Claim:** For bank liquidity, BCBS describes dynamic cash-flow projection and gap analysis under normal and institution-specific/market-wide stress scenarios, followed by contingency funding planning. For operational-risk capital, the Basel 2023 OPE25 version uses BI, BIC and ILM to calculate ORC; the 2027 version status must be checked for later effective use. For model risk, SR 26-2 describes risk-based model development/use, testing, validation, monitoring and outcome analysis. These are distinct method/governance branches, not substitutes for market VaR/ES, credit ECL or each other. **Locator:** BCBS LQY10 sections 10.31-10.34, 10.108-10.109 and 10.123-10.125; Basel OPE25 sections 25.1-25.9, 2023 in-force record; SR 26-2 sections on testing, model use, validation and monitoring. **Sources:** D011-BIS-LIQUIDITY-MANAGEMENT-CONSOLIDATED-2026, D011-BIS-OPERATIONAL-RISK-CAPITAL-SA-2023-CURRENT, D011-FED-SR26-2-2026 **Area context:** Fills the current methods gap beyond the stronger market, credit, CCR/CVA, ECL and margin coverage already indexed. The regulatory setting is banking; liquidity techniques also depend on currency, entity, product, horizon and stress design. **Limit:** The OPE25 source is a versioned capital standard and not an end-to-end operational risk taxonomy. SR 26-2 gives supervisory principles rather than one mandated validation algorithm. BCBS guidance does not prescribe one universal cash-flow model or stress library. **Relationship:** Liquidity assumptions and position data feed projections, mismatch/gap diagnostics and stress outputs; those results inform limits and contingency funding plans. BI and loss inputs feed BIC/ILM and an operational capital result. A risk model's purpose and data then determine suitable development tests, independent challenge and outcome monitoring.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Emerging predictive risk methods combine realized-volatility targets with econometric and machine-learning forecasts, but evaluation remains horizon- and loss-function-specific; recent comparisons report multiple criteria and downstream VaR/ES or utility diagnostics rather than a single universal winner. **Locator:** Federal Reserve FEDS 2025-061r1, revised September 2026; Journal of Economic Dynamics and Control 2024 learned realized-volatility forecasting study; 2026 realized-volatility review as a secondary synthesis. **Sources:** D011-FED-REALIZED-VOL-ML-COMPARE-2025-REV2026, D011-JEF-REALIZED-VOL-ML-2024, D011-LEUSHUIS-PETKOV-REALIZED-VOL-FORECASTING-REVIEW-2026 **Area context:** This represents a research/currently emerging forecasting design within market-risk modeling. It extends volatility estimation and forecast evaluation, not a replacement for exposure, credit, liquidity or regulatory-capital frameworks. **Limit:** The FEDS paper is preliminary author research on a specified US equity sample; the JEDC paper and review do not establish production adoption or outperformance across asset classes. Model performance depends on horizon, sample, targets and evaluation metric. **Relationship:** Realized-volatility construction and time-series foundations precede forecast model comparison; temporal validation and dependence-aware evaluation precede risk use; a forecast can inform VaR/ES, limits or portfolio decisions only after calibration, forecast-error analysis and downstream validation.
- **Claim:** Emerging predictive methods need separate evaluation by target and horizon. A full-text U.S. equity study compares intraday realized-volatility prediction using ARIMA/HAR/OLS/LASSO/XGBoost/MLP/LSTM, single-stock versus pooled training and market-volatility augmentation; it also tests transfer to stocks excluded from training. A separate publisher abstract describes mixed-frequency Elastic Net quantile regression for VaR and ES with bootstrap goodness-of-fit testing.
