These are distinct: the first predicts realized volatility, while the second targets conditional loss quantiles/tails. **Locator:** Zhang et al., Journal of Financial Econometrics 22(2), 2024, full text §§2–5 and out-of-sample evaluation; Li et al., North American Journal of Economics and Finance 80 (2025), publisher abstract and indexed highlights. **Sources:** D011-OUP-ML-INTRADAY-REALIZED-VOLATILITY-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-MIXED-FREQUENCY-ML-VAR-ES-2025 **Area context:** The equity paper supports a high-frequency market-risk forecast example; the VaR/ES abstract supports a separate tail-estimation lead. Neither substitutes for stress scenario design, credit loss modeling, regulatory backtesting or model validation. **Limit:** The full-text equity results are one U.S. stock sample and cannot establish rates/FX/commodity/credit performance. The VaR/ES full text and code were access-limited, so its estimator, baselines and reported performance remain provisional pending direct inspection and replication. **Relationship:** Choose the target first: realized volatility forecasts a volatility proxy; VaR/ES methods estimate conditional loss quantiles and require tail-appropriate scoring/calibration. Compare each with matched conventional baselines using chronological, out-of-sample protocols; a successful volatility forecast is not proof of calibrated tail loss or regulatory acceptance.
- **Claim:** A distinct emerging design forecasts distributions of market-specific stress indicators rather than only conditional volatility: the BIS study constructs Treasury, USD FX and money-market indicators from microstructure, liquidity and arbitrage-dislocation inputs, then compares random-forest quantile forecasts against autoregressive and multivariate quantile-regression baselines at 3–12 month horizons. This connects microstructure-based measurement, cross-market predictors and tail-quantile forecasting; it complements realized-volatility forecasting but is not the same task or an all-purpose stress test. **Locator:** Aldasoro et al., BIS Working Paper 1250 (2025), full text §§2–3; study's MCI construction and out-of-sample quantile forecast evaluation. **Sources:** D011-BIS-ML-MARKET-STRESS-2025 **Area context:** Optional emerging design for systemic market stress monitoring and distributional forecasting in the three studied US markets; it extends market/funding-liquidity foundations and does not replace credit ECL, portfolio VaR/ES, scenario design or bank supervisory stress testing. **Limit:** Single research paper, selected US markets and 3–12 month horizons; the reported comparison does not establish deployed practice, universal model superiority or formal structural-break robustness. **Relationship:** Market variables form the indicator; rolling PCA reduces the high-dimensional inputs using past information; AR/multivariate quantile regression provide benchmarks; random-forest quantiles estimate tail conditions; Shapley diagnostics summarize predictor contributions. Those components are the study's design, not an asserted universal learner prerequisite chain.
- **Claim:** A full-text credit-portfolio study compares AI-based and non-AI approximations against Monte Carlo for total portfolio VaR, marginal counterparty risk contribution, and VaR after correlation-parameter changes. The approaches are useful where repeated full simulations are costly for pricing, stress scenarios or calibration; results vary by use case and training-data availability, and the authors report non-AI regressions can equal or outperform AI methods. A separate graph-credit study found in this bounded search predicts borrower default and tests robustness, but does not estimate aggregate portfolio tail loss. A conference graph scenario-planning prototype likewise does not meet the inspectable portfolio-risk validation bar. **Locator:** Jakob et al. (2023), Digital Finance 5, 689–716, full open-access article §§2–4; Papalamprou and Terzis (2026), publisher abstract; Zhang and Feng et al. (2025), conference paper abstract/protocol. **Sources:** D011-SPRINGER-CREDIT-PORTFOLIO-AI-APPROXIMATION-2023, D011-JRMV-GNN-CREDIT-DEFAULT-ROBUSTNESS-2026 **Area context:** Adds an optional credit-portfolio computational branch to market-risk forecasting and system-stress methods. Learned approximations can accelerate repeated portfolio computations, but the selected estimator must match whether the task is total VaR, marginal contribution or a parameter stress. Borrower classification graphs support a different credit task and should not be displayed as portfolio-tail estimators. **Limit:** The credit-portfolio comparison is a simulation study and does not establish universal AI superiority, regulatory acceptance or production deployment. The graph-credit source is abstract-level and concerns borrower classification. No inspected graph/generative source met the stated evidence bar for aggregate VaR/ES or system-stress forecasting, so that candidate family remains bounded and unpromoted. **Relationship:** Credit-portfolio loss model and correlation assumptions -> Monte Carlo/reference loss distribution -> selected AI or non-AI approximation -> total VaR, counterparty marginal contribution or stressed VaR -> error/runtime comparison against the reference. Graph-based borrower default prediction is an upstream PD input only when its data and task justify the graph; it is not a direct substitute for portfolio loss aggregation or tail measurement.
- **Claim:** In credit-risk explainability, a separate method question follows prediction: if applicant features are dependent, standard Kernel-SHAP's independent-feature treatment can produce misleading attributions. A 2024 Lending Club P2P case compares methods for estimating feature dependence and reports improved explanation robustness when dependence is accounted for. This is a post-hoc explanation design; it does not improve or validate default prediction by itself. **Locator:** Famà et al. (2024), Statistics 58(5), publisher abstract and University of Bergamo repository record; related 2023 CLADAG proceeding abstract by Babaei, Pagnottoni and Do. **Sources:** D011-UNIBG-DEPENDENT-KERNEL-SHAP-CREDIT-2024, D011-TF-DEPENDENT-SHAP-CREDIT-2024 **Area context:** Optional emerging credit-model interpretation topic after learners understand the predictive model, feature dependence and Shapley attribution. Its P2P lending scope does not make it a universal prerequisite for market, liquidity, operational or model-risk work. **Limit:** The publisher full text is access-restricted; algorithm details, comparison metrics and replication are not established here. The abstract does not support a claim of causal interpretation, fairness, regulatory acceptance or predictive performance gain. **Relationship:** Fit and validate a credit prediction model first; then choose an attribution value function that reflects the feature dependence question. The explanation describes model behavior under its assumptions and must be evaluated separately from discrimination, calibration, fairness and lending decision review.
- **Claim:** Two credit-regime method designs answer different questions. Sequential stability tests monitor whether the drift/parameters of a structural firm-default model change, using distance-to-default-related processes as observations; a credit-threshold model instead uses credit/GDP or business/household-credit growth to forecast the probability of system financial stress. The former is a model-monitoring procedure; the latter is an early-warning forecast, not a PD model. Both complement rather than replace stable-baseline, calibration and out-of-sample checks. **Locator:** Andreou and Ghysels (2007/2008), full text §§2–4; Li and Xiao (2016), Bank of Canada paper §§2–3 and out-of-sample results. **Sources:** D011-UCY-STRUCTURAL-CREDIT-MODEL-QUALITY-CONTROL-2008, D011-BANKCANADA-CREDIT-REGIME-STRESS-2016 **Area context:** An optional credit-risk branch after structural/reduced-form model concepts, PD and distance-to-default or credit-condition measures. It adds break monitoring/systemic early warning without changing the area's market-risk, ECL, CCR/CVA or liquidity tasks. **Limit:** The structural-model paper is simulation/method evidence and its strongest optimality result has stated assumptions; the Canadian paper is one historical system-stress application. Neither establishes current adoption or universal effectiveness. **Relationship:** For firm PD, estimate asset/debt dynamics and distance to default, then monitor parameter stability as new observations arrive. For system stress, choose a credit-condition signal and threshold, estimate regime-dependent stress paths, and evaluate probabilities out of sample. These are distinct designs and outputs.
- **Claim:** Regime-aware realized-volatility methods can extend AR/HAR baselines through observed smooth transitions or latent Markov states; further variants allow transition probabilities to vary over time or variance to differ by regime. In the eight-index comparison, Markov-switching HAR with time-varying probabilities performs better at weekly/monthly horizons, while daily results do not clearly beat linear HAR. Thus method choice depends on horizon and the evaluation target rather than a universal nonlinear upgrade. **Locator:** Ding et al. (2025), full paper §§2–5 (model equations, eight-index data, out-of-sample and VaR/ES evaluations). **Sources:** D011-STIRLING-REGIME-SWITCHING-RV-RISK-2025 **Area context:** A source-inspected emerging/current research extension for market volatility and risk forecasting. It complements rather than replaces realized-volatility, GARCH, quantile, joint VaR/ES and stress-testing methods. **Limit:** Single comparative study and equity-index data; forecast gains vary by horizon. It is not a general break detector and not evidence for credit, liquidity or operational model performance. **Relationship:** HAR provides the persistent-volatility baseline; a transition function or latent Markov state allows parameters/regimes to vary; forecast tests and VaR/ES use assess the resulting outputs. Compare under a fixed horizon and evaluation protocol before choosing among the alternatives.
- **Claim:** Cross-asset evidence separates three emerging modeling questions. A full-text study directly forecasts VaR and ES jointly with stateful RNN/FNN designs and compares them to rolling, GARCH-type and GAS benchmarks across six series spanning equity indices, commodities and a currency. Separate volatility studies compare ML to HAR/linear models across global equity indices or several dataset classes; their abstracts report that nonlinear advantages vary by horizon/data and are not universal. Therefore realized-volatility forecasting and joint tail-risk forecasting are complementary but distinct tasks, and asset coverage alone does not prove generalization to credit, liquidity or operational risk. **Locator:** Qiu, Lazar and Nakata (2024), full paper §§3–5 and conclusion; Branco, Rubesam and Zevallos (2024), Journal of Empirical Finance 78 article 101524 publisher abstract/preview; TSMixer 2024 publisher abstract. **Sources:** D011-READING-QIU-LAZAR-NAKATA-JOINT-VAR-ES-RNN-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-BRANCO-RUBESAM-ZEVALLOS-HAR-CROSSMARKET-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-TSMIXER-REALIZED-VOLATILITY-2024 **Area context:** Optional emerging methods for market risk forecasting. The selected method follows the output needed: volatility, conditional VaR/ES, or market-stress indicators. These are not substitutes for credit ECL, default/recovery dependence, liquidity gap analysis, operational loss measurement or supervisory scenario design. **Limit:** One full-text joint VaR/ES paper and two abstract-level volatility comparisons; finite asset samples and differing objectives prevent pooled ranking. No independent reproduction or regime-break testing across all risk families is established. **Relationship:** Risk target and horizon determine the forecast object; historical returns and predictors feed either realized-volatility models or direct joint VaR/ES models. Forecast scoring/backtests follow estimation; portfolio or supervisory use requires separate calibration, governance and task-specific validation. Methods may be compared under a matched dataset but are not prerequisites for each other.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Future**
- **Claim:** Quantum simulation and quantum optimization are plausible future research routes for selected finance problems, including stress testing/macroeconomic analysis and asset-pricing optimization, but current sources characterize the technology as experimental and do not establish production risk-model superiority. **Locator:** BIS Paper 149 (2024), official publication page and executive summary; ESMA May 2026 quantum-finance maturity analysis as a counter-source on early-stage deployment and hardware constraints. **Sources:** D011-BIS-QUANTUM-FINANCE-OPPORTUNITIES-RISKS-2024, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026 **Area context:** Future-facing risk context is limited to quantum simulation/optimization research directions; it is a monitoring topic and should follow classical risk measures, stress/scenario design, numerical simulation and hardware-aware algorithm foundations. **Limit:** These sources do not demonstrate a quantum risk method that is currently more accurate, cheaper or deployable. The BIS paper is exploratory research; ESMA's outlook is not an exhaustive benchmark. No future date or guaranteed adoption is asserted. **Relationship:** Classical risk targets, scenarios, exposure/loss definitions and simulation baselines must be specified before comparing quantum approaches; encoding, circuit/resource estimates and error analysis are additional dependencies. Quantum-safe cryptography is a separate operational-resilience topic, not a risk estimator.
- **Claim:** Quantum Monte Carlo risk analysis is a future-facing method design that places stochastic risk-factor scenario generation inside a quantum circuit and combines it with quantum amplitude estimation (QAE) for market and credit risk quantities. The paper implements equity geometric Brownian motion, mean-reverting interest rates and structural/reduced-form/rating-migration credit examples; this addresses part of the classical bottleneck from preparing a precomputed distribution but remains a theoretical fault-tolerant-device architecture. **Locator:** Matsakos and Nield (2024), full Quantum 8, 1306 paper, especially §§1–3 and resource estimates; IBM/Woerner-Egger (2019) and Egger et al. (2021) abstracts provide earlier risk/credit examples; BIS/ESMA maturity sources provide supervisory countercontext. **Sources:** D011-QUANTUM-QMC-RISK-ANALYTICS-2024, D011-IBM-QUANTUM-RISK-ANALYSIS-2019, D011-IBM-QUANTUM-CREDIT-RISK-2021, D011-BIS-QUANTUM-FINANCE-OPPORTUNITIES-RISKS-2024, D011-ESMA-QUANTUM-FINANCIAL-MARKETS-2026 **Area context:** This is an advanced computational-risk research direction after classical stochastic models, portfolio loss construction, Monte Carlo, VaR/ES and QAE foundations. It integrates two required components—scenario generation and probability/risk-measure estimation—rather than simply replacing Monte Carlo with a quantum sampler. **Limit:** The 2024 paper assumes fault-tolerant circuits and ignores quantum errors; it estimates up to about 1,200 qubits and circuit depth on the order of 10^8, and says available hardware was years from production systems. Its circuit calculations ran on a classical zero-noise Qiskit simulator. No realized end-to-end speed, cost or decision-quality advantage is demonstrated; IBM records are abstract-only in this review. **Relationship:** The classical baseline defines risk factors, portfolio mapping, loss function and target statistic. QMC circuit state preparation encodes risk-factor evolution and scenario probabilities; QAE estimates a probability/expectation or tail quantity. Circuit depth, qubit count, discretization, state preparation and noise must be included in comparison with optimized classical Monte Carlo. Independent validation and regulatory governance precede any capital or limit use.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Variance-covariance, historical simulation and Monte Carlo are distinct established approaches named in the current US market-risk rule for covered institutions. They differ in how risk-factor variation and portfolio revaluation produce the VaR measure and must be selected and validated against the portfolio’s risk profile. **Locator:** 12 CFR §217.203(6), 2026 annual edition, names variance-covariance, historical simulation and Monte Carlo; §§217.203(d), 217.204–217.205 add validation, VaR and backtesting conditions. The current CFR codifies long-established method families; it does not provide a comparative accuracy ranking. **Sources:** D011-US-CFR-2026-217-203-MARKET-RISK-APPROACHES, D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT **Area context:** These form a core market-risk measurement branch in quantitative financial risk work; the method output is a loss quantile/VaR measure for a stated horizon/confidence, feeding but remaining distinct from regulatory capital and risk governance. **Limit:** The CFR scope is US Board-regulated institutions and applicable portfolios; Basel MAR32 implementation depends on local transposition. Historical simulation and Monte Carlo are not interchangeable with parametric assumptions, and VaR is not tail-severity ES. **Relationship:** Risk-factor data and valuation/revaluation feed the estimator; realized P&L supports backtesting; stress scenarios complement the statistical measure; ES capital under Basel MAR33 is a distinct tail measure and MAR32 VaR/PLA tests have a different validation purpose.
- **Claim:** Two distinct tail-estimation branches fill gaps left by a generic VaR-family list. CAViaR models a time-varying conditional VaR quantile directly with regression quantiles and provides a dynamic-quantile specification test. McNeil-Frey instead estimates conditional volatility with GARCH, applies EVT threshold methods to standardized residual tails, and derives conditional VaR and ES; its study also compares simulated multi-day risk with naive square-root-of-time scaling. CAViaR is a direct-quantile alternative; GARCH-EVT composes volatility and tail-distribution stages. **Locator:** Engle and Manganelli (2004), sections 2–6 and named CAViaR specifications/DQ test; McNeil and Frey (2000), sections 2–4 on GARCH filtering, EVT residual tails, backtesting and multi-day Monte Carlo forecasts. **Sources:** D011-ENGLE-MANGANELLI-CAVIAR-2004, D011-MCNEIL-FREY-GARCH-EVT-2000 **Area context:** These are market-loss tail-estimation techniques that follow portfolio P&L/risk-factor construction and precede forecast backtesting. They complement variance-covariance, historical simulation and Monte Carlo frameworks, but produce conditional quantile/tail estimates under different assumptions. **Limit:** Both are primary historical method papers with sample-specific empirical evidence. CAViaR forecasts VaR, not ES by itself; GARCH-EVT depends on volatility-filter adequacy, residual-tail assumptions and threshold choice. The multi-day scaling result is limited to McNeil-Frey's study and does not establish a universal correction or ranking. **Relationship:** CAViaR estimates the conditional quantile directly rather than requiring a full conditional distribution; the DQ test checks dynamic quantile adequacy. GARCH-EVT estimates conditional volatility first, then models residual extremes and can produce VaR/ES. Multi-day forecasts require an explicit horizon model; square-root-of-time scaling is an assumption to test, not an automatic dependency. VaR/ES outputs must then be evaluated with risk-measure-appropriate backtests.
- **Claim:** Primary comparison studies show that method rankings depend on asset sample, forecast horizon, backtest and scoring design. Le (2020) compares 12 VaR/ES models across 43 international indices and 1-, 5- and 10-day horizons, including historical simulation, GARCH-filtered simulation, CAViaR and EVT; its abstract reports MIDAS quantile approaches performing particularly well at longer horizons. Calmon et al. (2021) compare CAViaR, EVT, filtered historical simulation and time-varying higher conditional moments on 80 assets plus Monte Carlo, reporting EVT and FHS among the strongest most often. These results do not support one universal winner. **Locator:** Le (2020), publisher article page/full abstract, design and benchmark paragraphs; Calmon et al. (2021), Wiley publisher metadata and abstract. The latter full text was access-restricted. **Sources:** D011-LE-MIDAS-VAR-ES-COMPARISON-2020, D011-CALMON-ESTABLISHED-VAR-COMPARISON-2021 **Area context:** These are comparative market-risk forecasts using equity-index returns; they help learners understand how to compare method families at specified horizons and distinguish VaR from joint VaR/ES evaluation. They do not cover credit, liquidity, operational risk or all nonlinear portfolios. **Limit:** The 2020 article's detailed tables/code were not independently reproduced; the 2021 full paper was inaccessible, so its sample construction and exact test configurations remain unverified here. Both reported rankings are study-specific and may not transfer to other products, portfolios, regimes, confidence levels or data access conditions. **Relationship:** Choose a target risk measure and forecast horizon, hold portfolio/sample and evaluation windows consistent, then compare forecast calibration/backtests and scoring losses. Direct multi-horizon quantile models, one-day conditional-volatility forecasts, EVT and resampled FHS make different horizon assumptions; compare them under the same evaluation rather than treating one as a prerequisite or default winner.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Current**
- **Claim:** The 2026 U.S. market-risk rule recognizes variance-covariance, historical-simulation and Monte Carlo approaches as options for covered institutions' market-risk models; it does not rank them or make them interchangeable. **Locator:** 12 CFR §217.203(6), 2026 annual edition; paired provisions in §§217.203(d), 217.204(b) and 217.205 cover validation, backtesting and the VaR measure. **Sources:** D011-US-CFR-2026-217-203-MARKET-RISK-APPROACHES **Area context:** Quantitative Financial Risk Modeling: these are estimator alternatives for market-risk portfolios, selected against covered positions, material risks, data and nonlinear exposures. **Limit:** United States Board-regulated institution scope only; legal permission is not evidence of suitability for every portfolio or proof of relative accuracy. Other jurisdictional and firm requirements may differ. **Relationship:** Risk-factor and valuation/sensitivity inputs feed each approach; realized P&L and independent outcomes testing are downstream validation, not another estimator choice. Stress testing complements model measures for risks the models may miss.
- **Claim:** Basel market-risk capital uses expected shortfall under MAR33, while MAR32 prescribes VaR backtesting and P&L attribution as components of internal-model eligibility and validation. **Locator:** Current Basel Framework MAR32 §§32.1–32.5, 32.16–32.21 and 32.34–32.41; MAR33 §§33.1 onward. BIS chapter index identifies MAR32 and MAR33 as current, effective 1 January 2023. **Sources:** D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT, D011-BIS-MAR33-EXPECTED-SHORTFALL-2026 **Area context:** This is the bank prudential-capital context within financial risk modeling; it is not a universal forecasting loss or a generic investment-strategy backtest. **Limit:** Basel implementation depends on local transposition. Regulatory capital ES, VaR backtesting and PLA have related but different objectives and outputs. **Relationship:** The capital measure and validation tests consume portfolio valuation/P&L and model outputs; they do not replace measurement-method selection or firm-level model-risk governance.
- **Claim:** For in-scope EU non-cleared OTC derivatives, initial margin can be calculated by a standardised grid or an authorised model; the current pro forma model identified by EBA is ISDA SIMM. **Locator:** EBA Validation of pro forma initial margin models page (opened 2026-10-24); ISDA SIMM methodology v2.7+2412 effective 12 July 2025. **Sources:** D011-EBA-CENTRAL-VALIDATION-ISDA-SIMM-2026, D011-ISDA-SIMM-METHODOLOGY-V2-7-2025 **Area context:** SIMM is a distinct initial-margin technique for specified uncleared-derivative exposure; it is neither derivative fair-value pricing nor the Basel market-risk capital measure. **Limit:** EU/jurisdiction, counterparty and product scope applies. ISDA methodology is licensed; current entity thresholds and authorisation requirements must be checked in law. Do not infer a universal role requirement. **Relationship:** Pricing models may supply sensitivities, which SIMM maps and aggregates; margin output supports collateral exchange. It sits downstream of instrument, sensitivity and portfolio foundations and has a standardised-grid alternative where permitted.
- **Claim:** Basel's IRB approach estimates credit-risk components including PD, LGD, EAD and maturity, while the Foundation and Advanced IRB approaches differ in which LGD parameters the bank may estimate; for derivatives counterparty credit risk, SA-CCR produces EAD from replacement cost plus PFE, and IMM is a supervisory-approved alternative. **Locator:** Current Basel Framework CRE32 (effective 2023-01-01), especially §§32.1–32.5; CRE52 §§52.1–52.3 and 52.20 onward; CRE53 §§53.1–53.5 and 53.42–53.59. Basel 2024 CCR guidelines §§40.1 onward describe exposure/credit-quality interaction and management dimensions. Do not substitute forthcoming CRE32 text effective 2028-11-01 for the current chapter. **Sources:** D011-BIS-CRE32-IRB-RISK-COMPONENTS-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE52-SA-CCR-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE53-IMM-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CCR-MANAGEMENT-GUIDELINES-2024 **Area context:** Adds the credit-risk and derivatives counterparty branch to quantitative financial risk modeling: borrower/facility risk components feed regulatory capital calculations, while CCR models estimate current/future exposure profiles for derivatives and related transactions. **Limit:** These are Basel prudential frameworks whose legal effect depends on national adoption and scope. PD/LGD/EAD for regulatory capital are not the same as IFRS 9 expected-credit-loss estimates, fair value, CVA valuation, or a universally applicable credit score. SA-CCR versus IMM choice is constrained by transaction scope and approval. **Relationship:** IRB PD/LGD/EAD/maturity estimates feed risk weights and expected-loss components. SA-CCR's replacement-cost and PFE components combine into regulatory EAD; approved IMM generates an exposure distribution from which EPE and other management measures can be derived. CCR management adds stress, wrong-way-risk and counterparty-credit-quality analysis; these complement the regulatory exposure number rather than replace it.
- **Claim:** Accounting expected-credit-loss measurement is a distinct modelling output: IFRS 9's core requirement is summarized by IFRIC as unbiased probability-weighted expected cash shortfalls, discounted for time value and informed by reasonable, supportable forward-looking information; supervisory guidance describes coherent macroeconomic, PD, EAD and LGD component models and calls for model validation. **Locator:** Official IFRIC Update March 2022 summary of IFRS 9 §5.5.17; current Basel consolidated ECL guidelines §§20.47–20.48. IFRS Foundation standard PDF was attempted but required a subscription, so detailed standard clauses were not inspected. **Sources:** D011-IFRIC-IFRS9-ECL-5-5-17-2022, D011-BIS-ECL-MODEL-VALIDATION-GUIDELINES-2024, D011-IFRS9-ECL-STANDARD-ACCESS-LIMIT-2022 **Area context:** This is the accounting-loss forecasting branch of quantitative financial risk work, useful for expected allowance estimation and model validation. It shares credit data and risk components with regulatory-capital or stress models but targets a different accounting measure. **Limit:** The official IFRIC summary is a focused interpretive update, and the full IFRS 9 standard was inaccessible in this pass. Do not infer complete staging/measurement rules from it. Basel ECL guidelines are supervisory guidance and do not make accounting ECL equal to Basel IRB regulatory EL, CVA, or VaR/ES. **Relationship:** Macroeconomic scenarios and borrower/exposure models may feed a probability-weighted cash-shortfall calculation; PD, EAD and LGD components must be coherent across common inputs. Validation tests component and aggregate outputs. The same components can also inform prudential or stress analysis, but their horizon, calibration and objective must be specified for each use.
- **Claim:** Regulatory CVA risk capital is a separate branch from counterparty exposure and derivative fair-value valuation: Basel MAR50 provides BA-CVA, permits SA-CVA subject to supervisory approval, and defines SA-CVA sensitivities to counterparty spreads and market-risk factors as inputs. SA-CCR and approved IMM instead produce counterparty exposure/EAD measures. **Locator:** Current Basel Framework MAR50.3 and 50.9–50.11, version effective 1 January 2023; CRE52/CRE53 and Basel CCR Management Guidelines, opened 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-BIS-CVA-CREDIT-VALUATION-FRAMEWORK, D011-BIS-CRE52-SA-CCR-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CRE53-IMM-CURRENT, D011-BIS-CCR-MANAGEMENT-GUIDELINES-2024 **Area context:** This adds the derivatives-counterparty/CVA branch to current quantitative risk methods and makes three student-facing outputs legible: CVA valuation adjustment, CVA-risk capital, and CCR exposure/EAD. They are connected but are not synonyms or substitutes. **Limit:** Basel text is subject to jurisdictional adoption and specified entity/transaction scope. MAR50 is not a full accounting-CVA model manual; this mapping does not establish local adoption or a universal valuation convention. **Relationship:** Derivative pricing and exposure profiles feed CVA valuation; counterparty spreads and market-factor sensitivities feed regulatory CVA capital; SA-CCR or approved IMM estimates CCR exposure. Credit curves and exposure models may be shared inputs, but their outputs and objectives must remain separate.
- **Claim:** Credit dependence models must distinguish dependence among defaults from dependence between default and loss severity. The reviewed sources include structural/reduced-form default models, factor/copula portfolio aggregation, and empirical evidence that default and recovery processes can co-move; one model explicitly allows dependence across PD, LGD and EAD. This broadens the documented alternatives and identifies when an independence assumption may distort portfolio-loss tails, without establishing a universally superior family. **Locator:** Bade, Rösch and Scheule, European Financial Management 17(1), 2011, publisher abstract; Eckert, Jakob and Fischer, Journal of Credit Risk, abstract; Lee and Yang, International Review of Financial Analysis 66 (2019), publisher abstract; existing Fed credit-model comparison and BIS credit-risk framework sources. **Sources:** D011-WILEY-DEFAULT-RECOVERY-DEPENDENCE-2011, D011-FREY-MCNEIL-DEPENDENT-CREDIT-PORTFOLIOS-2002, D011-FED-CREDIT-MODEL-COMPARATIVE-ANATOMY-1999, D011-SPRINGER-COPULA-CREDIT-PORTFOLIO-MODELING-2015 **Area context:** These alternatives belong in credit portfolio risk where defaults, recoveries, exposures, concentration or sector spillovers shape aggregate loss and tail capital. They are not substitutes for IFRS 9 staging/ECL, CCR exposure simulation, or market VaR/ES. **Limit:** Some records are abstracts or hypothetical portfolios; data, estimation and validation differ. The evidence supports modeling the dependence question and comparing assumptions, not a head-to-head winner. IFRS 9 full text remains access-limited; accounting boundaries rely on official IFRIC/OSFI evidence. **Relationship:** Credit exposure and default/recovery data feed the selected joint or conditional model; dependence assumptions affect loss distribution and portfolio tail measures. Compare results under plausible recovery/default dependence and validate with portfolio-relevant observations; accounting ECL and regulatory/economic capital retain their own purposes and definitions.
- **Claim:** The historical primary literature documents CAViaR and GARCH-EVT as concrete alternatives to basic parametric and rolling historical VaR, while current Basel MAR32/MAR33 separately specifies bank internal-model backtesting/P&L attribution and expected-shortfall capital. The historical estimator papers explain method mechanics; they do not establish that these exact methods satisfy current regulatory eligibility or are commonly deployed today. **Locator:** Engle and Manganelli (2004), sections 2–5; McNeil and Frey (2000), sections 2–4; current Basel MAR32 and MAR33 chapters. **Sources:** D011-ENGLE-MANGANELLI-CAVIAR-2004, D011-MCNEIL-FREY-GARCH-EVT-2000, D011-BIS-MAR32-BACKTESTING-PLA-CURRENT, D011-BIS-MAR33-EXPECTED-SHORTFALL-2026 **Area context:** Useful as technical method alternatives and comparison baselines within market-risk modeling. A learner should distinguish method capability from current supervisory acceptance, local implementation and firm-specific use. **Limit:** The two research papers date to 2000 and 2004 and use their own historical datasets. Basel requirements are scoped to bank regulatory capital and local transposition. No adoption-frequency or current-production claim is made. **Relationship:** Select a risk measure and portfolio/horizon first; select and estimate a tail method next; evaluate VaR and ES forecasts with suitable diagnostics; separately test applicable Basel/internal governance requirements. Historical performance papers are not regulatory approval evidence.
- **Claim:** Current comparison evidence does not yield a single tail-estimation winner: one primary study reports MIDAS quantile VaR/ES methods performing especially well at multi-day horizons against historical simulation, GARCH/FHS, CAViaR and EVT benchmarks, while a second peer-reviewed comparison reports EVT and FHS performing best most often among CAViaR, EVT, FHS and time-varying higher-moment models. The studies differ in sample, horizon, models and evaluation; retain those conditions when presenting their results. **Locator:** Le (2020), 43 international indices/1-, 5- and 10-day OOS comparisons; Calmon et al. (2021), 80 assets and Monte Carlo comparison. Publisher abstracts inspected. **Sources:** D011-LE-MIDAS-VAR-ES-COMPARISON-2020, D011-CALMON-ESTABLISHED-VAR-COMPARISON-2021 **Area context:** This provides comparative evidence for choosing among current implemented statistical risk-forecasting approaches. It does not establish industrial prevalence, universal model superiority, or conclusions for other risk families. **Limit:** One publisher abstract contains detailed design and reported findings; the other full text was inaccessible. Exact test construction and results are not independently recomputed. Treat both as bounded peer-reviewed study evidence, not operational recommendations. **Relationship:** A selected estimator generates a risk forecast; backtests and consistent loss functions assess calibration and relative predictive accuracy. Horizon-specific direct estimation can complement or outperform naive scaling in some samples, but method choice remains conditional on portfolio, horizon, available data and validation protocol.
- **Claim:** For large dependent credit portfolios, dependence between obligors drives the tail of aggregate credit losses. Frey and McNeil express CreditMetrics, KMV and CreditRisk+ as Bernoulli-mixture models to compare loss-tail VaR and ES, and show why VaR's non-subadditivity can produce misleading aggregation/portfolio-optimisation results for skewed credit losses. This is a distinct technique branch from market-return VaR forecasting. **Locator:** Frey and McNeil (2002), full paper sections 2–3 and abstract; 15-page author-hosted manuscript inspected. **Sources:** D011-FREY-MCNEIL-DEPENDENT-CREDIT-PORTFOLIOS-2002 **Area context:** Applies to portfolio credit-loss aggregation where default dependence and skewness determine tail risk; it supports separating credit portfolio loss models from equity/market VaR estimators and motivates considering ES where aggregation coherence matters. **Limit:** The paper analyzes stylized large balanced/homogeneous portfolios and named historical industry-model formulations. It does not establish the correct copula/dependence model for a real portfolio, current market adoption or a complete modern credit-risk implementation. **Relationship:** Exposure/default inputs and obligor dependence feed a portfolio-loss distribution; quantiles and tail expectations produce VaR/ES. Dependence assumptions affect diversification and tail aggregation; outputs inform portfolio risk/capital decisions and must be challenged with alternative dependence and concentration scenarios.
- **Claim:** Counterparty credit risk is bilateral and combines future exposure with counterparty credit quality; correlations between exposure, credit spreads and market factors create wrong-way risk. Federal Reserve-hosted interagency guidance separates exposure metrics/aggregation, stress testing, CVA fair-value adjustment and CVA VaR, and calls for netting/margin, model validation and backtesting. CVA valuation is not SA-CCR/IMM exposure, accounting ECL or market-risk VaR. **Locator:** Interagency Supervisory Guidance SR 11-10 (2011), introduction and sections III.1–6, IV–V, especially CVA §§5 and wrong-way risk §6. **Sources:** D011-FED-INTERAGENCY-CCR-GUIDANCE-2011 **Area context:** Provides the method/context distinction for derivatives CCR: future exposure, counterparty credit, CVA valuation and CVA market-risk capital form related but separate model tasks. It complements Basel SA-CCR/IMM and CVA capital sources already indexed. **Limit:** U.S. banking supervisory guidance issued in 2011, not a current global formula or universal rule. It establishes supervisory concepts and practices, not every modern implementation detail; confirm applicable current jurisdictional rules. **Relationship:** Trade/market factors and netting/collateral terms generate future exposure profiles; counterparty credit inputs and exposure-credit dependence feed CVA and wrong-way stress; CVA risk estimates and backtests feed limits/hedging/model governance. Each output needs its own model validation and scope.
- **Claim:** Credit-portfolio models encode default and dependence differently. Gordy's Fed comparison explains how CreditMetrics and CreditRisk+ differ in functional form, distributional assumptions and approximations; the open Fischer–Jakob chapter compares rating-migration/latent-asset CreditMetrics with actuarial factor-based CreditRisk+ and evaluates Gaussian, t, generalized-hyperbolic, Archimedean and vine-copula alternatives. A 2026 publisher record signals robust Bernoulli-mixture methods for parameter/copula ambiguity, but only abstract/indexed text was inspected. **Locator:** Gordy, FEDS 1999-28, abstract and full paper; Fischer and Jakob (2015), open chapter sections comparing model structures, dependence families and portfolio-loss results; Ansari (2026), Wiley abstract/indexed record only. **Sources:** D011-FED-CREDIT-MODEL-COMPARATIVE-ANATOMY-1999, D011-SPRINGER-COPULA-CREDIT-PORTFOLIO-MODELING-2015, D011-ANSARI-ROBUST-BERNOULLI-MIXTURE-CREDIT-2026, D011-FREY-MCNEIL-DEPENDENT-CREDIT-PORTFOLIOS-2002 **Area context:** This is a portfolio-credit-loss modeling branch: obligor defaults, exposures, recovery/loss assumptions and dependence generate an aggregate loss distribution for tail-risk or economic-capital analysis. It is distinct from market-return VaR, IFRS 9 allowance estimation and counterparty exposure/CVA, even when data or risk components overlap. **Limit:** The Fed paper is dated working research; the Springer chapter's numerical illustration uses a hypothetical portfolio, finite historical PD samples and deterministic LGD, and its comparisons do not establish a universal best copula. The Wiley 2026 source was not available as full text. Model choice, calibration and validation remain portfolio-, horizon- and purpose-specific. **Relationship:** CreditMetrics and CreditRisk+ are alternative model architectures; dependence families are alternatives within a portfolio model, not prerequisites to taking every branch. Exposure/default inputs and dependence assumptions precede loss-distribution estimation; sensitivity and backtesting/benchmarking outputs inform capital or portfolio decisions. The 2026 robust-model signal motivates uncertainty analysis but is not yet a selectable established method claim.
- **Claim:** Credit-model selection depends on the decision and accounting/prudential context. IFRS 9 ECL implementation can use loss-rate, PD/LGD or other portfolio-appropriate methods with documented inputs, forward-looking scenarios, backtesting and independent validation; these produce accounting impairment allowances, not IRB capital. Within credit analysis, structural models connect firm asset value and default boundaries, while reduced-form models represent default timing/intensity; PD, LGD, exposure, rating migration and credit-spread curves support different model outputs. **Locator:** OSFI IFRS 9 guideline (revised April 2022), principles 1–6, §§58–60 and 91–97; IFRIC Update March 2022 summary of IFRS 9 §5.5.17; CFA Institute 2026 Credit Analysis Models reading overview; BIS Working Paper 160 (2004), theoretical framework and bond/CDS spread comparison; OSFI IRB implementation note (2026), PD/LGD/EAD quantification sections. **Sources:** D011-OSFI-IFRS9-ECL-GUIDELINE-2022, D011-IFRIC-IFRS9-ECL-5-5-17-2022, D011-CFA-CREDIT-ANALYSIS-MODELS-2026, D011-BIS-CREDIT-SPREAD-STRUCTURAL-REDUCED-FORM-2004, D011-OSFI-IRB-RISK-QUANTIFICATION-2026, D011-BIS-ECL-MODEL-VALIDATION-GUIDELINES-2024 **Area context:** This credit branch serves distinct accounting impairment, prudential capital and valuation/pricing tasks. It supplies model alternatives after the learner understands credit events, cash shortfalls, exposure and portfolio context; no single method is compulsory for every credit portfolio or institution. **Limit:** The full IFRS 9 standard was not accessible in this pass; the claim uses the official IFRIC summary and full OSFI guidance, which is Canadian supervisory guidance and does not replace the standard or other jurisdictions' rules. CFA's 2026 reading page is a curriculum overview, not the full licensed chapter. The BIS paper is historical empirical research; OSFI IRB guidance is jurisdiction- and implementation-scoped. **Relationship:** Exposure type, accounting basis, available data and decision determine whether the task estimates accounting ECL, IRB capital components, structural/reduced-form default risk or a fair-value credit adjustment. Method assumptions and inputs precede calibration and model validation; outputs should remain labeled by purpose and not substituted across branches.
- **Claim:** Market-liquidity risk and bank funding-liquidity risk are distinct but interacting questions. Liquidity-adjusted VaR (L-VaR) models the loss while liquidating a position, including the investor's own market impact, position size and an optimal liquidation strategy; the BOJ paper describes extensions for uncertain impact, multiple assets and nonlinear impact-volume relations. Funding-liquidity analysis instead forecasts cash inflows/outflows, assets, commitments and net funding shortfalls across horizons and stress scenarios. ECB analysis documents feedback between the two, but does not make their measures interchangeable. **Locator:** Hisata and Yamai (2000), official BOJ abstract, inspected 2026-10-26; BIS Basel Consolidated Guidelines, liquidity measurement §§10.31–10.32; ECB Financial Stability Review, May 2023, sections 1–2 and 4. **Sources:** D011-BOJ-LIQUIDITY-ADJUSTED-VAR-2000, D011-BIS-LIQUIDITY-MANAGEMENT-CONSOLIDATED-2026, D011-ECB-MARKET-FUNDING-LIQUIDITY-2023 **Area context:** Use L-VaR and liquidation/market-impact models when the question concerns the cost and loss of exiting a position under limited market depth; use cash-flow gap and stress methods for an entity's ability to meet funding needs. Their interaction matters in systemic or margin stress, and measurement choice follows the exposure and decision. **Limit:** The BOJ framework is historical research and the abstract does not establish a universal estimator or adoption. Basel cash-flow guidance is banking supervision; ECB indicators and empirical analysis are euro-area/system-level. No single measure captures every dimension of market liquidity, and jurisdictional requirements vary. **Relationship:** Position, market depth, trading volume and impact assumptions feed liquidation strategy and L-VaR; balance-sheet cash flows, contingent commitments and stress assumptions feed funding gaps and contingency decisions. Margin/haircut or dealer-capacity shocks can link the channels, but the model outputs remain separate.
- **Claim:** Kupiec's unconditional coverage test compares observed VaR exceedance frequency with the nominal rate; Christoffersen's conditional coverage adds whether exceptions cluster over time. For ES, the McNeil-Frey test uses VaR exceedance residuals and tests a one-sided zero-mean/iid condition; Acerbi-Szekely offers conditional, unconditional and quantile tests, with later minimally biased variants; Du-Escanciano uses cumulative violations. These test different forecast properties and require different information. **Locator:** CRAN rugarch 1.5-6 functions VaRTest and ESTest; MathWorks R2026b test-family overview; Acerbi-Szekely 2014 paper; Du-Escanciano 2017 Management Science abstract. **Sources:** D011-RUGARCH-CRAN-REFERENCE-AND-TESTS-2026, D011-MATHWORKS-ES-BACKTEST-TEST-FAMILIES-2026, D011-ACERBI-SZEKELY-ES-BACKTESTS-2014, D011-DU-ESCANCIANO-ES-BACKTEST-2017 **Area context:** The technique choices follow the risk measure being evaluated: hit-only VaR forecasts permit exception-count/independence tests; ES needs assessment of tail severity, often conditional on VaR hits and on modeled tail probabilities. **Limit:** A test's null/alternative, sample size and assumptions determine interpretation. Rugarch documents the McNeil-Frey test's iid excess-shortfall residual assumption; Acerbi-Szekely and other ES tests are sensitive to VaR accuracy. A passing test is not proof of correct model structure or future performance. **Relationship:** Risk model specification and out-of-sample VaR/ES forecasts precede backtesting. VaR exceptions provide hit indicators; exceedance residuals or tail-distribution draws supply ES severity information. Backtest diagnostics feed model review, but test selection and Basel regulatory approval are separate decisions.
- **Claim:** Liquidity gap analysis compares projected inflows/outflows and cumulative net surpluses or shortfalls under explicit behavioral assumptions; stress design distinguishes short-term/protracted and institution-specific/market-wide shocks. Basel operational capital calculations apply the version-specific BI/BIC/ILM construction. Model testing can compare out-of-sample/out-of-time outcomes, alternative assumptions/methods and input-data quality, with validation intensity tailored to model use/materiality. **Locator:** BCBS LQY10 sections 10.31-10.34, 10.54 and 10.108-10.109; Basel OPE25 sections 25.1-25.9; SR 26-2 model testing and validation sections. **Sources:** D011-BIS-LIQUIDITY-MANAGEMENT-CONSOLIDATED-2026, D011-BIS-OPERATIONAL-RISK-CAPITAL-SA-2023-CURRENT, D011-FED-SR26-2-2026 **Area context:** These named techniques add liquidity, operational-capital and model-validation procedures to the market-risk estimators already mapped. Their choice follows the exposure and intended decision, not a universal progression through every technique. **Limit:** The source documents establish supervisory descriptions, not comparative performance. Basel version and local adoption matter; SR 26-2 is not prescriptive and does not validate every model automatically. **Relationship:** Position data and behavioral assumptions precede horizon cash-flow projections and scenario analysis; those produce gap/stress diagnostics for funding actions. Capital calculations use defined BI/loss inputs to produce ORC/RWA. Model outcome tests compare forecasts/results with relevant observations and feed review, recalibration or restricted use.
- **Claim:** Maintained software shows how current risk techniques are implemented, while leaving model choice separate. ORE documents historical/Monte Carlo/semi- and fully parametric/hybrid VaR plus exposure simulation, XVA, sensitivities, stress and selected SA/BA-CCR calculations; its example connects market shocks to exposure simulation, XVA sensitivity, SA-CVA and BA-CVA/SA-CCR EAD. MathWorks documents PD/EAD/LGD and ECL modeling, credit portfolio analysis, VaR/ES and backtesting/validation metrics. SAS OpRisk VaR 6.1 documents frequency/severity fitting, dependence choices, goodness-of-fit, KRI inputs and simulation VaR for operational loss distributions. These are task-specific software implementations, not mutually exclusive estimators or proof of superior performance. **Locator:** ORE methodology catalogue and XVA Risk example; MathWorks Risk Management Toolbox R2026b; SAS OpRisk VaR 6.1 support page. Inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-ORE-RISK-ANALYTICS-DOCS-2026, D011-ORE-XVA-RISK-EXAMPLE-2026, D011-MATHWORKS-RISK-TOOLBOX-R2026B, D011-SAS-OPRISK-VAR-6-1-2026 **Area context:** The calculation determines the implementation: market positions and shocks can feed VaR/stress or counterparty exposure/XVA workflows; borrower inputs feed PD/LGD/EAD/ECL; operational loss/KRI histories feed frequency-severity models. This distinguishes risk technique from software product and preserves risk-family scope. **Limit:** This is capability evidence from official product documentation and examples. Vendor implementations and model choices require task-specific calibration, data governance and independent validation. SAS operational OpVaR is an internal/economic-capital modeling feature and should not be confused with the current Basel operational-risk capital formula. **Relationship:** Inputs and assumptions feed an estimator in the selected system; forecasts, exposure and scenario results are then backtested or otherwise validated before decision/report use. For CCR, SA-CCR exposure is an input to BA-CVA in the cited ORE example; it is not interchangeable with CVA sensitivities or market VaR.
- **Scope limits:** Seek independent and portfolio-specific comparisons/replications of credit dependence models beyond the indexed Bernoulli-mixture paper, the Fed's historical model comparison and the Springer chapter's hypothetical default-only illustration. Compare assumptions, calibration data, concentration, recovery variability, tail outputs and validation; do not claim a universal model-family winner. The IFRS 9 full text remains access-limited, so retain the official IFRIC/OSFI source boundary rather than claiming direct standard review.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Emerging**
- **Claim:** A source-supported emerging estimator family forecasts realized volatility by extending classical HAR/long-memory/time-series baselines with threshold, smooth-transition or Markov-switching dynamics and comparing them with XGBoost and neural networks. The reviewed evidence makes the machine-learning methods competitors/extensions within the same forecasting problem, not replacements for the risk target, data design or econometric baselines. **Locator:** Federal Reserve FEDS 2025-061r1 (revised September 2026), abstract and official methods/results summary; Branco, Rubesam and Zevallos, Journal of Empirical Finance (2024), publisher abstract; Leushuis and Petkov (2026) review indexed as secondary context. **Sources:** D011-FED-REALIZED-VOL-ML-COMPARE-2025-REV2026, D011-JEF-REALIZED-VOL-ML-2024, D011-LEUSHUIS-PETKOV-REALIZED-VOL-FORECASTING-REVIEW-2026 **Area context:** Applies to the market-volatility forecasting branch of quantitative risk. Models use past realized-volatility and, in an extended information set, selected predictors; estimation must preserve chronological evaluation and horizon-specific objectives. This is a current research frontier, not a required method for every risk specialty. **Limit:** Federal Reserve FEDS research is preliminary author work and its main universe is US equities; the 2024 peer-reviewed comparison covers ten global stock indices. Results are horizon- and loss-dependent and do not establish a universal ML advantage or adoption. The secondary review is synthesis, not independent replication. **Relationship:** High-frequency returns and realized-volatility construction precede HAR/ARFIMA/regime baselines; ML then tests whether nonlinear or high-dimensional predictors add value. Chronological validation, MSFE/MAE/QLIKE, Model Confidence Sets/Diebold–Mariano comparisons and economic utility precede translating a forecast into filtered-historical-simulation VaR/ES. VaR/ES backtesting is a downstream tail-risk validation step, not the same task as volatility-forecast accuracy.
- **Claim:** Two emerging estimation examples should not be conflated. The OUP study uses pooled high-frequency predictors with market realized volatility and tests ARIMA/HAR, regularized linear, boosted-tree and neural estimators, including held-out-stock transfer. The Elsevier abstract describes mixed-frequency Elastic Net quantile regression plus a bootstrap goodness-of-fit test to forecast VaR and ES. The first estimates realized volatility; the second targets joint tail-risk measures. **Locator:** OUP full article, methods and forecast-evaluation sections; Elsevier publisher abstract/highlights for Li et al. (2025). **Sources:** D011-OUP-ML-INTRADAY-REALIZED-VOLATILITY-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-MIXED-FREQUENCY-ML-VAR-ES-2025 **Area context:** These are optional research techniques for market-risk forecasting and tail estimation. Their placement depends on available high-frequency/mixed-frequency data and the actual loss forecast being evaluated. **Limit:** The OUP empirical scope is 100 liquid U.S. equities; the VaR/ES paper's full methods and code could not be inspected. Neither establishes universal model superiority, calibrated capital outputs or independent replication across asset classes. **Relationship:** Data alignment and leakage-safe time splits precede estimation; matched baselines and target-specific scoring follow. Realized volatility may be an input or proxy but does not replace quantile/tail-loss estimation, and the VaR/ES goodness-of-fit test does not replace regulatory validation.
- **Claim:** Random-forest quantile regression is a documented emerging estimator for the full conditional distribution of market-stress indicators: tree partitions capture nonlinearities and local predictor interactions, while quantile loss evaluates forecasted tails. In the BIS study, the method is compared with AR and multivariate quantile-regression benchmarks; Shapley values are a post-estimation predictor-contribution diagnostic, not a causal estimator or a risk forecast. **Locator:** Aldasoro et al., BIS Working Paper 1250 (2025), full text §§3–4; forecast definition, benchmark comparisons, quantile-loss evaluation and Shapley analysis. **Sources:** D011-BIS-ML-MARKET-STRESS-2025 **Area context:** This supplies an emerging tail-distribution forecasting technique for the studied Treasury/FX/money-market stress indicators. It differs from realized-volatility prediction, classical VaR/ES estimation and the distribution-free meaning of stress testing; placement remains optional research-stage evidence. **Limit:** Results are sample-, indicator-, predictor- and horizon-specific. The paper reports an upper-bound example of improvement, not a stable performance guarantee; Shapley values explain model attribution under the study setup and do not validate forecast calibration or establish causality. **Relationship:** Input construction and chronological rolling estimation precede quantile-forest forecasts; quantile loss compares forecasts with observed indicators; Shapley values inspect predictor contribution after fitting. Separate forecast calibration, regime stability and institutional validation remain necessary before decision use.
- **Claim:** Named credit-specific techniques include sequential change-point monitoring for structural-model parameters (including distance-to-default/return processes), threshold regression with a credit condition triggering regime-specific system-stress dynamics, and bootstrap simulation of future stress-index paths to form event probabilities. The threshold method uses credit/GDP, business-credit or household-credit growth as alternatives; these predictors are not interchangeable with firm-level PD inputs. **Locator:** Andreou and Ghysels full text §§2–4; Li and Xiao full text §§2.2–3. **Sources:** D011-UCY-STRUCTURAL-CREDIT-MODEL-QUALITY-CONTROL-2008, D011-BANKCANADA-CREDIT-REGIME-STRESS-2016 **Area context:** Optional techniques for structural credit-model monitoring and credit-sensitive systemic-stress forecasts. They belong to different units of analysis and should be taught as separate branches. **Limit:** No common benchmark between the two studies; one is model-stability simulation and one Canadian historical early-warning application. Do not infer that threshold regression validates borrower PD, or that monitoring detects every kind of structural break. **Relationship:** Sequential tests use new return/DD observations to flag parameter instability; threshold regression uses macro-credit predictors to switch stress dynamics; bootstrap paths yield event probabilities. Each output has a separate interpretation and downstream decision.
- **Claim:** The full-text study operationalizes three useful comparison choices: smooth-transition AR/HAR, latent Markov-switching AR/HAR, and Markov-switching models with time-varying transition probability or regime-specific variance. The study forecasts realized volatility, compares fit and out-of-sample accuracy, and derives VaR/ES for economic risk evaluation. An abstract-level USD study separately reports break detection followed by break-aware GARCH VaR; it is a distinct observed-break technique, not the same as latent-state switching. **Locator:** Ding et al. (2025), full paper §§2–5; Anjum and Malik (2020), publisher abstract only. **Sources:** D011-STIRLING-REGIME-SWITCHING-RV-RISK-2025, D011-ELSEVIER-USD-STRUCTURAL-BREAK-VAR-2020 **Area context:** These estimators are optional tools when volatility persistence or regime shifts are material to market-risk forecasting. Select the break/regime representation from the data and forecast objective; do not transfer their equity/FX evidence to every risk family. **Limit:** The open full-text evidence is equity-index RV; the USD VaR result is abstract-only. No universal performance ranking, production adoption or credit/liquidity application is established. **Relationship:** A detected break, smooth transition variable or latent state feeds a model that can adjust parameters/variance over time; the output is assessed against stable baselines with chronological forecasting and VaR/ES metrics. These are alternative ways to model nonstationarity, not steps all learners must take.
- **Claim:** A named emerging tail technique is joint VaR/ES estimation with stateful recurrent and feed-forward neural networks. The inspected paper uses the FZ0 joint score, simulated GARCH data and empirical daily returns; benchmarks include rolling-window, GARCH-type and GAS methods, with multiple VaR/ES backtests. Its six-asset empirical sample includes three international equity indices, two commodities and one currency. This is a direct tail-forecast method, not merely a volatility estimator. HAR, linear, regularized, tree and neural realized-volatility estimators remain a different forecast target; available comparative evidence shows model ranking changes by horizon and dataset. **Locator:** Qiu, Lazar and Nakata (2024), full text §§3–5 and conclusion; Branco et al. (2024) and TSMixer (2024), publisher abstracts/preview for counterevidence on volatility models. **Sources:** D011-READING-QIU-LAZAR-NAKATA-JOINT-VAR-ES-RNN-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-BRANCO-RUBESAM-ZEVALLOS-HAR-CROSSMARKET-2024, D011-ELSEVIER-TSMIXER-REALIZED-VOLATILITY-2024 **Area context:** This technique belongs in optional market-tail forecasting after learners understand return distributions, VaR, ES, time-series validation and backtesting. It should not be presented as a universal risk-model replacement or validated credit/operational estimator. **Limit:** The empirical comparison is one paper, six series and its selected backtests; publisher-access limits apply to the two volatility counterexample papers. No evidence here establishes regulatory acceptance, deployment, broad cross-risk performance or superiority over every estimator. **Relationship:** Define risk horizon, tail level and forecast target first; estimate VaR and ES jointly, then assess with joint scores and backtests against econometric baselines. Volatility forecasts may inform a separate tail model but are not equivalent to joint VaR/ES; benchmark comparison and outcome validation remain necessary.
- **Claim:** Two related but distinct computational techniques extend the risk-method set. Statistical learning estimates conditional VaR and ES jointly or across multiple quantile levels using neural quantile/least-squares regressions, with heavy-tail analysis and an a-posteriori Monte Carlo distance check; its financial case concerns dynamic initial margin. For credit portfolios, AI approximators learn expensive portfolio-loss/VaR calculations and are compared with non-AI regression approximations against Monte Carlo. These are not interchangeable: the first estimates conditional tail measures from loss information, while the second approximates outputs of a portfolio model for repeated computation. **Locator:** Barrera et al. (2025), Mathematical Finance, publisher full text; Jakob et al. (2023), Digital Finance, full open-access article §§2–4. **Sources:** D011-WILEY-STATISTICAL-LEARNING-VAR-ES-DYNAMIC-IM-2025, D011-SPRINGER-CREDIT-PORTFOLIO-AI-APPROXIMATION-2023 **Area context:** Conditional neural VaR/ES is an emerging optional technique after learners understand quantiles, tail measures, heavy-tailed loss and validation. Credit-portfolio approximations support repeated calculations where full simulation is costly, with use-case-specific error/runtime comparison. Neither removes the need to validate inputs and outputs against appropriate baselines. **Limit:** The conditional-learning paper's case study is dynamic initial margin rather than credit/rates risk. The credit approximation results are simulated and depend on training data and portfolio assumptions; they do not establish calibrated conditional forecasts, a general neural advantage or regulatory use. A distinct credit/rates study directly comparing quantile regression to joint VaR/ES with full tail-calibration/backtest protocol remains a bounded gap. **Relationship:** Specify the conditional loss/tail target -> estimate quantiles and ES with joint/quantile loss -> assess approximation distance and tail calibration. For a credit portfolio, specify obligor/dependence/correlation inputs -> construct a reference Monte Carlo loss/VaR -> train an approximation -> compare errors and runtime under changed portfolio/correlation cases. These outputs can support margin, portfolio pricing or stress analysis only when the task and model governance match.
- **Claim:** A rates-family example tests direct conditional quantile estimation rather than importing an equity volatility model: PCA-QREG uses yield-curve level, slope and curvature factors, EWMA factor volatility and quantile regression to estimate US Treasury yield distributions and bond-portfolio VaR. It is evaluated against historical simulation on 4,513 rolling daily observations with coverage/backtest tests, quantile loss and a modified Diebold–Mariano predictive-accuracy test. Separately, neural quantile regression extends traditional linear quantile VaR/CoVaR estimation to nonlinear bank spillover measures and systemic-risk network outputs. The two designs are complementary, not a direct same-sample benchmark; the rates study reports VaR, while joint VaR/ES neural estimation is supported by the other indexed multi-asset study. **Locator:** Pimentel, Risstad and Westgaard (2022), full text §§3–6; Keilbar and Wang (2022), full text §§2–5; Qiu, Lazar and Nakata (2024), full text §§3–5 for joint neural VaR/ES on different asset classes. **Sources:** D011-SPRINGER-PCA-QUANTILE-RATES-VAR-2022, D011-SPRINGER-NN-QUANTILE-SYSTEMIC-RISK-2022, D011-READING-QIU-LAZAR-NAKATA-JOINT-VAR-ES-RNN-2024 **Area context:** Place PCA-QREG as an optional rates-risk method after yield-curve/PCA and quantile-regression foundations. Place neural CoVaR as an optional systemic-risk research extension after VaR, linear quantile regression, bank dependence and model validation. VaR backtesting evidence applies to the stated Treasury study; neural CoVaR uses the stated linear baseline/out-of-sample design and is not a regulator-approved substitute. **Limit:** PCA-QREG's bond portfolio result concerns 5% VaR, not ES, with a short-end three-month misspecification and possible sensitivity to structural shifts/EWMA choice. Neural CoVaR's comparative result uses the study's historical bank sample and linear quantile baseline; it does not establish causality, observed exposure links or general deployment. No head-to-head rates comparison of joint VaR/ES was found in this bounded packet. **Relationship:** Yield-curve history -> PCA level/slope/curvature factors -> EWMA factor volatility -> quantile regression -> yield distribution and portfolio VaR -> coverage tests and quantile-loss model comparison. Separately, linear quantile VaR -> neural conditional quantile CoVaR -> derivatives of fitted quantiles -> inferred bank spillover network and SNRI/SFI/SHI outputs -> out-of-sample validation. These method branches connect through quantile-risk foundations but estimate distinct targets.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Future**
- **Claim:** Quantum amplitude estimation is the candidate future algorithmic counterpart to classical Monte Carlo sampling for estimating selected probabilities/expectations and derived risk measures; quantum Monte Carlo scenario-generation circuits can compose classical risk-factor models with QAE for risk estimation. This is a query-complexity research proposal with concrete finite-circuit examples, not an established risk estimator in deployment. **Locator:** Matsakos and Nield (2024), full paper §§1.2–3 and resource analysis; Woerner and Egger (2019) and Egger et al. (2021) research abstracts. **Sources:** D011-QUANTUM-QMC-RISK-ANALYTICS-2024, D011-IBM-QUANTUM-RISK-ANALYSIS-2019, D011-IBM-QUANTUM-CREDIT-RISK-2021 **Area context:** Potential uses include estimated CDF probabilities, VaR/CVaR/ES-like tail measures and credit economic-capital calculations, conditional on the encoded portfolio/loss model. It should follow classical Monte Carlo, loss distribution and tail-risk definitions, and quantum circuit/algorithm foundations. **Limit:** Quadratic query scaling does not establish end-to-end acceleration because circuit/state preparation, fault tolerance, error correction, hardware noise, data encoding, depth and measurement costs may dominate. Examples are theoretical or toy-scale; the Qiskit credit tutorial itself has internally inconsistent VaR/CVaR output. Do not imply regulatory validation or superiority. **Relationship:** Classical model and loss target -> circuit encoding of stochastic scenarios -> QAE probability/expectation estimation -> risk measure reconstruction -> error/resource accounting -> comparison with optimized classical Monte Carlo -> independent validation/backtesting. Each stage has a separate correctness and cost obligation.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Traditional**
- **Claim:** The 1996 RiskMetrics system is a historically important market-risk workflow, but its documentation separates three different things: VaR methodologies, volatility/correlation data, and calculation/reporting software. This is useful historical tooling context; the document does not establish that its original software remains current. **Locator:** RiskMetrics Technical Document, 4th ed. (December 1996), introduction §§1.1–1.3; the original technical document is hosted in MSCI's archive. **Sources:** D011-RISKMETRICS-TECHNICAL-DOCUMENT-1996 **Area context:** Places an established historical system at the intersection of market-risk methods, model inputs and portfolio VaR reporting, while preserving those as distinct selectable concepts. Its history can explain why covariance, market data and risk reporting became an integrated workflow. **Limit:** Historical documentation only; not evidence that RiskMetrics software is maintained, available or suitable for current regulatory or portfolio use. Current implementation tools require current versioned documentation and independent assessment. **Relationship:** Portfolio positions and market data feed volatility/correlation estimates and a chosen VaR methodology; software applies the method and produces a risk estimate/report. The method is not the data and neither is the calculation system.
- **Claim:** RiskMetrics' 1996 technical system is retained as a named historical market-risk implementation, not as current software. Its documentation separates VaR calculation methodology, risk-factor data and calculation/reporting functions. Current examples reviewed for this area show how the implementation layer later diversified into open-source libraries, commercial risk engines and model-governance systems; the index is representative by task and does not attempt a product-by-product software history. **Locator:** RiskMetrics Technical Document (1996), system and methodology sections; current ORE, MathWorks and SAS official documentation and version records inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-RISKMETRICS-TECHNICAL-DOCUMENT-1996, D011-ORE-RISK-ANALYTICS-DOCS-2026, D011-MATHWORKS-RISK-TOOLBOX-R2026B, D011-SAS-RISK-ENGINE-DOCS-2026 **Area context:** This is a historical tool context for bank market-risk calculation and reporting, contrasted with present task-specific implementations. It does not imply that modern risk work follows one product lineage or that this historical system remains available/current. **Limit:** The 1996 record is historical documentation and the current records are representative capability pages, not evidence of product adoption, comparative accuracy or a complete history of risk software. **Relationship:** Historical risk-measure concepts and data inputs can be compared with current implementations, but students should choose software from the present calculation, data and validation need rather than infer a required migration path from the historical example.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Current**
- **Claim:** Current software examples include a research/engineering toolbox with documented VaR and ES estimation, credit PD/EAD/LGD/ECL modeling and backtesting functions, and a commercial portfolio-risk platform with holdings-based factor risk, full-revaluation stress tests and reporting. These are different tool choices, not an exhaustive market inventory. **Locator:** MathWorks Risk Management Toolbox R2026b documentation and VaR/ES backtesting page; MSCI BarraOne current product page, all opened 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-MATHWORKS-RISK-TOOLBOX-R2026B, D011-MATHWORKS-RISK-BACKTESTING-R2026B, D011-MSCI-BARRAONE-RISK-PLATFORM-2026 **Area context:** Provides students two contrasting implementation contexts: coded/statistical modeling and testing with documented functions versus an integrated holdings-based risk/reporting platform. Tool selection follows risk type, portfolio, data access, model governance and output need. **Limit:** Both are vendor descriptions. They establish stated capabilities only, not comparative accuracy, regulatory approval, adoption, price, or superiority; the product set and licensing require follow-up. A platform output is not a method or standard. **Relationship:** Financial data, instrument representation and risk assumptions feed model estimation; outputs can include VaR/ES forecasts, stress results and validation diagnostics. Those require independent calibration, data/assumption checks, backtesting and applicable governance before use.
- **Claim:** Current open-source volatility tooling has distinct univariate and multivariate roles: CRAN tsgarch is the maintainer-named successor candidate to rugarch for univariate GARCH specification, estimation, forecasts and walk-forward evaluation; rugarch remains a documented option with VaR/ES tests but feature development is ending; rmgarch implements DCC, GO-GARCH and Copula-GARCH and currently depends on rugarch. Python arch provides a separate implementation family with analytical, simulated and residual-bootstrap forecast methods. These are selectable tools for different model structures and lifecycle constraints, not equivalent packages. **Locator:** CRAN tsgarch 1.0.4, rugarch 1.5-6 and rmgarch 1.4-3 reference manuals; rugarch maintainer README; arch 7.2 volatility and forecasting documentation; all inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-TSGARCH-CRAN-REFERENCE-2026, D011-RUGARCH-CRAN-REFERENCE-AND-TESTS-2026, D011-RUGARCH-MAINTENANCE-TRANSITION-2025, D011-RMGARCH-CRAN-MULTIVARIATE-2026, D011-ARCH-VOLATILITY-PROCESSES-2026, D011-ARCH-UNIVARIATE-MODELS-2026 **Area context:** Univariate conditional volatility forecasts can feed distribution-based VaR/ES; multivariate conditional covariance/correlation and conditional densities support portfolio loss aggregation and dependence modeling. Package and dependence-family choice follows the input data and portfolio question. **Limit:** Documentation does not establish comparative accuracy or regulatory approval. GARCH family assumptions, distribution choice, convergence and out-of-sample evaluation remain necessary. rugarch feature development is ending, and rmgarch's dependency on rugarch needs explicit maintenance checks; verify API parity before migrating to tsgarch. **Relationship:** Return series and mean specification feed a conditional variance model; residual distribution and forecast method produce volatility or density forecasts; univariate forecasts may feed risk quantiles, while multivariate dependence models produce covariance/correlation or portfolio-density outputs. VaR exception and ES tail-severity tests then evaluate different forecast properties; a tool function does not make those tests interchangeable.
- **Claim:** Risk-library and data-source choices depend on the risk output. Riskfolio-Lib 7.4 documents portfolio optimization using dispersion, downside/tail and drawdown measures, risk-parity/hierarchical allocation and risk contribution; it can support portfolio-level downside-aware construction, but does not replace instrument-level pricing or bank market, credit, counterparty or liquidity systems. For macro-financial covariates and scenario/backtest research, FRED/ALFRED provides named series metadata, observations and historical vintages; Federal Reserve Board research pages provide paper-specific datasets, definitions, frequencies and replication artifacts; ECB disseminated statistics are available through SDMX 2.1, while research microdata use separate eligibility/access procedures. **Locator:** Riskfolio-Lib 7.4 maintainer documentation (portfolio measures and optimization); PyPI project metadata; St. Louis Fed FRED API overview; Federal Reserve Board Economic Research Data catalogue, including its stated update frequencies; ECB official data access page, sections Data API and Access to microdata. Inspected 2026-10-26. **Sources:** D011-RISKFOLIO-LIB-DOCS-2026, D011-RISKFOLIO-LIB-PYPI-7-4-2026, D011-FRED-ALFRED-API-DATA-2026, D011-FED-ECON-RESEARCH-DATA-CATALOG-2026, D011-ECB-SDMX-DATA-ACCESS-2026 **Area context:** These sources fit portfolio allocation/downside measurement and macro-financial research/scenario contexts. Frequency, vintages, definitions and access terms must fit the particular risk factor and holding period; high-frequency pricing, issuer/obligor data, transaction data, collateral/exposure data and production bank risk engines need separate sources. **Limit:** Riskfolio-Lib documentation is maintainer capability evidence, not an independent benchmark or validation. The ECB dataset-catalogue endpoint returned 503 on the 2026-10-26 check, so this claim relies on its official data-access page for the API and microdata boundary, not a claim that specific catalogue datasets are currently available. Public aggregate or research series do not establish suitability, licensing or complete point-in-time history for a specific model. **Relationship:** Choose the measure/model first, then select an implementation that supports its assumptions and output; independently validate it. Select data by instrument, factor, frequency, vintage and access rights. A public macro series can enrich a scenario or historical research design but cannot stand in for the positions, market quotes, transaction-level credit or exposure data required for a production risk calculation.
- **Claim:** Current risk software spans different jobs and access models. Open Source Risk Engine v1.8.17.0 documents historical, Monte Carlo, semi/full-parametric and hybrid VaR; exposure simulation, XVA, sensitivities, stress and selected SA/BA-CCR/capital calculations, with user-supplied trade and market inputs and public examples under a Modified BSD repository license. MathWorks R2026b Risk Management Toolbox documents market VaR/ES and validation/backtests, credit PD/EAD/LGD/ECL and portfolio models, and climate-scenario analysis; its separate Modelscape product handles model inventory, validation workflow, test, deployment and monitoring across MATLAB/Python/R/SAS or external models. SAS vendor documentation lists a broad near-real-time market/credit/liquidity/CVA engine, SAS OpRisk VaR 6.1 for loss/KRI modeling and simulation, and SAS Risk Management for Banking 3.4 with liquidity calculations. These tools are alternatives or complements by calculation task, not interchangeable all-risk packages. **Locator:** ORE official documentation/methodology catalogue and v1.8.17.0 release record (released 2026-09-15); ORE XVA Risk example; MathWorks Risk Management Toolbox and Modelscape R2026b documentation; SAS Risk Engine product page; SAS OpRisk VaR and Risk Management for Banking support/version pages. Inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-ORE-RISK-ANALYTICS-DOCS-2026, D011-ORE-RELEASE-1-8-17-2026, D011-ORE-XVA-RISK-EXAMPLE-2026, D011-MATHWORKS-RISK-TOOLBOX-R2026B, D011-MATHWORKS-MODELSCAPE-R2026B, D011-SAS-RISK-ENGINE-DOCS-2026, D011-SAS-OPRISK-VAR-6-1-2026, D011-SAS-RISK-MGMT-BANKING-3-4-2026 **Area context:** This maps maintained software options to market portfolio risk, derivative CCR/XVA, credit estimation, liquidity scenarios, operational-loss analysis and model governance.
