Trade-strategy methods then choose benchmarks/schedules/algorithms, while post-trade TCA measures implementation shortfall, spreads, impact, delay and execution quality. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Trade Strategy and Execution and Trading Costs and Electronic Markets readings; SEC Investor.gov order-type bulletin updated 2026-08-18; Almgren and Chriss (2001); Cartea and Jaimungal (2015), publisher abstract on market/limit-order execution. **Sources:** D011-CFA-TRADE-STRATEGY-EXECUTION-2026, D011-CFA-TCA-2026, D011-SEC-INVESTOR-ORDER-TYPES-UPDATED-2026, D011-JOR-ALMGREN-CHRISS-OPTIMAL-EXECUTION-2001, D011-CARTEA-JAIMUNGAL-EXECUTION-ORDERS-2015 **Area context:** After a target portfolio and orders exist, learners examine how order instruction and execution strategy respond to urgency, liquidity, expected alpha decay, risk, market impact and completion probability. Separate the order type, execution schedule/algorithm and cost-evaluation method as related but distinct choices. **Limit:** CFA content is one current professional curriculum; the SEC bulletin is a non-exhaustive retail U.S.-equity description, while academic execution papers study specified models/venues. Order types, routing and market structure differ across broker, venue, asset class and jurisdiction. No single execution algorithm or benchmark is universally best. **Relationship:** Portfolio targets yield required trades; trade/order characteristics and market state inform the execution method; fills and unfilled quantity create realized costs and opportunity risk; TCA compares results with a suitable benchmark and feeds portfolio/strategy review. Algorithms implement an execution design; TCA evaluates it rather than replacing it.
- **Claim:** Investment mandate and decision process are separate dimensions: active versus passive/index describes the intended investment objective; benchmark-relative limits or evaluation can apply to active management; discretionary versus systematic describes how investment decisions are generated and is a choice within active strategies. These are not mutually exclusive rungs in one learning sequence. Execution then branches by instrument/market, with different structure and liquidity across equities, fixed income, listed/OTC derivatives and FX. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Active Equity Investing: Portfolio Construction; Analysis of Active Portfolio Management; Liability-Driven and Index-Based Strategies; Trade Strategy and Execution readings; Fama and French (1993) publisher abstract for a historically bounded stock/bond factor example. **Sources:** D011-CFA-ACTIVE-EQUITY-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-PORTFOLIO-ANALYSIS-2026, D011-CFA-LIABILITY-DRIVEN-INDEX-STRATEGIES-2026, D011-CFA-TRADE-STRATEGY-EXECUTION-2026, D011-ELSEVIER-FAMA-FRENCH-COMMON-RISK-FACTORS-1993 **Area context:** This helps students choose a coherent route without conflating why a portfolio is managed (active, passive or liability-relative), how decisions are made (discretionary or systematic), how results are judged (absolute or benchmark-relative), and how resulting trades are implemented in the relevant market. **Limit:** These are curriculum-defined distinctions and examples, not an exhaustive taxonomy of investment mandates or proof that all firms use the same labels. Systematic techniques can support either return seeking or risk/index replication; benchmark-relative analysis does not by itself make a strategy systematic. The CFA execution material is broad but does not supply every market's venue/order protocol. **Relationship:** Mandate/objective and benchmark shape the investment problem; decision process generates candidate positions/signals; portfolio constraints convert them to weights; market-specific execution turns targets into orders/fills; attribution and transaction-cost analysis evaluate results against the chosen objective. The branches reconnect at portfolio targets and downstream execution/evaluation.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Current**
- **Claim:** When many strategies or model variants have been searched, there is no single interchangeable ‘multiple testing’ remedy: White’s Reality Check and Hansen’s SPA compare searched candidates to a benchmark; Romano–Wolf StepM performs stepwise familywise-error testing; Model Confidence Set returns a set of best/indistinguishable candidates; DSR adjusts Sharpe-ratio significance for selection and non-normality; PBO/CSCV estimates selection-related backtest overfitting. **Locator:** White (2000), Hansen (2005), Romano & Wolf (2005), Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011), Bailey & López de Prado (2014), and Bailey et al. (2017) source records; current `arch` 7.2.0 multiple-comparison module reference documents Reality Check, SPA, StepM and MCS inputs/outputs. **Sources:** D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-2005, D011-ROMANO-WOLF-STEPM-2005, D011-HANSEN-LUNDE-NASON-MCS-2011, D011-BAILEY-LOPEZ-DSR-2014, D011-PBO-BACKTEST-OVERFIT-2017, D011-ARCH-MULTIPLE-COMPARISON-DOCS **Area context:** These are complementary/alternative validation designs for systematic strategy and predictive-model selection after a search, each answering a different inferential question and requiring an explicit candidate universe, benchmark/loss, temporal dependence treatment and sample. **Limit:** Several primary records were inspected at publisher-abstract level; implementations and assumptions vary. No one method repairs omitted trials, leakage, unrealistic trading costs, changing regimes or weak data. These are not universal regulatory requirements or proof of deployable profit. **Relationship:** Chronological, purged/embargoed or otherwise leakage-aware evaluation establishes valid time separation first; data-snooping and selection procedures then address search multiplicity/overfitting for a specified universe; economic cost, capacity and live/paper-trading checks remain additional downstream validation. DSR is Sharpe-specific; MCS is a model set; PBO/CSCV is not identical to benchmark superiority testing.
- **Claim:** Cost-aware systematic investing has a distinct portfolio-choice branch. A peer-reviewed review derives dynamic-programming methods for portfolio choice with small proportional transaction costs, illustrates explicit solutions under mean-reverting expected returns, and describes policy iteration for more complex cases. This complements target-weight optimization and execution-cost estimation; its continuous-time small-cost assumptions differ from large market-impact execution models. **Locator:** Muhle-Karbe, Reppen and Soner (2017), Annual Review of Financial Economics 9:301-331, publisher abstract inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-ANNUAL-REVIEWS-TRANSACTION-COST-PORTFOLIO-CHOICE-2017 **Area context:** After a mandate and return/risk model are specified, the learner can compare a cost-blind target allocation with a dynamic no-trade/rebalance policy when trading frictions materially affect the decision. The cost-aware solution changes the portfolio decision itself; downstream execution still estimates realized fills and impact. **Limit:** Abstract-level evidence in this packet; theoretical scope is small transaction costs and specified models. It does not establish empirical superiority, suitability for all assets/horizons, or a replacement for empirical transaction-cost analysis and execution algorithms. **Relationship:** Expected-return/risk and mandate inputs + proportional-cost assumptions -> dynamic target/no-trade region or policy-iteration solution -> desired holdings/rebalance decision -> execution algorithm and realized-cost measurement. The portfolio policy and execution controller are complementary, not interchangeable.
- **Claim:** Selection-bias corrections in systematic research have different targets and outputs. White's Reality Check evaluates whether the best candidate in the declared search beats a benchmark; its full-universe bootstrap can be conservative when many poor alternatives are included. Hansen's SPA retains the benchmark question but uses studentization and a sample-dependent null intended to improve power. Romano-Wolf StepM returns candidates identified as superior to a benchmark under stepwise familywise-error control. Hansen-Lunde-Nason MCS instead returns a confidence set under a user-selected loss without a fixed benchmark. Deflated Sharpe Ratio adjusts Sharpe significance for selection and non-normality; PBO/CSCV targets the probability of strategy-selection overfit; factor-discovery thresholds address a different cross-sectional discovery problem. They do not substitute for one another or for forward temporal testing, economic costs and a complete search log. **Locator:** Original papers by White (2000), Hansen (2005), Romano and Wolf (2005), Hansen, Lunde and Nason (2011), Bailey and López de Prado (2014), Bailey et al. (2017), Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016); versioned ARCH 7.2.0 and CRAN MCS 0.2.1 implementation references; inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-ARCH-MCP-IMPLEMENTATION-CODE-7-2-2026, D011-CRAN-MCS-IMPLEMENTATION-0-2-1-2026, D011-HSU-HAN-WU-CAO-PORTFOLIO-DATA-SNOOPING-2018, D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-FULLTEXT-UNIVERSITY-COPY-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-FULLTEXT-CITESEERX-2005, D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-2005, D011-ROMANO-WOLF-STEPM-2005, D011-HANSEN-LUNDE-NASON-MCS-2011, D011-BAILEY-LOPEZ-DSR-2014, D011-PBO-BACKTEST-OVERFIT-2017, D011-HARVEY-LIU-ZHU-FACTOR-MULTIPLE-TESTING-2016 **Area context:** Use these after a researcher has generated multiple forecasts, factor candidates, strategy variants or parameter searches and before interpreting the selected backtest as evidence. The chosen procedure follows the question: benchmark superiority, which candidates beat a benchmark, a set of statistically indistinguishable candidates, Sharpe significance after trial selection, selection-overfit risk, or factor-discovery evidence. **Limit:** Every result is conditional on the disclosed candidate universe, benchmark or loss function, sample, dependence structure and implementation. Data-driven/effective trial counts can be hard to recover after undocumented exploration. The empirical portfolio source is available only at publisher abstract/preview scope; it supports one bounded illustration, not a general asset-class result. None of these methods repairs leakage, omitted candidates, weak economic rationale, unmodeled costs or simulation-to-live differences. **Relationship:** Candidate-search log + time-aligned candidate losses/returns + declared benchmark/criterion -> choose a correction matching the inferential target -> report adjusted p-value, identified superior candidates, retained confidence set, deflated Sharpe statistic or PBO estimate -> retain an untouched/forward evaluation and economic cost analysis. Each output answers a distinct question; a passing result does not automatically establish another.
- **Claim:** Multiple-testing methods answer context-specific questions and should be applied to the searched candidate universe, benchmark/loss and mandate actually studied. White Reality-Check-family corrections applied to 16 basic, 126 learning and nearly 2,000 extended portfolio allocations across developed-country equity indexes, DJIA stocks and NYSE stocks found that most apparent 1/N-relative winners did not survive the study's data-snooping tests. A separate global factor-allocation study applies Hansen SPA and extensions to equity and fixed-income factor strategies, evaluates 2006–2019 and uses cash as the natural long-short benchmark plus the equity market as an alternative; its indexed results report the simple equal-weighted factor mix was difficult to beat in that test universe. Harvey–Liu–Zhu instead address the cross-sectional discovery of equity-return factors and motivate a higher discovery hurdle than a conventional t>2. These applications do not make SPA/Reality Check, factor t-thresholds, DSR or PBO interchangeable: the first group tests portfolio candidates against a benchmark, while the factor threshold addresses repeated cross-sectional discoveries. Existing ML/LLM strategy generation increases candidate search, but this bounded pass found no distinct peer-reviewed LLM-specific inferential procedure; record trials and use existing selection-aware and temporal validation methods unless such evidence emerges. **Locator:** Hsu, Han, Wu and Cao (2018), Journal of Banking & Finance 97, publisher abstract/article preview; Dichtl, Drobetz and Wendt (2021), European Financial Management 27, publisher metadata and indexed article excerpts; Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016), Review of Financial Studies 29(1), NBER and publisher records; original White/SPA, StepM, MCS, DSR, PBO papers and version-pinned ARCH 7.2.0 / CRAN MCS 0.2.1 implementations; inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-HSU-HAN-WU-CAO-PORTFOLIO-DATA-SNOOPING-2018, D011-DICHTL-DROBETZ-WENDT-FACTOR-ALLOCATION-SPA-2021, D011-HARVEY-LIU-ZHU-FACTOR-MULTIPLE-TESTING-2016, D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-2005, D011-ROMANO-WOLF-STEPM-2005, D011-HANSEN-LUNDE-NASON-MCS-2011, D011-BAILEY-LOPEZ-DSR-2014, D011-PBO-BACKTEST-OVERFIT-2017, D011-ARCH-MCP-IMPLEMENTATION-CODE-7-2-2026, D011-CRAN-MCS-IMPLEMENTATION-0-2-1-2026, D011-GOYAL-WELCH-ZAFIROV-EQUITY-PREMIUM-2022-LOOK-2024, D011-OLAGOKE-LLM-TRIAL-ADJUSTED-OUTSAMPLE-GATE-2026 **Area context:** Once a strategy or factor search has generated a disclosed candidate set, choose validation from the decision question: benchmark-superiority procedures for a declared portfolio benchmark and aligned losses; cross-sectional discovery thresholds for proposed return factors; Sharpe selection correction or PBO for a selected backtest; retain temporal holdout, data provenance, costs and implementation review. The relevant comparison depends on the mandate: developed-market indexes, equity stock selection and cross-asset factor allocation have different universes and benchmarks. This evidence supports conditional evaluation branches, not a universal compulsory correction sequence or guaranteed performance. **Limit:** Hsu evidence is equity-only and accessible at abstract/article-preview scope; Dichtl's full text could not be fetched in this pass, so its sample/result claims are restricted to publisher metadata and indexed article excerpts. HLZ's proposed threshold applies to cross-sectional equity-factor discovery under its assumptions, not all portfolio tests. The LLM gate is an unreviewed, abstract-limited single-market preprint and does not establish a distinct inferential method. No evidence here ranks corrections across every asset class, benchmark or regulation; the current claim is limited to the compared equity and global equity/fixed-income factor examples. **Relationship:** Candidate portfolio returns/losses + declared benchmark + cost-aware performance criterion -> benchmark-superiority or model-confidence procedure (Reality Check/SPA/StepM/MCS as question requires); selected Sharpe/backtest -> DSR/PBO/CSCV as separate diagnostics; cross-sectional factor hypotheses -> factor-discovery threshold/control. Point-in-time candidate generation and trial ledger feed these tests; validated outputs then feed mandate-specific portfolio review, out-of-sample evaluation, transaction costs and execution. ML/LLM generation changes the number/rate of candidates but does not replace this mapping or supply a distinct valid test by itself.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Machine-learning portfolio research is best treated as an alternative design around a defined investment objective, portfolio constraints and estimation risk, rather than as an independent alpha engine. Studies of learned covariance shrinkage and data-driven portfolio optimization compare against explicit classical baselines and depend on the training/evaluation design. **Locator:** El Karoui and Lim (2018) on machine learning and portfolio optimization; Mattera et al. (2023) on reinforcement-learning covariance shrinkage; Neural nonlinear shrinkage 2026 paper and the CFA 2026 real-world allocation constraints reading. **Sources:** D011-ELKAROUI-LIM-ML-PORTFOLIO-2018, D011-MATTERA-RL-COVARIANCE-SHRINKAGE-2023, D011-NEURAL-NONLINEAR-SHRINKAGE-2026, D011-CFA-REAL-WORLD-ALLOCATION-CONSTRAINTS-2026 **Area context:** This is a current research design at the intersection of statistical learning and constrained portfolio construction. It belongs after portfolio objectives, covariance estimation and leakage-aware validation are understood, and alongside classical/regularized alternatives. **Limit:** The papers use specified datasets, models and objectives; research evidence does not show universal superiority, live adoption or that every portfolio problem benefits from ML. RL shrinkage should not be confused with RL trade execution. **Relationship:** Point-in-time asset/return data and a portfolio objective feed model estimation; learned parameters or covariance estimates feed constrained allocation; temporal holdouts and comparison to sample/factor/shrinkage baselines precede cost-aware paper/live evaluation.
- **Claim:** Financial reinforcement learning must be split by the decision it solves: direct action selection, portfolio allocation, forecast/model selection and execution are sequential decision tasks with different states, actions, rewards, constraints and output metrics. A 2025 peer-reviewed review/meta-analysis compares financial RL literature with traditional methods and highlights MDP design, explainability, robustness and benchmarking as unresolved challenges. A separate 2026 intraday systematic review reports highly heterogeneous studies and predominantly historical/simulation evidence; its publisher page was access-limited in this pass, so its claims are abstract/indexed-text level only. Neither review supports a general RL superiority or live-readiness claim. **Locator:** Bai et al. (2025), Annual Review of Statistics and Its Application 12:209–232, publisher abstract; Argyriou et al. (2026), Applied Sciences 16(20), 10060, publisher-indexed abstract/text (direct fetch 429). **Sources:** D011-ANNUALREVIEWS-RL-FINANCIAL-APPLICATIONS-2025 **Area context:** Place RL as an optional emerging method after the learner can define a target task, objective and baseline. A portfolio policy, an execution scheduler and a direct trading agent should be contextualized separately; each needs temporally valid data and a task-matched classical baseline, validation and cost/risk treatment. **Limit:** The 2025 article is review-level evidence across heterogeneous finance applications; the 2026 systematic review is only indexed/abstract-level here and details were not fully inspected. Neither establishes live deployment, profitability, robust transfer or universal advantage. **Relationship:** Define the financial task and decision horizon -> state/action/reward and constraints -> compare RL policy with an appropriate established method -> test on temporal holdouts with fees, spreads, slippage, liquidity and market impact -> report task-specific economic and risk outputs. Outputs are not interchangeable across forecasting, allocation, execution and trading.
- **Claim:** Emerging finance ML/RL methods branch by the decision they support. A contextual LinUCB bandit can choose one portfolio at a time from a prebuilt candidate pool; this is not the same as an allocation policy learning a state-transition process. Model-predictive control is a receding-horizon optimizer for multi-period mean-variance or risk-parity allocation, while imitation plus RL has been proposed for multi-price-level market making. Offline RL for parent-order execution consumes order-book context and inventory/time state. A recent hybrid adds a separately trained regime forecaster that selects behavioral position-sizing adjustments around an actor–critic policy; the forecaster, policy and sizing layer therefore have distinct outputs and validation needs. A 2025 seven-equity-dataset study covering over 300 OOS years found SAC did not systematically beat 1/N and its turnover erased gains at 0.1% costs, providing a counterexample to general superiority. These methods complement or compete with traditional portfolio rules only under a matched mandate, benchmark, constraints, data window and friction model. **Locator:** Ni et al. (2023), Expert Systems with Applications publisher abstract (CSI 300, CART portfolio pool + LinUCB); Li, Uysal and Mulvey (2022), EJOR publisher abstract (multi-period mean-variance/risk parity MPC; 2006–2020 out-of-sample, market-impact costs); Niu et al. (2024), IJCAI Main Track full text (four datasets; imitation + RL for multi-price market making); Zhang et al. (2023), IJCAI Main Track full text (offline RL execution using historical limit-order-book context and simulator); Charkhestani and Esfahanipour (2026), Scientific Reports full text (TimesNet-regime forecast + behavioral sizing + actor–critic policy, crypto and DJIA walk-forward); Finance Research Letters 75 (2025), publisher abstract (SAC versus 1/N, seven equity datasets, cost/turnover counterexample); Bai et al. (2025), Annual Review review/meta-analysis; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-IJCAI-IMM-IMITATIVE-MARKET-MAKING-2024, D011-ESWA-CONTEXTUAL-BANDIT-PORTFOLIO-2023, D011-FRL-DRL-BEAT-1N-2025, D011-EJOR-MPC-MULTIPERIOD-PORTFOLIO-2022, D011-FRL-CHATGPT-RISK-APPETITE-PORTFOLIO-2025, D011-FRL-GEMINI-NAIVE-PORTFOLIO-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2025, D011-JRFM-LLM-AUTONOMOUS-PORTFOLIO-ALLOCATORS-2026, D011-SPRINGER-DRL-PORTFOLIO-SYSTEMATIC-REVIEW-2026, D011-RISKNET-GENAI-EQUITY-FEATURE-DISCOVERY-2026, D011-NATURE-BEHAVIORAL-DRL-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-IJCAI-GENERALIZABLE-RL-EXECUTION-2023, D011-ANNUALREVIEWS-RL-FINANCIAL-APPLICATIONS-2025, D011-WANG-GAO-LI-RL-EXECUTION-2026, D011-MATTERA-RL-COVARIANCE-SHRINKAGE-2023, D011-NEURAL-NONLINEAR-SHRINKAGE-2026, D011-FINRL-META-NEURIPS-2022-BENCHMARKS-2026, D011-QLIB-MICROSOFT-RESEARCH-PAPER-2020 **Area context:** This is an optional specialist branch after the learner can state the investment objective, baseline, data timing, constraints and costs. For allocation, compare optimizer/MPC or RL output weights with fixed-mix/equal-weight, mean-variance, risk-parity or mandate-specific baselines. For execution, first define a parent order and implementation shortfall/market-impact objective, then compare TWAP/VWAP or classical control with data-driven policies. For market making, use inventory, quote, fill-probability and adverse-selection context; it is a separate task. A contextual bandit chooses among an already formed action/portfolio set, while full RL learns a sequential policy. Results flow into turnover, cost, risk, benchmark and live-monitoring checks; no one method is a universal next step. **Limit:** Evidence is heterogeneous and not a common leaderboard. Ni et al. is publisher-abstract level and a single CSI 300 sample; the SAC result is publisher-abstract level and covers seven equity datasets for one algorithm/protocol; the portfolio-MPC result is abstract-level and uses specified multi-asset/industry universes; the IJCAI papers are full text but simulator/historical-data research. The 2025 Annual Review identifies broad RL design/robustness concerns but combines tasks. No evidence establishes current industry prevalence, production deployment, universal outperformance or cross-asset transfer. **Relationship:** Chosen mandate/universe + point-in-time data + benchmark/cost model -> select the task branch: forecast/signal (model output), portfolio allocation (weights; classical optimizer OR MPC OR tested RL), parent-order execution (schedule/order actions; TWAP/VWAP or classical stochastic control OR RL), market making (quotes/inventory; model-based quoting or imitation+RL), or candidate-set adaptation (contextual bandit). Their output types and loss/reward functions differ. All routes feed held-out/walk-forward tests, turnover, fees/spreads/impact, risk and operational controls; portfolio allocation feeds target holdings to execution, while market making is not a prerequisite for ordinary long-horizon allocation.
- **Claim:** Generative AI has at least four distinct portfolio-research roles: extract or synthesize features that feed a separate quantitative forecaster; propose assets in response to a stated risk appetite; directly emit candidate portfolio weights; and generate strategy candidates for subsequent quantitative scoring. These outputs must not be conflated with contextual bandits selecting from an existing candidate pool, RL policies trained on sequential states/rewards, or MPC solving an explicit finite-horizon objective. Published findings are mixed and setup-dependent; none supplies a normalized same-data, same-cost comparison across these branches and classical optimizers. **Locator:** Risk.net/Journal of Investment Strategies publisher abstract on retrieval-grounded feature discovery; 2025 Finance Research Letters ChatGPT risk-appetite and Gemini/anonymized-data publisher records; 2026 JRFM publisher-indexed autonomous-allocation methods/results; existing LLM candidate-generation paper and trial-aware OOS preprint; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-FRL-CHATGPT-RISK-APPETITE-PORTFOLIO-2025, D011-FRL-GEMINI-NAIVE-PORTFOLIO-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2025, D011-JRFM-LLM-AUTONOMOUS-PORTFOLIO-ALLOCATORS-2026, D011-RISKNET-GENAI-EQUITY-FEATURE-DISCOVERY-2026, D011-OLAGOKE-LLM-TRIAL-ADJUSTED-OUTSAMPLE-GATE-2026, D011-IEEE-AGENTIC-LLM-STRATEGY-GENERATION-2026 **Area context:** This branch is relevant after the learner understands portfolio objectives, benchmarks, point-in-time information, and the difference between selecting assets, predicting returns, generating candidate rules and calculating weights. If the LLM supplies features, those feed a separate estimator/optimizer; if it emits weights directly, validate constraints, concentration, turnover, costs and OOS comparisons; if it generates strategy candidates, all prompts/versions become trials in the selection ledger. Client-facing recommendations additionally invoke suitability, disclosure and regulatory context, distinct from proprietary research. **Limit:** Two Finance Research Letters studies and the JRFM study were not available as directly inspected full text in this pass; publisher snippets/abstracts support only reported high-level designs and outcomes. Samples are limited (U.S./European equities or 50 S&P 500 names), model/prompt dependent, and do not establish broad transfer, causal value, live trading or adviser suitability. The single short LLM-gating preprint remains unreviewed and does not establish a separate validated statistical correction. **Relationship:** Historical/public text + point-in-time prices + risk preference -> (retrieval-grounded LLM feature -> separate quantitative forecaster -> portfolio optimizer) OR (LLM directly proposes/outputs weights -> mathematical constraint, concentration and risk checks) OR (LLM generates strategy candidates -> versioned trial ledger -> selection-aware/walk-forward validation) -> cost-aware portfolio comparison -> orders/fills and performance/risk review. Bandit, RL, optimizer and LLM outputs are distinct at the decision stage; any complementary chain must pass outputs in a type-consistent way.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Future**
- **Claim:** Quantum portfolio optimization is a future-facing alternative for selected constrained allocation problems, not a replacement learning path for ordinary portfolio construction. Current research proposes different formulations: a 2024 quantum-access algorithm for a risk-return frontier and a peer-reviewed end-to-end QAOA pipeline for discrete global minimum variance with binary encoding, initial states, cost operator, ansatz and a classical optimizer. The 2026 QAOA study reports that realistic thermal-relaxation noise precludes quantum advantage in its tested regime; a favorable shot-scaling result is conditional on future hardware improvement. **Locator:** Rebentrost and Lloyd (2024), Künstliche Intelligenz 38, 327–338, MIT author-final manuscript record and abstract; Yuan et al. (2026), Quantum Science and Technology 11, Cambridge repository published-version metadata and abstract, DOI 10.1088/2058-9565/ae4a48. **Sources:** D011-MIT-QUANTUM-PORTFOLIO-ALGORITHM-2024, D011-CAMBRIDGE-QAOA-PORTFOLIO-OPT-2026 **Area context:** These proposals apply to portfolio allocation/optimization after the learner understands risk-return objectives, constraints, covariance/return inputs and classical optimization baselines. They show two different quantum approaches and assumptions; choosing QAOA or quantum-access algorithms depends on the optimization formulation, hardware and data-access model. **Limit:** The 2024 algorithm's complexity assumes quantum access to historical returns; full end-to-end data-loading cost and realistic constraints are not established by the abstract. The 2026 paper studies a particular discrete global minimum-variance problem and reports simulation results; its abstract says realistic thermal relaxation prevents advantage. Neither source proves deployed performance, broad asset-class utility or superiority to best classical solvers after transaction costs, turnover, liquidity and model uncertainty. **Relationship:** Mandate, risk objective and portfolio constraints define the classical optimization problem first; the quantum encoding and circuit optimizer then target that formulation. Data loading/quantum access, encoding error, noise, optimizer convergence and output feasibility must be measured against a matched classical solver. Only after portfolio weights are validated do rebalance scheduling, trading costs and execution follow.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Established strategy-selection methods answer different multiplicity questions: White's Reality Check and Hansen's SPA test whether a searched strategy/model family beats a specified benchmark; Romano–Wolf StepM controls familywise error while identifying benchmark-beating candidates; Hansen–Lunde–Nason MCS returns a set not distinguishable from the best under a chosen loss; DSR adjusts a selected Sharpe ratio for trial selection and non-normality; PBO/CSCV estimates how often an in-sample-selected strategy ranks poorly out of sample. Harvey–Liu–Zhu's higher significance hurdle concerns factor discovery across many tested factors and is not itself a strategy-level backtest procedure. **Locator:** White (2000), Journal of Econometrics 99(1); Hansen (2005), Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 23(4); Romano and Wolf (2005), Annals of Statistics 33(4); Hansen, Lunde and Nason (2011), Econometrica 79(2); Bailey and López de Prado (2014), Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5); Bailey et al. (2017), Journal of Computational Finance 20(4); Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016), Review of Financial Studies 29(1); ARCH 7.2.0 multiple-comparison documentation for software inputs/outputs. **Sources:** D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-2005, D011-ROMANO-WOLF-STEPM-2005, D011-HANSEN-LUNDE-NASON-MCS-2011, D011-BAILEY-LOPEZ-DSR-2014, D011-PBO-BACKTEST-OVERFIT-2017, D011-HARVEY-LIU-ZHU-FACTOR-MULTIPLE-TESTING-2016, D011-ARCH-MULTIPLE-COMPARISON-DOCS **Area context:** These techniques belong after a systematic researcher has defined the candidate universe, benchmark or objective, return/loss measure and time-aware evaluation. They help interpret strategy or factor selection evidence; they do not generate investment signals or establish that a strategy will be profitable. **Limit:** Several records were verified from publisher abstracts or author-hosted manuscripts; the implementation documentation covers one software package and is not a validation guarantee. Dependence, bootstrap design, trial counting, candidate-set completeness, return distribution and sample size affect interpretation. None is a universal regulatory requirement or a substitute for realistic costs, capacity, leakage controls or prospective evaluation. **Relationship:** Time ordering and leakage control establish a valid evaluation design first. Benchmark-based tests, familywise-error procedures, model-set inference, Sharpe adjustment, PBO and factor-discovery thresholds then address distinct selection questions when their assumptions fit. Their outputs are diagnostics for research review; portfolio allocation, execution-cost analysis and paper/live monitoring remain separate downstream steps.
- **Claim:** Implementation checks confirm that these selection procedures share candidate-loss inputs but not conclusions. ARCH 7.2.0 exposes benchmark-versus-candidate loss arrays for SPA/Reality Check and StepM, and a candidate-loss matrix for MCS; it supports stationary, circular and moving-block bootstraps, with explicit block size, replication count, seed and (for SPA) studentization/nested-bootstrap options. Its default block size is an API default rather than a generally justified choice. CRAN MCS 0.2.1 additionally exposes forecast-specific squared/absolute, volatility and quantile losses; its documentation distinguishes moving-block resampling from iid resampling and states stationarity, dependence and moment conditions, plus degeneracy behavior. The technical-rule and portfolio-allocation studies illustrate that apparent winners may not remain superior after accounting for the searched universe. **Locator:** ARCH v7.2.0 version-pinned source and module docs; CRAN MCS 0.2.1 manual and source; White (2000) and Hansen (2005) full-text inspection copies cross-checked to DOI records; CEPR DP1976 and Hsu et al. (2018) publisher record; inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-ARCH-MCP-IMPLEMENTATION-CODE-7-2-2026, D011-CRAN-MCS-IMPLEMENTATION-0-2-1-2026, D011-HSU-HAN-WU-CAO-PORTFOLIO-DATA-SNOOPING-2018, D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-FULLTEXT-UNIVERSITY-COPY-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-FULLTEXT-CITESEERX-2005, D011-WHITE-REALITY-CHECK-2000, D011-HANSEN-SPA-2005, D011-ROMANO-WOLF-STEPM-2005, D011-HANSEN-LUNDE-NASON-MCS-2011, D011-BAILEY-LOPEZ-DSR-2014, D011-PBO-BACKTEST-OVERFIT-2017, D011-HARVEY-LIU-ZHU-FACTOR-MULTIPLE-TESTING-2016 **Area context:** This is an implementation-level comparison for systematic-strategy and forecast evaluation. Preserve aligned per-period losses for every candidate and the benchmark, choose loss based on the decision (forecast error, volatility, quantile or portfolio result), then choose a dependence-aware resampling design and report block/replication settings. It complements ordinary holdout and economic validation; it is not itself a strategy-generation algorithm. **Limit:** The default sqrt(T) block length is not a universal answer; test sensitivity to dependence and block settings. CRAN explicitly requires the original MCS stationarity/dependence/moment conditions for nondegenerate inference. The 2018 allocation study is at abstract/preview scope in this pass. Neither package implementation constitutes independent correctness certification or proves predictive/portfolio benefit. **Relationship:** Full candidate universe -> comparable, timestamp-aligned loss matrix -> (benchmark test / stepwise benchmark selection / no-benchmark MCS / Sharpe-specific adjustment / CSCV overfit estimate) -> inferential report with chosen loss, benchmark, trial definition, bootstrap design and limits -> forward portfolio and cost validation. Candidate losses are shared inputs, but outputs and null hypotheses differ.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Current**
- **Claim:** Current systematic portfolios can use structured covariance estimators—sample covariance, linear/nonlinear/quadratic shrinkage and factor structures—because optimizer inputs are noisy and method choice changes allocation behavior. These are alternatives or complements selected by dimensionality, data and portfolio objective, not necessarily sequentially required methods. **Locator:** Ledoit and Wolf (2004, 2012, 2022); Conlon, Cotter and Kynigakis (2025); Goldberg, Gurdogan and Kercheval (2025); CFA Institute 2026 asset-allocation and real-world-constraints readings. **Sources:** D011-LEDOIT-WOLF-SHRINKAGE-2004, D011-LEDOIT-WOLF-NONLINEAR-SHRINKAGE-2012, D011-LEDOIT-WOLF-QUADRATIC-SHRINKAGE-2022, D011-CONLON-COTTER-KYNIGAKIS-FACTOR-COVARIANCE-2025, D011-GOLDBERG-GURDOGAN-KERCHEVAL-EIGENVECTOR-SHRINKAGE-2025, D011-CFA-ASSET-ALLOCATION-2026 **Area context:** The estimator family supports risk-input construction for portfolio optimization; it belongs between return/risk data preparation and constrained allocation, with portfolio-specific validation. **Limit:** Theoretical and empirical results vary with sample size, asset universe, structure and objective. These papers do not establish a single best estimator or remove estimation error; factor and shrinkage approaches encode different assumptions. **Relationship:** Historical returns and universe definition feed covariance estimation; the estimated matrix enters an optimizer with expected returns and constraints; portfolio turnover, concentration, realized risk and trading costs are downstream checks.
- **Claim:** Covariance-estimator choice cannot be ranked apart from the portfolio objective and implementation design. A same-sample rolling equity comparison evaluates sample/maximum-likelihood, linear and nonlinear shrinkage, and POET estimates with GMV allocation, changing LASSO sparsity and an explicit turnover constraint; in that design LASSO alone can increase turnover as its tuning changes, while a separate turnover constraint controls it. A 2025 risk-based portfolio study reports that long-only asset limits and transaction-cost penalties can reduce the apparent advantage of alternative covariance estimators under constrained GMV/risk parity, although time-series dynamics remain useful for volatility. Historical stock-model evidence likewise cautions that additional factors need not improve covariance forecasts or optimized outcomes, while benchmark tracking error can alter the ranking. Thus estimator, objective (GMV, risk parity, benchmark-aware), constraints, forecast horizon, rebalance rule and costs interact; they are task-specific complements/alternatives rather than a single prerequisite ladder. **Locator:** Husmann, Shivarova and Steinert (2022), full open text, rolling S&P 500 design and conclusion; Dom et al. (2025), peer-reviewed Quantitative Finance article, Lancaster accepted manuscript/repository abstract; Chan, Karceski and Lakonishok (1999), NBER record and abstract; scikit-learn stable LedoitWolf 1.9.1 API; CRAN POET 2.0 record/manual; Qiao et al. (2023), author-hosted Journal of Empirical Finance full text. Inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-HUSMANN-SHIVAROVA-STEINERT-SPARSITY-STABILITY-MINVAR-2022, D011-DOM-HOWARD-JANSEN-LOHRE-BEYOND-GMV-2025, D011-CHAN-KARCESKI-LAKONISHOK-COVARIANCE-PORTFOLIO-1999, D011-SCIKIT-LEARN-COVARIANCE-LEDOITWOLF-1-9-1-2026, D011-CRAN-POET-2-0-IMPLEMENTATION-2026, D011-QIAO-BU-GIBBERD-LIAO-WEN-LI-TIMEVARYING-COSTS-2023 **Area context:** After defining the investable universe, risk objective and data horizon, the learner can compare a sample covariance baseline with shrinkage, factor-residual/POET or time-varying estimators; then test each within the chosen allocation objective and constraints. A GMV/risk-parity learner should assess out-of-sample risk, turnover and costs under the actual rebalance schedule. A return-seeking or benchmark-relative portfolio also needs expected-return/benchmark design; covariance selection does not replace forecasting or strategy definition. The named scikit-learn and POET APIs are reproducible implementation examples with different assumptions, not mandatory tools. **Limit:** The strongest same-design estimator/constraint comparison uses surviving S&P 500 constituents, daily returns, 504-observation rolling estimates and study-specific tuning over 1998–2018; it retains survivorship bias, assumes homoscedasticity and does not cover other asset classes. The 2025 study's accessible repository evidence is the abstract, and the 1999 comparison is abstract-level historical stock evidence. scikit-learn documents a general-purpose estimator; POET 2.0 is an older package and its factor-count/threshold choices require validation. The 2023 event-triggered rebalancing paper is one proposed empirical design. No study supports a universal winner, horizon, rebalance frequency, factor count or production-adoption claim. **Relationship:** Point-in-time returns/universe + chosen objective/benchmark -> estimate covariance (sample OR linear/nonlinear shrinkage OR factor structure such as POET; time-varying model where dynamics matter) -> combine with mean/forecast inputs only for objectives that use them + constraints (long-only, concentration, benchmark, sparsity) -> optimize target weights -> decide rebalance schedule (fixed or covariance-change-triggered) -> measure realized risk, turnover, costs and benchmark error. Estimators are alternatives at the covariance-input stage; portfolio constraints and turnover controls are complementary, and the latter can change estimator rankings. Outputs then feed execution/TCA and risk review, while strategy/forecast design remains a separate upstream input.
- **Claim:** Return, variance and distribution forecasts are distinct model outputs, and their usefulness depends on the downstream objective and evaluation. Long-sample U.S. equity-premium evidence shows predictor performance can decay out of sample; Campbell–Thompson's sign-restricted regressions provide a conditional alternative to an unrestricted regression/historical-average baseline. Volatility forecasts form separate branches (ARCH/GARCH-family, option-implied, realized-volatility and combinations) with horizon- and backtest-dependent evidence. Across 13 portfolio strategies, a 2026 study finds ordinary RMSE can misstate economic forecast value: expected-return error is central for portfolios that use mean forecasts, while covariance error gains importance in turbulent conditions and for some diversification strategies. A 14-year daily international-ETF study contrasts forecast-enhanced return/volatility objectives (mean-variance and Omega) with VaR/CVaR/downside objectives and reports different gains by objective and volatility regime, without attributing them to lower trading costs. The learner should compare a simple benchmark, forecast target/horizon and cost-aware portfolio utility under the selected mandate rather than treating statistical accuracy as portfolio value. **Locator:** Timmermann (2018) Annual Review of Financial Economics; Goyal, Welch and Zafirov (2024) RFS full text, predictor extension through 2021; Campbell and Thompson (2008) RFS / Harvard repository copy; Salcher et al. (2026) Journal of Forecasting full text, 13 portfolio strategies and Fama–French 12-industry calibration; Yu et al. (2020) International Review of Economics & Finance publisher abstract, 14-year daily international ETFs; Leushuis and Petkov (2026) realized-volatility review and Kambouroudis et al. (2016) GARCH/implied/realized comparison already indexed. Inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-TIMMERMANN-FORECASTING-METHODS-FINANCE-2018, D011-GOYAL-WELCH-ZAFIROV-EQUITY-PREMIUM-2022-LOOK-2024, D011-CAMPBELL-THOMPSON-RETURN-PREDICTION-2008, D011-SALCHER-RISK-ADJUSTED-FORECAST-ERROR-2026, D011-YU-CHIOU-LEE-LIN-RETURN-FORECAST-PORTFOLIO-OBJECTIVES-2020, D011-LEUSHUIS-PETKOV-REALIZED-VOL-FORECASTING-REVIEW-2026, D011-JFUTURES-GARCH-IMPLIED-REALIZED-2016, D011-ARCH-VOLATILITY-PROCESSES-2026 **Area context:** After choosing instrument universe, target and decision horizon, a learner may estimate expected-return signals, conditional variance/correlation, or a return distribution; these are complementary inputs only when the selected objective consumes them. Mean-variance/Omega objectives trade return against volatility, GMV/risk parity emphasize risk allocation, and VaR/CVaR/downside objectives emphasize loss-tail criteria. Each branch then compares forecasts to simple baselines and evaluates portfolio outcomes with relevant risk, benchmark, utility, turnover and transaction costs. Covariance estimation is one input-stage choice; it does not substitute for expected-return forecasting, allocation objective, signal selection or execution. **Limit:** Evidence is contrasted, not a single common-data leaderboard: U.S. aggregate equity-premium predictors through 2021, U.S. industry-portfolio-based simulation/empirical forecast evaluation, and daily international ETFs over 14 years. The 2024 RFS extension includes original discovery periods and is not an independent replication; Campbell–Thompson evidence is one U.S. sample; the ETF evidence is publisher-abstract scope. The volatility comparison sources cover specified stocks and horizons. None establishes universal forecast superiority, investor utility across markets, or a prescribed sequence for every systematic mandate. **Relationship:** Point-in-time data + task/mandate + forecast horizon -> (expected-return model OR conditional-volatility/correlation model OR distribution/quantile model; combine only as the portfolio objective requires) -> objective branch (return-risk, minimum-risk/risk-parity, benchmark-aware, or tail/downside) + constraints -> weights/holdings -> objective-matched out-of-sample forecast and portfolio evaluation -> turnover/transaction-cost and execution checks. Statistical forecast loss and portfolio economic value are related but not interchangeable; covariance and mean forecasts are complementary inputs for some strategies, while risk-only/diversification strategies can use other structures.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Reinforcement-learning execution is a research-stage extension of optimal execution: current studies parameterize policies against explicit cost/risk objectives and order-book or simulated-market states, while testing generalization and model misspecification remains necessary. **Locator:** Bertimas and Lo (1998) and Almgren & Chriss (2001) establish dynamic-programming and cost/risk execution baselines; IJCAI 2023 generalizable offline-RL paper and Wang, Gao & Li, Finance and Stochastics 30 (2026), publisher article, describe learned execution policies and bounded simulator/historical-order-flow comparisons. **Sources:** D011-BERTIMAS-LO-EXECUTION-1998, D011-ALMGREN-CHRISS-EXECUTION-2001, D011-IJCAI-GENERALIZABLE-RL-EXECUTION-2023, D011-WANG-GAO-LI-RL-EXECUTION-2026 **Area context:** This method belongs after understanding order execution, market impact, transaction costs, risk tolerance and sequential decision-making; it addresses order scheduling/policy choice rather than portfolio alpha discovery or derivative fair-value pricing. **Limit:** Research results use specified simulations/data and assumptions; the 2026 analysis has conditional convergence assumptions and identifies out-of-distribution/model-misspecification concerns. No evidence here establishes live-market superiority, safe deployment or an industry-wide future requirement. **Relationship:** The classical execution objective supplies baselines and interpretable costs; RL consumes states/rewards and outputs an execution policy. Backtest controls, realistic fill/impact models, robustness and transaction-cost analysis are downstream checks; policy learning complements or competes with classical schedule optimization only under matched objectives and constraints.
- **Claim:** The method families produce different actions and need different inputs: contextual LinUCB updates selection among a fixed portfolio candidate pool from context/reward observations; full RL maps state to sequential actions under an MDP/reward; imitation learning transfers a signal-based expert policy and can be combined with RL exploration for multi-level market-making quotes; MPC repeatedly solves a model-based finite-horizon optimization rather than learning a policy from reward. For order execution, the IJCAI 2023 offline-RL study uses historical LOB context, private time/inventory state and a data-driven simulator; it finds limited context samples/high-dimensional context can overfit and tests context aggregation against TWAP, momentum and other RL baselines. The 2025 portfolio counterexample shows turnover and 0.1% cost can reverse gross SAC results. These are alternatives only within matched tasks and objective; imitation, learned representation, costs and validation can also be complementary components. **Locator:** IJCAI 2023 and IJCAI 2024 full papers; Ni et al. (2023) contextual portfolio bandit publisher abstract; Li et al. (2022) portfolio-MPC publisher abstract; Finance Research Letters 75 (2025) SAC study publisher abstract; Bai et al. (2025) Annual Review publisher page; current FinRL-Meta benchmark card and Qlib workflow/data cards. Inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-IJCAI-IMM-IMITATIVE-MARKET-MAKING-2024, D011-ESWA-CONTEXTUAL-BANDIT-PORTFOLIO-2023, D011-FRL-DRL-BEAT-1N-2025, D011-EJOR-MPC-MULTIPERIOD-PORTFOLIO-2022, D011-FRL-CHATGPT-RISK-APPETITE-PORTFOLIO-2025, D011-FRL-GEMINI-NAIVE-PORTFOLIO-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2025, D011-JRFM-LLM-AUTONOMOUS-PORTFOLIO-ALLOCATORS-2026, D011-SPRINGER-DRL-PORTFOLIO-SYSTEMATIC-REVIEW-2026, D011-RISKNET-GENAI-EQUITY-FEATURE-DISCOVERY-2026, D011-NATURE-BEHAVIORAL-DRL-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-IJCAI-GENERALIZABLE-RL-EXECUTION-2023, D011-ANNUALREVIEWS-RL-FINANCIAL-APPLICATIONS-2025, D011-WANG-GAO-LI-RL-EXECUTION-2026, D011-MATTERA-RL-COVARIANCE-SHRINKAGE-2023, D011-NEURAL-NONLINEAR-SHRINKAGE-2026, D011-FINRL-META-NEURIPS-2022-BENCHMARKS-2026, D011-QLIB-MICROSOFT-RESEARCH-PAPER-2020 **Area context:** Teach the technique only after defining what action is being chosen and what information is available at decision time. Allocation consumes features/forecasts and risk/cost constraints to produce weights; contextual bandits assume a candidate action pool and reward feedback; execution RL consumes market/order-book and order-state data to produce a schedule or order action; market making produces quotes and inventory decisions. MPC requires an explicit transition/cost model and repeatedly resolves a constrained horizon. Data-driven methods require time-ordered splits, realistic fees/spread/impact, turnover reporting and a paper/simulation-to-live gap assessment. Current frameworks FinRL-Meta and Qlib are reproducibility/reference infrastructure, not validation or proof of deployment. **Limit:** The IJCAI execution and market-making papers offer detailed formulations but use research datasets/simulators, not live broker execution. Ni, SAC and portfolio-MPC claims remain publisher-abstract level; their reported samples and results are study-specific. FinRL-Meta/Qlib document benchmark/workflow support, not a universal hardware requirement. No normalized cross-method compute, GPU, latency or capital requirement comparison was found in the inspected sources; absent a task-specific published benchmark, do not invent one. Commercial or operational hardware needs depend on data granularity, retraining frequency, latency and execution venue. **Relationship:** Order-book/market-state and order/inventory state -> execution or market-making action policy (classical schedule, MPC where an explicit model is optimized, contextual bandit when selecting from a defined action set, imitation+RL or RL where sequential policy learning is studied) -> fills, implementation shortfall, impact, inventory/adverse-selection and risk metrics. Separately, candidate portfolio + contextual feedback -> bandit selection; or forecasts/risk estimates + multi-period model -> MPC/RL allocation weights -> target holdings -> downstream execution. Do not connect by generic 'AI' label: add an edge only where the action/output actually feeds the next task and shared constraints are respected.
- **Claim:** Generative AI may produce features for a separate tabular forecaster, candidate assets, or weight vectors, but it does not inherently optimize a formal risk-return objective or enforce execution constraints; these must be checked downstream. LLM-generated candidate rules feed trial accounting and selection-aware/walk-forward safeguards. Published studies use differing prompts, risk preferences, universes, model versions, rebalance horizons and cost assumptions, and report mixed findings; none provides a normalized comparison to RL, contextual bandits, MPC or classical optimizers across the same task and datasets. **Locator:** 2025 Finance Research Letters publisher-indexed ChatGPT risk-appetite and Gemini/anonymized-data studies; 2026 JRFM publisher-indexed autonomous-allocation methods/results; existing LLM candidate-generation paper and trial-aware OOS preprint; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-FRL-CHATGPT-RISK-APPETITE-PORTFOLIO-2025, D011-FRL-GEMINI-NAIVE-PORTFOLIO-COUNTEREXAMPLE-2025, D011-JRFM-LLM-AUTONOMOUS-PORTFOLIO-ALLOCATORS-2026, D011-RISKNET-GENAI-EQUITY-FEATURE-DISCOVERY-2026, D011-IEEE-AGENTIC-LLM-STRATEGY-GENERATION-2026, D011-OLAGOKE-LLM-TRIAL-ADJUSTED-OUTSAMPLE-GATE-2026 **Area context:** Place prompt-based allocation after portfolio objectives and risk constraints, as an optional experiment. The learner must validate whether returned weights meet long-only/short, concentration, turnover and mandate rules and compare with equal-weight, market-cap, mean-variance, Black–Litterman or other relevant baselines under matched data and costs. If an LLM gives only a textual signal, pass it to a separate quantitative estimator/optimizer. LLM candidate creation increases the number of tested configurations and must be counted in the research log. **Limit:** Direct full-text inspection was limited by publisher access controls; the claim is restricted to abstract/indexed methods and outcome summaries. No study demonstrates regulated personalized advice, execution safety, general out-of-sample advantage, or a standard LLM-specific multiple-testing adjustment; broad hardware/latency comparisons are absent. **Relationship:** LLM prompt/model/version + timestamped inputs -> (retrieval-grounded feature -> separate forecaster -> optimizer) OR proposed asset set/weight vector -> explicit constraint/suitability check OR candidate strategy -> trial ledger and selection-aware validation -> time-ordered, cost-aware out-of-sample portfolio evaluation -> execution and monitoring. RL/bandit/MPC are not automatic successors to an LLM; choose only when the task requires sequential action, candidate-set adaptation or explicit finite-horizon optimization.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Excel is a documented spreadsheet environment with Solver optimization and basic statistical-analysis add-ins, and university course materials show it applied to finance tasks such as computing return/covariance matrices, constructing efficient frontiers and preparing data for backtesting. This supports Excel as a selectable learning/prototyping tool in portfolio analysis, distinct from specialized backtest and execution platforms. **Locator:** Microsoft Support pages for Solver and Analysis ToolPak; University of Warsaw Computational Finance registry (2025L/2026L); HSUHK/edX Portfolio Management course page. **Sources:** D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-SOLVER-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-ANALYSIS-TOOLPAK-2026, D011-UWARSAW-COMPUTATIONAL-FINANCE-EXCEL-2026, D011-HSUHK-EXCEL-PORTFOLIO-MOOCCOURSE-2019 **Area context:** The finance-course records place the spreadsheet after return and covariance foundations for exploratory portfolio analysis and educational optimization, with Bloomberg backtest-data preparation as a later handoff. **Limit:** Course examples do not prove industry prevalence or suitability for large, point-in-time, automated or production research. Solver and Analysis ToolPak documentation describes features, not financial-model validity, data provenance or robust numerical conditioning. **Relationship:** Clean return series feed descriptive/statistical analysis and covariance estimates; constraints and objective feed Solver to produce candidate weights/frontier; those outputs can become inputs to a specialist backtest where realistic universe, costs, rebalancing, fills and validation are modeled. Excel is complementary to advanced statistical/programming/backtesting tools and not a substitute for them.
- **Claim:** The traditional spreadsheet branch fits small educational and exploratory portfolio models: Excel Solver exposes objective, decision and constraint cells and supports a documented maximum of 200 variable cells; worksheets are limited to 1,048,576 rows, and Power Query can import/transform data subject to refresh/schema/locale/volume limitations. Excel's supported Show Changes history is retained for up to 60 days, not an immutable model or data-lineage log. A peer-reviewed spreadsheet-risk review supports independent testing and clear input/output structure, while warning that reported error rates come from old, heterogeneous studies and should not be generalized. When the portfolio optimization needs reusable objectives/constraints, solver alternatives, rolling rebalancing or larger datasets, R PortfolioAnalytics and Python PyPortfolioOpt provide code-based alternatives; an integrated platform such as LEAN connects research code to event-driven backtesting and live order/fill workflows, but explicitly requires reconciliation because simulated and live execution can differ. **Locator:** Microsoft Excel specifications, Solver and Show Changes pages; Microsoft Power Query Excel connector limitations; Powell, Baker and Lawson, Decision Support Systems 46 (2008), 128–138; CRAN PortfolioAnalytics 2.0.0 docs; PyPortfolioOpt 1.5.4 docs; QuantConnect Research Engine and Trading and Orders docs; inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-WORKSHEET-LIMITS-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-SOLVER-202-VARIABLE-LIMIT-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-SHOW-CHANGES-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-POWERQUERY-EXCEL-CONNECTOR-2026, D011-POWELL-BAKER-LAWSON-SPREADSHEET-ERROR-REVIEW-2008, D011-CRAN-PORTFOLIOANALYTICS-OPTIMIZATION-DOCS-2026, D011-PYPORTFOLIOOPT-OPTIMIZATION-DOCS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-RESEARCH-BACKTEST-LIVE-RECONCILIATION-2026 **Area context:** After return, covariance and portfolio-constraint foundations, Excel can make an initial allocation model visible and easy to inspect. A reusable R/Python optimizer is appropriate when the method needs explicit solver/objective/constraint variants or repeated rebalancing; a research/backtest platform is a further layer for point-in-time data, event-driven orders, fills, fees and slippage. Reporting in Excel can remain complementary after calculation moves to code/platforms. **Limit:** This is a function-based learning/tool map, not a universal tool ladder or role requirement. Excel's 200-variable Solver limit is not a universal 200-security limit; package documentation does not certify numerical results; LEAN's integrated backtest/live path is vendor-specific and does not eliminate data, parameter or fill-model error. Spreadsheet-error research is historical and heterogeneous, so it motivates tests/review rather than a general error-rate claim. **Relationship:** Small transparent portfolio objective + bounded dataset -> Excel Solver prototype and inspectable weights/report -> if the model exceeds its decision-variable/data/governance needs, port the same input/constraint/objective definitions into tested R/Python optimization code -> connect validated code to point-in-time backtest, cost/fill model and paper/live reconciliation. This is a scale/governance decision path, not a prerequisite claim that every learner must abandon Excel.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Current**
- **Claim:** Maintained tools can operationalize distinct parts of the systematic workflow: scikit-learn's TimeSeriesSplit preserves temporal ordering under its equal-spacing assumptions; ARCH implements bootstrap-based model-comparison procedures; LEAN documents a modular flow from research signals through target portfolio, risk adjustment and execution orders. **Locator:** Official scikit-learn time-series cross-validation guide; ARCH stable 7.2.0 multiple-comparison reference; QuantConnect LEAN Algorithm Framework v2 overview and module contracts. **Sources:** D011-SCIKIT-TIME-SERIES-SPLIT, D011-ARCH-MULTIPLE-COMPARISON-DOCS, D011-QUANTCONNECT-PORTFOLIO-TO-EXECUTION-FLOW **Area context:** These tools support time-aware evaluation, selected inferential checks and a research-to-order implementation pipeline; their functions are complementary and they are not substitutes for trading methods or validated market data. **Limit:** Project documentation proves feature/API behavior for the documented versions, not financial validity or universal institutional workflow. TimeSeriesSplit alone does not address overlapping labels, look-ahead, strategy search or execution-cost realism; LEAN is a vendor platform example. **Relationship:** Chronological splits and leakage controls precede model/strategy evaluation; statistical tests consume specified model-loss or return inputs; portfolio construction and risk modules transform signals into targets before orders, while executions and costs feed post-trade analysis.
- **Claim:** A current algorithmic research framework can separate signal generation, portfolio construction (converting insights to target holdings), risk management, and execution; it also exposes fill and slippage models for backtests. LEAN documents that built-in backtests assume complete fills unless customized and that its documented platform does not model market impact by default, while live fills are asynchronous and can differ from backtest assumptions. **Locator:** QuantConnect LEAN Algorithm Framework, portfolio-construction, fill-model and live reconciliation documentation opened 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-PORTFOLIO-CONSTRUCTION-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-FILL-MODELS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-BACKTEST-LIVE-RECONCILIATION-2026 **Area context:** A selectable computational implementation example that exposes where model outputs pass into target holdings and simulated execution, plus what those simulations omit unless explicitly modeled. **Limit:** Platform-specific documentation, not a neutral comparison or assurance that a backtest is realistic. Data resolution, broker, fees, fills, latency, market impact, corporate actions and survivorship/point-in-time behavior need task-specific checks. **Relationship:** Signal/Insight objects feed portfolio targets; targets feed risk checks and orders; fill/fee/slippage assumptions affect simulated returns; live reconciliation must compare actual fills/costs with the backtest. This implementation chain is complementary to, not a replacement for, statistical validation and multiple-testing controls.
- **Claim:** For Nigerian listed-market implementation, NGX publicly documents FIX real-time/delayed/end-of-day market-data and trading connectivity, an API for real-time/delayed/EOD data display with separate pricing/registration, FIX certification and ad-hoc application testing, and broker/dealer DMA through an OMS from a Certified Independent Software Vendor. CRSP describes U.S. listed equities; LSEG's documented dated-index example is not a guarantee for every market or field; DataScope breadth is a commercial coverage claim; QuantRocket relies on upstream products. Exact licensed dataset fields, history depth, non-U.S./futures/options/Nigerian coverage, missing event treatment and entitlements remain product-specific and must be sampled before use. **Relationship:** Dated security/index membership + identifier history + corporate-action and delisting events -> point-in-time investable universe and returns -> signal/portfolio estimation -> backtest outputs. A missing or retrospectively adjusted event can alter features, returns, weights and measured strategy performance; data flags do not by themselves validate fills, fees or live execution.
- **Claim:** The tool chain is a set of distinct layers, not competing all-in-one choices. Excel Solver is useful for transparent small optimizer prototypes but has documented workbook/variable limits; R PortfolioAnalytics and Python PyPortfolioOpt encode objectives and constraints, while the learner must supply appropriate inputs. scikit-learn time splits and ARCH comparison routines address separate validation operations. Qlib provides point-in-time quant-research/data/model workflows; FinRL-Meta packages RL research environments/benchmarks; neither is a live broker. LEAN links signal, target holdings, risk and order execution and documents how fills/backtest and live orders can diverge. QuantRocket catalogs upstream dataset coverage, while WRDS/CRSP, LSEG and NGX provide provider- or venue-specific data/access contexts. Select by task, data rights, asset coverage, reproducibility and output compatibility; do not infer that a solver or backtest engine supplies complete point-in-time data or realistic fills. **Locator:** Official Microsoft Solver and Excel worksheet/solver limits; CRAN PortfolioAnalytics and PyPortfolioOpt project documentation; scikit-learn TimeSeriesSplit and ARCH multiple-comparison API docs; Qlib current workflow/point-in-time documentation and FinRL-Meta repository; QuantConnect LEAN Framework, fill-model and live-reconciliation docs; QuantRocket dataset catalog; WRDS/CRSP and LSEG data-product records; NGX Technology Services; sources inspected 2026-10-27 to 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-SOLVER-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-WORKSHEET-LIMITS-2026, D011-MICROSOFT-EXCEL-SOLVER-202-VARIABLE-LIMIT-2026, D011-CRAN-PORTFOLIOANALYTICS-OPTIMIZATION-DOCS-2026, D011-PYPORTFOLIOOPT-OPTIMIZATION-DOCS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-PORTFOLIO-TO-EXECUTION-FLOW, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-PORTFOLIO-CONSTRUCTION-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-FILL-MODELS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-BACKTEST-LIVE-RECONCILIATION-2026, D011-QUANTROCKET-DATASET-DELISTED-COVERAGE-2026, D011-QLIB-CURRENT-REPO-WORKFLOW-DATA-SCOPE-2026, D011-FINRL-META-CURRENT-RESEARCH-REPO-2026, D011-WRDS-CRSP-STOCK-IDENTITY-CORPORATE-ACTIONS-DELISTING-2026, D011-LSEG-HISTORICAL-INDEX-CONSTITUENTS-API-2026, D011-NGX-TECHNOLOGY-SERVICES-FIX-API-DMA-2026, D011-ARCH-MULTIPLE-COMPARISON-DOCS, D011-SCIKIT-TIME-SERIES-SPLIT **Area context:** For a learner in systematic investing: establish point-in-time data and a defined universe first; use spreadsheet or code to prototype an objective/constraint set; choose a maintained research framework when versioning, repeated experiments or larger data demand it; validate chronological splits and selection bias; construct target weights; then model fills, fees, slippage and impact before any paper/live comparison. Excel is a reasonable bounded entry/prototype tool; code libraries support explicit reproducibility; Qlib/FinRL-Meta/LEAN serve different workflow roles. Nigeria adds NGX feed entitlements and certified participant/OMS requirements; this is a separate market-access layer, not a software-method prerequisite for every learner. **Limit:** This mapping compares documented functions and documented caveats, not price, empirical performance or institutional prevalence. Vendor/provider pages cannot establish data completeness; Excel limits are version-specific; open-source libraries require suitable inputs and independent validation; Qlib and FinRL-Meta are research infrastructure; LEAN's model assumptions need task-specific fill/impact calibration; NGX service descriptions do not grant access or prove the user's legal authorization. A sample-based audit and paper/live execution reconciliation remain implementation-specific and cannot be completed from public docs alone. **Relationship:** Point-in-time vendor/venue data + identifiers/events -> research features -> portfolio objective/constraints solved in a spreadsheet or code optimizer -> chronological/selection-aware validation -> targets and risk controls in a workflow engine -> fill/fee/slippage/impact model -> paper/live or venue reconciliation -> performance/cost report. Each stage has alternatives within its function, but inputs and outputs must match: an optimizer is not a data vendor, a research framework is not a market-access license, and a backtest is not live evidence.

**Mapped cell evidence — Tools, software and data, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Qiskit Finance 0.4.1 is an available, optional research-learning tool for inspecting portfolio optimization and related quantum-finance examples. Its tutorial demonstrates a software implementation route; the release record identifies 0.4.1 (February 2024) as the latest release reviewed. This is an existing research artifact, not a future-only tool or production platform. **Locator:** Qiskit Finance tutorial index, including portfolio optimization; official 0.4.1 release record and package metadata, inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-PRICING-TUTORIALS-0401, D011-QISKIT-FINANCE-RELEASE-0-4-1 **Area context:** In systematic investment, the tutorial supports an optional lab after learners can formulate a portfolio objective and compare it with classical optimization. It is useful for understanding encoding, circuit-based optimization and simulation boundaries, not for building a production strategy stack. **Limit:** The version is old and the tutorial does not establish current maintenance, hardware readiness, practical advantage or independently validated portfolio performance. Qiskit Finance is one research tool, not an exhaustive inventory of systematic-investment software. **Relationship:** Mandate, objective, constraints and classical baseline define the allocation problem first; Qiskit Finance then provides a research implementation path for selected quantum formulations. The resulting portfolio must still be evaluated with the same data, costs, constraints and out-of-sample controls as classical alternatives.
- **Claim:** Two distinct, optional open research frameworks extend the systematic-investment toolset. FinRL-Meta provides financial reinforcement-learning market environments and benchmark workflows that separate data, environment and agent layers so methods can be compared under shared conditions; its NeurIPS benchmark paper identifies low signal-to-noise, survivorship bias and backtest overfitting as material evaluation problems. The maintained project positions FinRL-Meta as a research/benchmark layer and distinguishes production-oriented FinRL-X/FinRL-Trading. Microsoft Qlib is a broader AI-oriented investment research framework supporting supervised prediction, market-dynamics modeling and reinforcement learning, with dataset/model/backtest/evaluation workflows, experiment recording and a point-in-time database. Its supplied examples cover selected US and China datasets, not every market. Neither framework is interchangeable with the other, a universal requirement, or proof of profitable or production-ready trading. **Locator:** FinRL-Meta, NeurIPS 2022 Datasets and Benchmarks paper and current project README; Microsoft Research Qlib paper; Qlib 0.9.7 stable documentation and current repository inspected 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-FINRL-META-NEURIPS-2022-BENCHMARKS-2026, D011-FINRL-META-CURRENT-RESEARCH-REPO-2026, D011-QLIB-MICROSOFT-RESEARCH-PAPER-2020, D011-QLIB-DOCS-0-9-7-AND-POINT-IN-TIME-2025, D011-QLIB-CURRENT-REPO-WORKFLOW-DATA-SCOPE-2026 **Area context:** After learners can define a strategy hypothesis, point-in-time data, temporal evaluation and classical baselines, Qlib can support broader predictive/model/backtest experiments while FinRL-Meta can support RL policy experiments in explicit market environments and shared benchmarks. Choose by research question: forecast/model comparison versus policy learning in an environment. The learner should retain a simple benchmark and record data, code, configuration and experiment versions before interpreting results. **Limit:** Framework documentation and a benchmark paper establish available workflows and known evaluation risks, not comparative performance, alpha, adoption, data completeness, licensing, live readiness or suitability for any particular market. Bundled example datasets are limited; verify current release/tag, data provenance, point-in-time semantics, temporal splits, transaction costs, slippage, execution and market-specific entitlements. The current repository and stable/PyPI releases can differ. **Relationship:** Point-in-time data + hypothesis + classical baseline -> (Qlib: features/prediction or market-dynamics model -> portfolio targets/backtest/evaluation) OR (FinRL-Meta: state/reward/action design + market environment -> learned policy/actions -> benchmark evaluation). These are alternative research workflow branches for different questions; their outputs feed portfolio and execution review only after temporal leakage, costs, baselines and environment assumptions are checked. A policy-action result is not automatically an executable order or live performance claim.
