- **Claim:** Established systematic-investment learning can be taught as a sequence from quantitative methods and portfolio principles into constrained construction, backtesting and evaluation. CFA's CBOK lists probability, regression, time-series/forecasting, volatility and model governance; its Portfolio Development and Construction module recommends prior portfolio-management and basic financial-modeling familiarity, then exercises IPS/constraints, MPT statistics, covariance matrices, efficient frontiers, optimization, backtesting and performance measures. **Locator:** CFA Institute CBOK page (2027 topic outline, inspected 2026-10-26); Portfolio Development and Construction Practical Skills Module page, including duration/prerequisite and stated learning objectives. **Sources:** D011-CFA-CBOK-2026, D011-CFA-PORTFOLIO-DEVELOPMENT-PSM-2026, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-PORTFOLIO-ANALYSIS-2026, D011-CFA-TRADE-STRATEGY-EXECUTION-2026 **Area context:** These resources give students an inspectable route from return/risk and portfolio foundations to research and portfolio outputs; the CFA module is one optional professional pathway, not a universal prerequisite or complete systematic-trading course. **Limit:** CFA curriculum evidence establishes its own learning objectives and recommended prerequisites. It does not establish universal employer requirements, method effectiveness, or that every learner needs the CFA credential. **Relationship:** Statistics, time-series analysis and financial modeling precede portfolio objectives and constraints; portfolio construction then produces weights/targets that can be backtested and reviewed using risk, return and benchmark measures before execution.

**Mapped cell evidence — Standards, credentials and learning resources, Current**
- **Claim:** Algorithmic trading is subject to venue- and jurisdiction-specific controls in addition to quantitative model validation: EU MiFID II Article 17 and ESMA supervisory materials address resilient systems, thresholds/limits, testing and monitoring; US SEC Rule 15c3-5 addresses risk-management controls for market access; Nigeria’s FX Code supplies conduct and disclosure expectations for the Nigerian FX market. **Locator:** Official ESMA MiFID II Article 17 text and 2026 supervisory briefing; SEC Rule 15c3-5 text/FAQ; Central Bank of Nigeria Nigerian FX Code 2025 primary code and implementation materials. **Sources:** D011-ESMA-MIFID-II-ARTICLE-17-ALGO-TRADING, D011-ESMA-ALGO-TRADING-SUPERVISORY-BRIEFING-2026, D011-SEC-RULE-15C3-5-FINAL-2011, D011-SEC-MARKET-ACCESS-FAQ-STAFF, D011-CBN-NIGERIAN-FX-CODE-PRIMARY-2025, D011-CBN-NIGERIAN-FX-CODE-ALGO-DISCLOSURE-2025 **Area context:** These standards and rules constrain development, testing, access and operation of systematic/algorithmic trading in their stated entities and markets; they complement quantitative strategy and execution learning rather than teach a single algorithm. **Limit:** Rules differ by jurisdiction, firm category, instrument and activity. Do not generalize the EU/US regimes to Nigeria or treat the Nigerian FX Code as a global trading regulation; verify current legal text and entity-specific scope. **Relationship:** Pre-deployment testing, risk limits, monitoring and market-access controls surround strategies and order execution. They do not establish alpha validity; strategy validation and execution-cost measurement remain separate technical tasks.
- **Claim:** Nigeria's current primary statute is the Investments and Securities Act 2025 (Act No. 2), published in the Federal Gazette; SEC Nigeria states it repealed the 2007 Act. The SEC website still lists its Robo-Advisory Rules as dated 30 August 2021 and describes them under the prior statutory framework. Therefore the older Robo-Advisory rules, derivatives rules and exchange materials must be checked against the 2025 Act and current subsidiary instruments before being presented as current obligations. The Act's existence/repeal context is established; the exact current algorithmic-trading rule status is not resolved by this source packet. **Locator:** Investments and Securities Act 2025, Official Gazette title page and SEC Nigeria's current Act notice; SEC Rules for FinTechs page, Robo-Advisory section dated 30 August 2021; opened 2026-10-27. **Sources:** D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ISA-2025-OFFICIAL-GAZETTE, D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ROBO-ADVISORY-RULES **Area context:** This local regulatory finding affects whether Nigerian systematic strategies can be researched, advised, routed or operated by a particular entity and venue. Keep algorithmic strategy governance, robo-advisory portfolio management, exchange membership and derivatives surveillance as separate regulatory questions. **Limit:** No legal advice or detailed interpretation. The source packet has not matched every legacy subsidiary rule to the 2025 Act, determined commencement/transitional effects or reviewed current NGX Regulation rules. Do not claim that the 2021 robo-advisory rule is repealed or remains fully operative without exact legal reconciliation. **Relationship:** Identify activity (research, investment advice, portfolio management, brokerage, exchange dealing, derivatives) + entity + instrument + venue -> retrieve current Act and subsidiary/exchange rules -> verify registration, controls and approval -> document jurisdiction-specific implementation. A broad term 'algorithmic trading' does not by itself determine the applicable rule.
- **Claim:** Algorithmic-trading controls are layered by jurisdiction, entity and venue rather than supplied by one universal rule. EU MiFID II Article 17 places system resilience, limits, testing, monitoring and records on investment firms engaging in algorithmic trading; ESMA's 2026 briefing is nonbinding supervisory guidance on governance, testing, outsourcing and pre-trade controls. U.S. securities Rule 15c3-5 concerns broker-dealer market access. In U.S. futures, the CFTC's final Electronic Trading Risk Principles apply to DCMs, including participant rules, pre-trade controls on electronic orders and significant-disruption notices; the distinct Regulation AT proposal was withdrawn in 2020. In Nigeria, ISA 2025 gives SEC rulemaking jurisdiction over derivatives and digital/virtual-asset services, while the SEC-approved NGX derivatives rulebook available here is dated 2019 and documents member-side erroneous-order, product/position-limit and trade-reporting controls. Current consolidated Nigerian subsidiary-rule status remains unverified. Professional curricula and credentials (CFA/GARP) teach relevant knowledge but are not, by themselves, legal authorization or universal job requirements. **Locator:** Official ESMA MiFID II Article 17 and 2026 supervisory briefing; SEC Rule 15c3-5 and staff FAQ; CFTC 17 CFR Part 38 Electronic Trading Risk Principles final rule (2021) and Regulation AT withdrawal (2020); Nigeria Investments and Securities Act 2025 §§3, 355; SEC Nigeria current rules listing; NGX derivatives rulebook (2019) Rules 5.2, 5.8 and 5.9/current NGX interpretative-guidance index; CFA/GARP current curriculum cards. **Sources:** D011-ESMA-MIFID-II-ARTICLE-17-ALGO-TRADING, D011-ESMA-ALGO-TRADING-SUPERVISORY-BRIEFING-2026, D011-SEC-RULE-15C3-5-FINAL-2011, D011-SEC-MARKET-ACCESS-FAQ-STAFF, D011-CFTC-ELECTRONIC-TRADING-RISK-PRINCIPLES-2021, D011-CFTC-REG-AT-WITHDRAWAL-2020, D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ISA-2025-OFFICIAL-GAZETTE, D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ROBO-ADVISORY-RULES, D011-NGX-DERIVATIVES-RULEBOOK-SEC-APPROVED-2019, D011-GARP-FRM-CURRICULUM-2026, D011-CFA-TRADE-STRATEGY-EXECUTION-2026, D011-CFA-CBOK-2026 **Area context:** This is a contextual standards/resource layer around systematic research and order implementation. Learners first identify activity, entity, instrument and venue; then study the exact controls relevant to that setting. The EU/US examples are comparative, while Nigerian activity requires its own current SEC, NGX and applicable intermediary-rule verification. **Limit:** Not legal advice or a complete compliance analysis. The SEC Rule 15c3-5 page is broker-dealer market-access scope; MiFID II has EU entity/activity scope; CFTC principles primarily bind DCMs; ESMA briefing is nonbinding; the NGX rulebook is dated and not reconciled against all post-2025 instruments. Do not teach withdrawn Regulation AT proposals as law, or infer that a CFA/GARP credential confers trading permissions. **Relationship:** Strategy research and backtest validation -> exchange/broker/venue access and instrument selection -> entity- and venue-specific governance, testing, limits, monitoring and records -> orders/fills and post-trade review. These controls complement strategy validity and execution-cost analysis; credentials/resources support learning, while legal permissions and obligations are a separate jurisdictional branch.
- **Claim:** The Nigeria branch must distinguish securities/derivatives venue activity, regulated advisory, proprietary dealing, client-account service, and digital-asset service. ISA 2025 empowers SEC rulemaking/registration in derivatives and digital/virtual-asset areas. FMDQ's official materials document SEC-approved derivatives rules amended in May 2024, clearing and member categories for own-account versus client trading, and FGN bond and Naira FX futures (with separate cleared/OTC FX products). NGX publishes its 2019 SEC-approved derivatives rulebook and 2022 interpretative guidance; its current rules index shows SEC-approved 2026 trading-hours/pricing amendments but does not show a clearly named post-2019 derivatives-rule amendment in this search. SEC's current public materials still list robo-advisory rules and digital-asset rules, while the 2024 digital-asset amendments document is expressly an exposure draft; 2025–2026 ARIP notices show conditional VASP onboarding, not a full licence. No exchange-listed options were identified in the inspected FMDQ/NGX product catalogs, and no single public rule specifically covering every Nigerian algorithmic trading activity was found. Apply controls by entity, activity, product, venue and client/proprietary context; do not treat proposed text or professional credentials as law/authorization. **Locator:** ISA 2025 Official Gazette §§3 and 355; SEC current Rules/FinTech rule pages, SEC-hosted digital-assets exposure draft and ARIP VASP framework/status notice; FMDQ SEC-approved derivatives rules and 2024 annual-report amendment confirmation, ETD product and trading-membership records; NGX 2019 derivatives rulebook, NGX RegCo 2022 interpretative guidance, current SEC-approved rules archive; indexed and inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D011-FMDQ-DERIVATIVES-RULES-AMENDED-2024, D011-FMDQ-ETD-PRODUCTS-AND-MARKET-STRUCTURE-2026, D011-FMDQ-DERIVATIVES-MEMBERSHIP-OWN-CLIENT-2026, D011-NGX-DERIVATIVES-INTERPRETATIVE-GUIDANCE-2022, D011-NGX-TRADING-MEMBER-RULES-ARCHIVE-2026, D011-SEC-DIGITAL-ASSET-RULES-AMENDMENT-EXPOSURE-2024, D011-SEC-ARIP-VASP-FRAMEWORK-2024, D011-SEC-ARIP-STATUS-AUG-2026, D011-SEC-REGISTERED-FINTECH-OPERATORS-2025, D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ISA-2025-OFFICIAL-GAZETTE, D011-SEC-NIGERIA-ROBO-ADVISORY-RULES **Area context:** For this area, standards/resources appear as a conditional implementation branch after a learner has specified whether they are studying listed securities, exchange-traded/OTC derivatives, automated client advice, client execution, proprietary dealing, or virtual-asset services. The activity determines which SEC, exchange, clearing/member and market-access materials apply. FMDQ/NGX rule documents contextualize Nigerian futures and execution; US/EU sources in the preceding claim remain comparative examples, not Nigerian rules. **Limit:** Bounded public-source map, not legal advice or exhaustive current-law certification. The SEC digital-asset amendment is a draft; NGX direct archive fetch timed out and the 2019 rulebook has not been legally reconciled provision-by-provision with ISA 2025; FMDQ's latest derivatives amendments located are May 2024, but later member notices/directives may exist. Catalog absence does not establish that options or OTC contracts are unavailable in Nigeria. SEC approval-in-principle is not final authorization. Verify live rules and entity permissions with the regulator, exchange and clearing member before operational use. **Relationship:** Learning in the market/task -> classify actor (software provider, adviser, fund manager, dealer, broker/dealer, trading member, VASP) + product (equity/security, FGN bond/FX futures, OTC/cleared FX, virtual asset) + venue/client relation -> select relevant SEC rules, exchange rules, clearing/member controls and local access requirements -> pre-trade risk/order checks -> reporting, clearing and monitoring. **Mapped cell evidence — Outputs and downstream role context, Traditional**
- **Claim:** A systematic investment workflow produces distinct outputs in sequence: a forecast or signal, portfolio targets/weights, orders and an execution schedule, realized fills and costs, then benchmark-relative and risk-adjusted performance measures. Optimal-execution research explicitly trades off expected market-impact costs against price-volatility risk; current curriculum distinguishes active-return attribution and ex-ante from realized risk/return. **Locator:** Almgren and Chriss, Journal of Risk (2001) publisher abstract; CFA Institute 2026 Active Portfolio Management reading; LEAN portfolio-construction docs for signal-to-target interface. **Sources:** D011-JOR-ALMGREN-CHRISS-OPTIMAL-EXECUTION-2001, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-PORTFOLIO-ANALYSIS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-PORTFOLIO-CONSTRUCTION-2026 **Area context:** Defines traditional decision and work-product boundaries from active forecast through allocation/execution and evaluation. These outputs connect investment research to portfolio-management and trading tasks without collapsing them into one item. **Limit:** The execution paper is abstract-level and curricula are instructional. These sources do not establish universal organizational handoffs, return targets or role prevalence; exact route/task links require current canonical role evidence. **Relationship:** Research signal informs target positions; risk limits and portfolio constraints adjust targets; execution design turns orders into time/price/quantity decisions; fills and costs feed realized attribution/performance. Backtest metrics are only credible when the simulated execution/cost assumptions fit the intended data and market.
- **Claim:** A portfolio-analysis learning workflow can yield explicit return and covariance matrices, efficient-frontier portfolios, minimum-variance and optimal-risky weights; these are allocation outputs that can be exported for later backtesting. The selected course uses Excel for those calculations and backtest-data preparation, while active-management curriculum evaluates active-return attribution and risk-adjusted outcomes. **Locator:** HSUHK/edX Portfolio Management course page; University of Warsaw Computational Finance registry; CFA Institute 2026 Active Portfolio Management curriculum. **Sources:** D011-HSUHK-EXCEL-PORTFOLIO-MOOCCOURSE-2019, D011-UWARSAW-COMPUTATIONAL-FINANCE-EXCEL-2026, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-PORTFOLIO-ANALYSIS-2026 **Area context:** Separates spreadsheet-derived candidate allocations from strategy research and later execution/performance outcomes, making an actionable route from portfolio foundations into optimization and evaluation visible. **Limit:** Instructional artifacts show course assignments, not validated live performance or universal professional outputs. The output depends on return estimation, constraints, benchmark and risk preferences; a spreadsheet frontier is not itself a robust investment recommendation. **Relationship:** Estimated returns/covariance and investor constraints feed optimization; candidate weights move downstream into risk controls, backtesting and order generation; fills and costs then change realized portfolio and performance attribution. Each transition needs its own data and validation checks.
- **Claim:** Systematic investing yields a linked but separable evidence and decision record: research tests candidate signals/models; portfolio construction converts approved forecasts or risk views into target holdings under a mandate and benchmark; execution converts targets to orders and schedules; fills, explicit costs, slippage and market impact determine realized positions and net results; performance measurement reports total return/risk, attribution explains the return/risk sources, and appraisal evaluates the process against suitable benchmarks and constraints. O*NET's broad quantitative-financial-analyst task profile explicitly includes developing portfolio-construction, optimization, performance-measurement, attribution and P&L tools; current employer records separately show research, trading, development and risk-analysis examples. These are conditional handoffs, not interchangeable role duties. **Locator:** CFA Institute 2026 Portfolio Performance Evaluation (public page: learning outcomes and summary); CFA Institute 2026 Active Portfolio Management; O*NET 13-2099.01 tasks; current indexed Jane Street, Citadel, Point72 and BlackRock task sources; LEAN framework documentation and Almgren–Chriss (2001). Inspected/source-checked 2026-10-28 or in the dated prior task pass. **Sources:** D011-CFA-PORTFOLIO-PERFORMANCE-EVALUATION-2026, D011-SEC-ADVISER-MARKETING-PERFORMANCE-FAQ-2026, D011-OXFORD-EQUITY-PORTFOLIO-CAPACITY-2012, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-EQUITY-PORTFOLIO-2026, D011-CFA-ACTIVE-PORTFOLIO-ANALYSIS-2026, D011-CFA-TRADE-STRATEGY-EXECUTION-2026, D011-CFA-TCA-2026, D011-ONET-QFA-2026, D011-JS-QUANT-RESEARCHER-2026, D011-JS-QUANT-TRADER-2026, D011-P72-QUANT-DEV-TRADING-RESEARCH-2026, D011-BLACKROCK-QUANT-INVESTING-ANALYST-2026, D011-BLACKROCK-RQA-CAREER-2026, D011-NGX-TECHNOLOGY-SERVICES-FIX-API-DMA-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-PORTFOLIO-CONSTRUCTION-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-FILL-MODELS-2026, D011-QUANTCONNECT-LEAN-BACKTEST-LIVE-RECONCILIATION-2026, D011-JOR-ALMGREN-CHRISS-OPTIMAL-EXECUTION-2001 **Area context:** This connects financial research and portfolio optimization to implementation and review, while preserving separate decisions: a signal is not a portfolio, a target is not a fill, gross backtest return is not realized net performance, and appraisal is not the same operation as return measurement. **Limit:** CFA curriculum and O*NET describe broad analytical tasks; employer examples are task- and employer-specific; LEAN is one platform implementation and its fill/cost behavior is platform-specific. The outputs do not prove strategy validity or guaranteed profitability. The current exact 23/23 route dispositions remain conditional or bounded and do not alter stored fit/routes. **Relationship:** Point-in-time data and tested research -> candidate signal/forecast -> mandate, benchmark, constraints and risk model -> target weights/positions -> order strategy/schedule -> actual fills and transaction costs -> holdings/returns/risk -> measurement -> attribution -> appraisal and monitoring. **Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Traditional**
- **Claim:** An established vehicle-control foundation needs consistent vehicle-motion vocabulary and a clear distinction between geometric path-tracking assumptions and actual vehicle/actuator response. The historical Pure Pursuit implementation uses a vehicle-frame geometry and a lookahead path point but explicitly does not model vehicle capability or actuator lag; it therefore cannot by itself establish that requested curvature will be realized. **Locator:** ISO 8855:2011 public status/abstract; Coulter, CMU-RI-TR-92-01, full text reopened 2026-10-26, sections 1–3 and 4.3 (rear-axle frame, geometric curvature, actuator/dynamics limits). **Sources:** D166-ISO-8855-2011-VEHICLE-DYNAMICS, D166-CMU-PURE-PURSUIT-1992 **Area context:** This distinguishes the geometric controller concept from the dynamics and interface knowledge needed to apply its command to a real vehicle. It supports vehicle frames, motion terminology, path geometry and awareness of plant/actuator assumptions as foundational knowledge for this area. **Limit:** ISO 8855 is a terminology standard, and the CMU report describes a historical mobile-robot/NavLab implementation. These sources do not form a complete vehicle-dynamics curriculum or quantify tire/friction, stability or actuator models for modern AV platforms. **Relationship:** Coordinate/vehicle-motion terms and the rear-axle reference support interpretation of the path geometry; the geometric curvature command then depends on the vehicle and actuator dynamics to become actual motion. The report explicitly identifies this model gap; it is not a universal teaching sequence.
- **Claim:** Vehicle-motion control builds on vehicle axes/equations of motion, longitudinal/lateral dynamics, tire slip/force generation and friction limits, steering/actuator response, and estimation of states not measured directly. The needed model fidelity depends on speed, slip, combined braking/cornering, vehicle and operating domain. **Locator:** University of Zagreb 2025/26 course schedule/outcomes; Autoware MPC model options; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D166-UNIZAGREB-VEHICLE-DYNAMICS-CONTROL-2025-26, D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-MATHWORKS-VEHICLE-DYNAMICS-BLOCKSET-R2026B **Area context:** Foundations for converting planned paths/speeds into motion commands and choosing a vehicle model for the actual operating regime. **Limit:** Sources do not set a universal threshold for kinematic versus dynamic models; it depends on vehicle, tire, ODD and validation evidence. **Relationship:** Trajectory/speed + estimated pose/velocity/actuator state -> select suitable vehicle/tire model -> compute steering/longitudinal command -> validate tracking, stability and comfort. Detailed suspension/powertrain knowledge is conditional on whether it affects the controlled plant.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Current**
- **Claim:** A current vehicle-control foundation must connect the planned trajectory to the estimated vehicle state, steering feedback, a vehicle-response model and the interface that realizes commands. Autoware's controller documentation makes these dependencies concrete, including reference trajectory, odometry, steering state, model assumptions and downstream command-realization assumptions. **Locator:** Autoware Trajectory Follower Nodes, MPC Lateral Controller and PID Longitudinal Controller; sections Purpose, Design, Assumptions/Known Limits and Inputs/Outputs/API, reopened 2026-10-26. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-TRAJECTORY-FOLLOWER-CONTROL, D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-AUTOWARE-PID-LONGITUDINAL-CONTROLLER **Area context:** This establishes the control-area bridge between upstream planning/localization and vehicle actuation: learners need to understand state/reference/model alignment and actuator-interface assumptions before interpreting a tracking controller's output. **Limit:** These are Autoware interface and implementation assumptions, not a complete vehicle-dynamics curriculum or universal AV prerequisite list. Full foundations in tire forces, friction limits, actuator dynamics, sampling, delay and stability still need independent source mapping by vehicle regime. **Relationship:** Planning supplies a reference trajectory; localization/vehicle feedback supplies current state and steering; the selected vehicle model and controller produce tracking commands; the vehicle interface must realize those commands. Those are data/task dependencies in this project, not all mandatory course-order edges.
- **Claim:** Vehicle-motion control builds on vehicle axes/equations of motion, longitudinal/lateral dynamics, tire slip/force generation and friction limits, steering/actuator response, and estimation of states not measured directly. The needed model fidelity depends on speed, slip, combined braking/cornering, vehicle and operating domain. **Locator:** University of Zagreb 2025/26 course schedule/outcomes; Autoware MPC model options; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D166-UNIZAGREB-VEHICLE-DYNAMICS-CONTROL-2025-26, D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-MATHWORKS-VEHICLE-DYNAMICS-BLOCKSET-R2026B **Area context:** Foundations for converting planned paths/speeds into motion commands and choosing a vehicle model for the actual operating regime. **Limit:** Sources do not set a universal threshold for kinematic versus dynamic models; it depends on vehicle, tire, ODD and validation evidence. **Relationship:** Trajectory/speed + estimated pose/velocity/actuator state -> select suitable vehicle/tire model -> compute steering/longitudinal command -> validate tracking, stability and comfort. Detailed suspension/powertrain knowledge is conditional on whether it affects the controlled plant.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Emerging**
- **Claim:** A source-inspected emerging model-adaptation path keeps a nominal physical vehicle model and adds a learned residual from recorded vehicle behavior. Its prerequisites therefore include a usable nominal model, synchronized motion/steering/acceleration data, training/validation separation, simulation evaluation and checks of mismatch/generalization; the evidence also documents failure under one large heavy-bus mismatch. **Locator:** Autoware Smart MPC Trajectory Follower documentation, reopened 2026-10-26; training-data conversion, training/validation directory handling, residual fitting, simulation tests and limitations; cross-check with ICRA 2024 LMPC paper record/abstract. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-SMART-MPC-LEARNING-CONTROL, D166-ICRA-LMPC-ERROR-DYNAMICS-IAC-2024 **Area context:** This is an emerging competency branch for learning-augmented vehicle dynamics/control research, following the learner's understanding of the nominal plant and conventional MPC baseline; it is not a prerequisite for ordinary tracking-controller work. **Limit:** One experimental Autoware project and one IAC research program, with ICRA full text unavailable in this pass. Neither establishes on-road maturity, universal safety, transfer to production fleets or general benefit from learning. **Relationship:** Nominal vehicle dynamics and measured vehicle data support residual-model estimation; validation data and simulation test parameter variation; only then is the learned residual considered for integration into the model-based controller. The implementation reports mismatch limits, so generalization remains a separate validation task.
- **Claim:** Emerging control includes model-residual learning around MPC/iLQR/MPPI, learned local policies and end-to-end/foundation-model systems that may emit trajectories or direct actuation. Evidence spans Autoware experiments, racing/off-road demonstrations and research reviews; public-road transfer and safe production use remain unestablished. **Locator:** Autoware Smart MPC docs; IAC racing papers; CMU-RI-TR-25-55; 2026 foundation-model and end-to-end reviews; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-SMART-MPC-LEARNING-CONTROL, D166-ICRA-LMPC-ERROR-DYNAMICS-IAC-2024, D166-SONG-ETAL-IAC-FBL-MPC-2026, D166-CMU-OFFROAD-RL-VEHICLE-CONTROL-2025, D166-FOUNDATION-MODELS-ADS-SURVEY-2026, D166-E2E-ADS-ARCHITECTURES-CONTROL-REVIEW-2026 **Area context:** Optional research branch after model-based controller, vehicle dynamics and closed-loop simulation foundations; residual learning, local policy and direct actuation are different designs with different interfaces. **Limit:** Racing/off-road results are ODD-specific; reviews/prototypes do not show public-road safety, certification or universal performance gains. **Relationship:** Nominal model/controller -> collect representative data or define policy -> train residual/local policy -> simulate for robustness/constraints -> HIL/vehicle evaluation and safety monitoring. If the learned output is a trajectory, a conventional tracker may consume it; direct actuation needs explicit vehicle interface and fallback evidence.

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Traditional**
- **Claim:** A documented conventional tracking design separates lateral path tracking from longitudinal speed/acceleration tracking: Pure Pursuit is a geometric lateral tracker, while PID feedback is used for longitudinal velocity tracking in Autoware's current follower. A bounded autonomous-racing integration report also describes geometric lateral plus PID longitudinal control. These are distinct axis-specific method examples, not three interchangeable controllers or a universal AV architecture. **Locator:** Coulter, CMU-RI-TR-92-01, sections 1–3; Autoware trajectory follower mode documentation reopened 2026-10-26; A2RL 2024 competition lessons publisher/indexed text, inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D166-CMU-PURE-PURSUIT-1992, D166-AUTOWARE-TRAJECTORY-FOLLOWER-CONTROL, D166-AUTOWARE-PID-LONGITUDINAL-CONTROLLER, D166-A2RL-COMPETITION-LESSONS-2024 **Area context:** Maps baseline controller designs to the core trajectory-following task and shows why the path-tracking and speed-control branches should be explained separately before introducing constrained predictive or learned methods. **Limit:** CMU is a 1992 historical implementation report; Autoware documents one maintained stack; A2RL is a single competition context. This evidence does not rank controllers, generalize racing results to road vehicles, or show that every stack uses this pairing. **Relationship:** A reference path and current pose feed geometric lateral tracking; desired speed/acceleration and speed feedback feed longitudinal PID; the two command streams are synchronized by the stack before vehicle-specific execution. Their composition is documented only in these implementations.
- **Claim:** A trajectory plus odometry/steering feedback enters lateral and longitudinal controllers, which emit steering and velocity/acceleration commands. Autoware documents Pure Pursuit or MPC for lateral tracking and PID for longitudinal tracking; Apollo documents an LQR lateral implementation. They are axis- and interface-specific alternatives, not a single prerequisite ladder. **Locator:** Autoware trajectory follower, Pure Pursuit, MPC and PID API/design pages; Apollo control tuning guide; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-TRAJECTORY-FOLLOWER-CONTROL, D166-AUTOWARE-PURE-PURSUIT-CONTROLLER-CURRENT, D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-AUTOWARE-PID-LONGITUDINAL-CONTROLLER, D166-APOLLO-CONTROL-TUNING **Area context:** Control methods after trajectory/state inputs and vehicle dynamics; selection depends on axis, model, speed/curvature, actuator delay, constraints, compute period and validation target. **Limit:** Project docs establish implementations, not independent ranking or road safety. **Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Current**
- **Claim:** A maintained AV stack combines distinct lateral- and longitudinal-control designs: Autoware configures lateral tracking as MPC or Pure Pursuit, while its documented trajectory-follower node currently uses PID for longitudinal velocity tracking. These address different axes and should not be displayed as three interchangeable choices for one task. **Locator:** Autoware Trajectory Follower Nodes, Parameters section (`lateral_controller_mode`: `mpc` or `pure_pursuit`; currently only PID longitudinal controller), reopened 2026-10-26; corresponding MPC/PID design pages. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-TRAJECTORY-FOLLOWER-CONTROL, D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-AUTOWARE-PID-LONGITUDINAL-CONTROLLER **Area context:** Shows one current controller architecture and method choice for following a planner trajectory: lateral path tracking is selected separately from longitudinal target-speed/acceleration tracking. **Limit:** This documents Autoware's current configuration only; it does not rank MPC against Pure Pursuit, prove PID is the universal longitudinal method, or establish that the same design fits every vehicle, speed, ODD or safety case. **Relationship:** Reference path and vehicle state enter lateral control; reference speed/acceleration and speed state enter longitudinal control. **Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Current research demonstrates distinct learning-augmented designs: LMPC can add locally learned error dynamics to a nominal nonlinear physics model; a racing RL design uses risk-aware jump-start/curriculum learning with nonlinear MPC; and a separate full-scale racing framework uses high-level feedback-linearized MPC with lower-level yaw-rate/acceleration controllers. These are different architectures and evidence levels, not one compulsory ladder. **Locator:** ICRA 2024 LMPC bibliographic record/abstract; PubMed abstract for risk-conscious jump-start RL, IEEE Transactions on Cybernetics 55(2), 2025; Control Engineering Practice 174 (2026) article metadata/abstract for reduced-order feedback-linearized MPC. **Sources:** D166-ICRA-LMPC-ERROR-DYNAMICS-IAC-2024, D166-RISK-AWARE-JUMPSTART-RL-RACING-2025, D166-SONG-ETAL-IAC-FBL-MPC-2026 **Area context:** These research designs extend model-based control through local learned corrections, policy learning or hierarchical linearized MPC for autonomous-racing trajectory tracking. They belong as optional emerging method branches after vehicle dynamics, trajectory tracking and MPC/model assumptions are understood. **Limit:** The papers concern specific racing vehicles/tracks; ICRA and 2026 publisher full texts were inaccessible here, and the RL record is abstract-only. They do not establish road-vehicle transfer, production prevalence, safety approval or comparative superiority. **Relationship:** Learned error models complement nominal dynamics inside one LMPC design; nonlinear MPC constrains action generation in one RL design; the feedback-linearized study decomposes high-level and low-level control loops. These are study-specific architectures, not relationships that must be combined for every learner.
- **Claim:** Emerging control includes model-residual learning around MPC/iLQR/MPPI, learned local policies and end-to-end/foundation-model systems that may emit trajectories or direct actuation. Evidence spans Autoware experiments, racing/off-road demonstrations and research reviews; public-road transfer and safe production use remain unestablished. **Locator:** Autoware Smart MPC docs; IAC racing papers; CMU-RI-TR-25-55; 2026 foundation-model and end-to-end reviews; inspected 2026-10-28. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-SMART-MPC-LEARNING-CONTROL, D166-ICRA-LMPC-ERROR-DYNAMICS-IAC-2024, D166-SONG-ETAL-IAC-FBL-MPC-2026, D166-CMU-OFFROAD-RL-VEHICLE-CONTROL-2025, D166-FOUNDATION-MODELS-ADS-SURVEY-2026, D166-E2E-ADS-ARCHITECTURES-CONTROL-REVIEW-2026 **Area context:** Optional research branch after model-based controller, vehicle dynamics and closed-loop simulation foundations; residual learning, local policy and direct actuation are different designs with different interfaces. **Limit:** Racing/off-road results are ODD-specific; reviews/prototypes do not show public-road safety, certification or universal performance gains. **Relationship:** Nominal model/controller -> collect representative data or define policy -> train residual/local policy -> simulate for robustness/constraints -> HIL/vehicle evaluation and safety monitoring. If the learned output is a trajectory, a conventional tracker may consume it; direct actuation needs explicit vehicle interface and fallback evidence.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Pure Pursuit selects a path goal at a lookahead distance, transforms that goal into vehicle coordinates, computes the connecting arc's curvature and requests steering. The lookahead parameter changes convergence/oscillation behavior; the report warns that the technique omits vehicle/actuator dynamics and can lose tracking when path curvature or steering lag exceeds its assumptions. **Locator:** Coulter, CMU-RI-TR-92-01, full text reopened 2026-10-26; sections 2.0, 3.3, 4.1 and 4.3; Autoware current trajectory-follower mode docs confirm Pure Pursuit remains one selectable lateral implementation in that stack. **Sources:** D166-CMU-PURE-PURSUIT-1992, D166-AUTOWARE-TRAJECTORY-FOLLOWER-CONTROL **Area context:** This supplies an item-level explanation of how a traditional geometric path-tracking technique turns a reference path and current pose into a steering-curvature request, and why model-based controllers add vehicle response and constraint information. **Limit:** Historical robot/NavLab report and one current software implementation; not a current comparative benchmark, parameter recommendation or assurance that Pure Pursuit meets a vehicle's handling/safety envelope. **Relationship:** Path points and vehicle pose determine a lookahead goal; the goal geometry produces curvature; the vehicle controller converts that request into steering. Vehicle dynamics and actuator behavior determine whether the request tracks the path, so those are complementary modeling/validation concerns rather than part of the geometric formula itself.
- **Claim:** A trajectory plus odometry/steering feedback enters lateral and longitudinal controllers, which emit steering and velocity/acceleration commands. **Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Current**
- **Claim:** Autoware's lateral MPC predicts vehicle response and solves a QP, with kinematic bicycle models (with or without steering delay) and a dynamic bicycle model including slip angle; it offers an unconstrained least-squares solver or OSQP. Its longitudinal PID design combines reference-acceleration feedforward with velocity-error feedback, plus configurable slope/delay compensation. These are implementation techniques with explicit configuration and model assumptions. **Locator:** Autoware MPC Lateral Controller, Design, model/solver options, trajectory-reference and filtering sections; Autoware PID Longitudinal Controller, feedforward/feedback and slope-compensation sections, reopened 2026-10-26. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-MPC-LATERAL-CONTROLLER, D166-AUTOWARE-PID-LONGITUDINAL-CONTROLLER **Area context:** Provides concrete selectable techniques for designing and tuning vehicle tracking controllers, and exposes the dependency on model choice, solver, trajectory parameterization, filtering, vehicle feedback and interface behavior. **Limit:** Project documentation establishes available implementations and known assumptions, not accuracy or safety comparisons. The MPC defaults target a named Lexus RX configuration below 40 km/h; PID slope compensation has interface caveats and may be unnecessary for vehicles exposing target speed. **Relationship:** The vehicle model and current pose/steering predict response; the QP selects lateral commands. The longitudinal feedforward term uses trajectory acceleration and slope, while feedback corrects tracking error. Controller output depends on the vehicle's lower-level interface and must be validated with its dynamics and actuator response.

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Emerging technical alternatives include locally regressing model-error dynamics within LMPC; expert-initialized, risk-conscious policy mutations trained across track difficulty while NMPC supplies constrained actions; and reduced-order feedback linearization with separate yaw-rate and acceleration loops. They differ in what is learned, where optimization remains, and the output/controller contract. **Locator:** ICRA 2024 LMPC abstract/metadata; PubMed abstract for risk-conscious jump-start RL (2025); publisher abstract/record for full-scale IAC feedback-linearized MPC (2026). **Sources:** D166-ICRA-LMPC-ERROR-DYNAMICS-IAC-2024, D166-RISK-AWARE-JUMPSTART-RL-RACING-2025, D166-SONG-ETAL-IAC-FBL-MPC-2026 **Area context:** These algorithmic choices are research-level control techniques that build on vehicle-state/dynamics representations, conventional control objectives and trajectory tracking; their evidence belongs in an emerging branch, not in compulsory basic control selection. **Limit:** Available sources are limited to abstracts and one racing evaluation program. They provide no matched cross-method benchmark, public-road safety evidence or generalization guarantee. **Relationship:** Local residual regression modifies the predictive model; RL learns a policy but retains an NMPC action component in the cited design; feedback linearization changes the control decomposition. Each yields a different route for evaluating tracking and constraint behavior; none implies learning must precede or replace the other methods.

The docs describe model mismatch failures as well as improvements. **Relationship:** Logged vehicle data and a nominal control model feed residual-model training; held-out logs and simulation test generalization; only selected trained model files are loaded into the trajectory follower. Vehicle/simulator configuration and mismatch conditions shape the reported result; the tool is an optional emerging research path.

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Vehicle integration foundations include consistent coordinate frames, units, timestamp semantics and sensor/vehicle interface contracts. ROS REP 103/105 provide explicit frame conventions; IEEE 1588 supplies a general network clock-synchronization protocol; ISO 23150-20 specifies a bounded automated-driving sensor input/supportive interface. **Locator:** ROS REP 103 and REP 105 sections on units, frames, map/odom/base_link semantics; IEEE 1588-2019 official status/scope; ISO 23150-20:2026 official abstract; Autoware vehicle-interface design notes. **Sources:** D166-ROS-REP-103-COORDINATE-CONVENTIONS, D166-ROS-REP-105-MOBILE-PLATFORM-FRAMES, D166-IEEE-1588-2019-PTP, D166-ISO-23150-20-SENSOR-INTERFACES-2026, D166-AUTOWARE-VEHICLE-INTERFACE-DESIGN-2026 **Area context:** These are interface literacy prerequisites for correctly interpreting sensor measurements, vehicle state and commands across components; timing/frame consistency enables fusion and control but does not itself perform them. **Limit:** ROS conventions are ecosystem-specific and informational; IEEE 1588 performance depends on profile and implementation; the ISO abstract is not the full paid standard and excludes electrical/mechanical interfaces. **Relationship:** Sensors and vehicle components emit measurements with units, frames and timestamps; middleware/interface contracts preserve or transform these; localization, perception and control consume them. This is an engineering data dependency, not proof of a universal course sequence.
- **Claim:** Traditional CAN CC integration separates data-link/physical-layer responsibilities from higher-layer services: CAN frames carry content identifiers that arbitrate bus access, while ISO 15765-5 specifies an OSI-layered DoCAN connection from external diagnostic equipment through a vehicle DLC to a CAN network. **Locator:** CiA CAN CC knowledge page sections 'CAN data link layer' and 'Error detection and fault confinement'; ISO 11898-1:2024 catalogue scope; ISO 15765-5:2023 OBP sections 1 and 5, especially OSI layers and DLC-to-CAN connection. **Sources:** D166-CIA-CAN-CC-KNOWLEDGE, D166-ISO-11898-1-2024-CATALOG, D166-ISO-15765-5-2023-OBP **Area context:** Established/traditional CAN CC and DoCAN foundation retained in current standards catalogues; this is a layered vehicle-network/diagnostic interface example, not the complete contemporary vehicle network stack. **Limit:** No timing determinism, deadline guarantee, security/authentication, safety integrity, deployment prevalence or universal architecture is inferred. ISO 11898-1:2024 includes CAN CC/FD/XL options; this claim is deliberately limited to CAN CC and DoCAN framing. **Relationship:** {'type': 'prerequisite', 'explanation': 'Vehicle command and diagnostic semantics depend on lower-layer network transport and physical connectivity; the standards define distinct layers and do not supply the application contract or vehicle-specific safety behavior.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Current**
- **Claim:** Current integration work spans vehicle signal and sensor contracts, clock/frame alignment, runtime/service communication, diagnostics and health/update management. AUTOSAR Adaptive documents one current production-oriented service platform; ISO 23150-20 defines a sensor input interface scope; current Autoware interface documentation gives a concrete open-stack example. **Locator:** AUTOSAR Adaptive R25-11 overview; ISO 23150-20:2026 scope; Autoware vehicle-interface design documentation, inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D166-AUTOSAR-ADAPTIVE-PLATFORM-R25-11-CURRENT, D166-ISO-23150-20-SENSOR-INTERFACES-2026, D166-AUTOWARE-VEHICLE-INTERFACE-DESIGN-2026, D166-ISO-14229-1-2026-UDS-CURRENT **Area context:** This situates system integration between ADS applications and vehicle sensors/ECUs/compute, including diagnostics and lifecycle concerns rather than only connecting software modules. **Limit:** AUTOSAR is an example rather than a universal deployed stack; ISO requirements are abstract-limited here; a project document cannot establish industry prevalence or safety compliance. **Relationship:** Application services and sensor/vehicle interfaces depend on correct signal, timing and diagnostic contracts; health/fault state feeds monitoring and fallback behavior; updates and configuration must preserve validated system behavior.
- **Claim:** Integration requires consistent message semantics, units/frames, timestamps, communication and feedback status; control intent is not the same as measured actuation or mode. **Locator:** Autoware Vehicle Interface design sections 2-4 and vehicle interface current message/API docs; ROS REP 103 and IEEE 1588 source-index records. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-VEHICLE-INTERFACE-TUTORIAL, D166-IEEE-1588-2019-PTP, D166-ROS-REP-103-COORDINATE-CONVENTIONS **Area context:** Interface contract and integration foundation, not planning/controller design. **Limit:** Autoware and ROS examples are ecosystem-specific; IEEE 1588 is generic timing and does not guarantee achieved system accuracy. **Relationship:** {'type': 'prerequisite', 'explanation': 'Correct command/status interpretation presupposes compatible message, unit, frame and timing conventions; exact implementation varies.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Emerging**
- **Claim:** An emerging integration trend is service-oriented, high-performance compute connected to legacy ECUs, sensors and software-defined-vehicle diagnostics. AUTOSAR Adaptive R25-11 describes signal-to-service bridging and lifecycle services; ASAM SOVD 1.0.0 extends diagnostic access for software-rich/HPC systems while explicitly coexisting with UDS. **Locator:** AUTOSAR Adaptive R25-11 current platform overview; ASAM SOVD 1.0.0 scope/version and relation to UDS, inspected 2026-10-23/24. **Sources:** D166-AUTOSAR-ADAPTIVE-PLATFORM-R25-11-CURRENT, D166-ASAM-SOVD-1-0-0-CURRENT, D166-ISO-14229-1-2026-UDS-CURRENT **Area context:** This adds service discovery, software lifecycle, distributed diagnostics and mixed-platform integration to the area’s foundations, relevant where AV compute is integrated with production vehicle systems. **Limit:** Standards-body descriptions establish intended interfaces and versions, not universal adoption, implementation quality, achieved latency or functional-safety assurance; SOVD adoption/version status must be rechecked. **Relationship:** High-performance applications and legacy ECU signals are bridged through platform services; diagnostics and health data support service supervision and repair; this works alongside established UDS pathways rather than simply replacing them.
- **Claim:** An emerging vehicle-integration foundation is understanding how a service-oriented Adaptive Platform can coexist with Classic ECU software through standardized interfaces and signal-to-service translation, and how redundant service instances may support fail-operational designs; CAPI 1.0 adds a common implementation initiative, but platform capability is not proof of any vehicle's redundancy or safety behavior. **Locator:** AUTOSAR Adaptive Platform page, lines 148-163: service-oriented runtime, standardized interfaces, Signal-to-Service Translation, redundant service mirroring/takeover and Classic/Adaptive coexistence; CAPI 1.0 release page, lines 141-150, identifies the 2026 executable implementation and code generators. **Sources:** D166-AUTOSAR-ADAPTIVE-PLATFORM-R25-11-CURRENT, D166-AUTOSAR-CAPI-1-0-2026 **Area context:** Emerging integration foundation as of 2026-10-26: platform capabilities have existed in the Adaptive standard, while the common executable implementation is newly released. Neither maturity label means universal industry use. **Limit:** Official standard/issuer pages only; no full technical specification, CAPI code, fault-injection test, timing analysis, safety case, implementation conformance or vehicle deployment was inspected. Licensing/access and independent adoption remain unresolved. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'Classic and Adaptive can coexist and translate signals/services at their boundary; redundant service execution can complement fault-tolerance design but does not replace end-to-end vehicle safety analysis or evidence.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Methods and designs, Future**
- **Claim:** ConvIO is a 2026 research method for designing centralized zonal automotive E/E architectures: its five-step process assigns I/O to chassis-aware zones, selects zone counts/locations, and generates communication paths around an HPC. In a single BEV-model case study, the authors report 68.7-69.9% lower combined LV cable length than a domain-oriented baseline across three network topologies; this is not evidence of production deployment, safety validation or universal optimality. **Locator:** Mauser et al., IEEE Access 14 (2026), pp. 98616-98632, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3707952. Full published text: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/408232334_ConvIO_A_Framework_for_Convergence_of_Inputs_and_Outputs_in_Automotive_Zonal_EE_Architectures; institutional record: https://portal.fis.tum.de/en/publications/convio-a-framework-for-convergence-of-inputs-and-outputs-in-autom/. **Sources:** D166-MAUSER-CONVIO-ZONAL-EE-ARCH-2026 **Area context:** Future/futuristic candidate for next-generation SDV/zonal E/E integration methods, published in 2026; the horizon is not evidence of production maturity or adoption. **Limit:** Single modeled BEV case and reported wiring-length outcome; generalization across platforms/I/O distributions is unproven. Full production constraints, independent reproduction, timing/cybersecurity and comprehensive functional-safety analysis are not established; fault-containment extensions are future work. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'A physical E/E architecture-design method complementary to software/middleware/interface design; it does not define service APIs or prove a complete or universally optimal vehicle architecture.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Traditional**
- **Claim:** Traditional integration techniques include coordinate/unit transforms, timestamp synchronization, signal adaptation and command conversion between generic ADS outputs and vehicle-specific actuator/chassis interfaces. ROS frame conventions and the Autoware/Apollo interface examples make these transformations inspectable. **Locator:** ROS REP 103/105; IEEE 1588-2019 scope; Autoware vehicle-interface and raw-command converter docs; Apollo chassis command schema. **Sources:** D166-ROS-REP-103-COORDINATE-CONVENTIONS, D166-ROS-REP-105-MOBILE-PLATFORM-FRAMES, D166-IEEE-1588-2019-PTP, D166-AUTOWARE-VEHICLE-INTERFACE-DESIGN-2026, D166-AUTOWARE-RAW-VEHICLE-CMD-CONVERTER-2026, D166-APOLLO-CHASSIS-COMMAND-SCHEMA-2026 **Area context:** These are concrete transformation and synchronization techniques at subsystem boundaries; they prevent semantic mismatch but do not substitute for calibration, state estimation or vehicle control. **Limit:** The technique evidence is project/convention specific; clock synchronization and frame transforms require configuration and validation, while command conversion alone cannot demonstrate safe actuation. **Relationship:** Sensor/state values are normalized into the consumer frame and time base; control messages are translated to vehicle-specific commands; vehicle response and status return to the ADS through the reverse interface.
- **Claim:** An archived Autoware.Auto vehicle-interface reference specifies timestamped normalized acceleration/steering commands, vehicle-state commands, odometry/status feedback, and concrete command-handling behaviors: map normalized inputs to actuators, hold commands between updates, reject unsafe commands or sequences, fall back to a stop after command timeout, and allow manual override. These are bounded interface techniques in one project reference design, not universal vehicle-interface requirements. **Locator:** Autoware.Auto Vehicle-Interface-Reference-Implementation, Scope and Reference Implementation, lines 22-33; timestamped control-command schema and rationale, lines 40-68; output/state-report contract, lines 144-174 and 237-252; Behaviors, lines 253-263 and linked sections Command mapping, Zero order hold, Unsafe Command Rejection, Timeout Fallback Behavior and Manual Override. **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-AUTO-VEHICLE-INTERFACE-REFERENCE-IMPLEMENTATION-2019 **Area context:** Established/traditional interface techniques documented in an archived Autoware.Auto reference design; the document defines its minimal contract for compatible Autoware.Auto-derived stacks and does not establish OEM adoption or current prevalence. **Limit:** Archived reference design, not evidence of adoption across OEMs or validation of a particular vehicle. It does not specify universal calibrated limits, safe-stop performance, fault coverage, measured timing, certification or public-road safety. The timeout-stop behavior must be validated for the actual vehicle and operating context. **Relationship:** {'type': 'output_dependency', 'explanation': 'The interface consumes controller-level motion commands and produces physical-actuation requests plus vehicle-state/odometry feedback. This is a component boundary, not proof of a universal learner sequence or that the interface replaces vehicle-specific ECU/network integration and validation.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Current**
- **Claim:** Current integration techniques include service-to-signal bridging, UDS/SOVD diagnostic requests and logging, sensor-interface health/calibration metadata, and standardized message exchange among simulation components. They solve distinct production, diagnostic and virtual-test handoffs. **Locator:** AUTOSAR Adaptive R25-11 signal/service translation; ISO 14229-1:2026 UDS; ASAM SOVD 1.0.0; ISO 23150-20:2026; ASAM OSI 3.8.0. **Sources:** D166-AUTOSAR-ADAPTIVE-PLATFORM-R25-11-CURRENT, D166-ISO-14229-1-2026-UDS-CURRENT, D166-ASAM-SOVD-1-0-0-CURRENT, D166-ISO-23150-20-SENSOR-INTERFACES-2026, D166-ASAM-OSI-3-8-0 **Area context:** These are implementation techniques supporting service integration, diagnostics and simulation interoperability across a mixed ADS/vehicle system. **Limit:** The techniques cannot be collapsed into a single alternative set: production signal bridging, ECU diagnostics, sensor metadata and simulator messages operate at different layers; editions and adoption vary. **Relationship:** Vehicle signals and sensor metadata enter runtime services; diagnostic protocols expose state/logging to tools; simulator messages connect virtual components for tests; integration verification checks end-to-end contracts.
- **Claim:** Current vehicle-interface implementations adapt generic acceleration and steering targets into vehicle-specific actuation using calibrated command maps and feedback, instrument command-to-publish latency, and expose mode/fault state; an Apollo Devkit example gates auto engagement on actuator response and transitions to a configured emergency mode for selected faults. **Locator:** Autoware raw_vehicle_cmd_converter documentation, Overview/reference-data/Vehicle Adaptor/Latency Measurement sections (lines 1082-1123); Apollo Chassis schema, DrivingMode/ErrorCode and status/timestamp fields (lines 731-875); Apollo Devkit controller, EnableAutoMode response checks and SecurityDogThreadFunc fault transition (lines 2971-3033 and 3558-3684). **Sources:** D166-AUTOWARE-RAW-VEHICLE-CMD-CONVERTER-2026, D166-APOLLO-CHASSIS-COMMAND-SCHEMA-2026, D166-APOLLO-DEVKIT-CONTROLLER-EXAMPLE-2026 **Area context:** Current software-to-vehicle interface integration at the actuation boundary: generic controller targets are converted to a particular drive-by-wire interface and accompanied by vehicle status/mode/fault reporting; this is distinct from trajectory tracking algorithm design and from a system safety case. **Limit:** Project documentation/code does not establish vehicle deployment, safety certification or universal practice. Autoware's latency metric ends at software publication, not measured physical actuation. Its vehicle-adaptor feature is labeled under development. Apollo fault thresholds and emergency commands are platform-specific; no safe-stop efficacy, timing guarantee, or independent validation is shown. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'Command adaptation complements the trajectory controller by translating its desired acceleration/steering into vehicle-specific signals and returning state/diagnostics. Interface-level fault handling consumes platform feedback; it does not replace the vehicle safety concept, independent fallback validation, or controller stability analysis.'}

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Emerging**
- **Claim:** Emerging interface techniques include REST/JSON vehicle diagnostics for distributed software, standardized sensor health/calibration input metadata and reusable simulator/XIL interfaces; event-specific remote emergency signaling and integrated logging supply additional bounded racing examples. **Locator:** ASAM SOVD 1.0.0; ISO 23150-20:2026 abstract; ASAM OSI/XIL; Formula Student Germany Driverless Specification 2026 v1.1 and A2RL 2024 engineering report. **Sources:** D166-ASAM-SOVD-1-0-0-CURRENT, D166-ISO-23150-20-SENSOR-INTERFACES-2026, D166-ASAM-OSI-3-8-0, D166-ASAM-XIL-3-0-0, D166-FSG-DRIVERLESS-SPEC-2026-V1-1, D166-A2RL-COMPETITION-LESSONS-2024 **Area context:** These examples extend integration from point-to-point signals to observable software services and standardized test setups, including explicit emergency/logging interfaces in constrained race vehicles. **Limit:** Competition and simulator interfaces are not public-road vehicle interfaces; ISO scope is abstract-limited; ASAM SOVD is a published but evolving standard and does not prove fleet adoption. **Relationship:** Sensor/vehicle services and remote diagnostics expose state; test automation and simulation interfaces support repeated component/system checks; event emergency signaling terminates or disables the test vehicle in that competition context.
- **Claim:** Näke et al. formulate zonal control-unit placement and component assignment as a p-median/location-covering integer linear program, and cable routing as a capacitated multi-commodity-flow integer linear program minimizing wire length. The exact optimum is conditional on the stated graph, objective and constraints; evaluation uses a simplified vehicle topology and synthetic randomized nets. **Locator:** Näke et al., Efficient Architecture Evaluation and Generation of Automotive Wiring Harnesses, IEEE ITEC Asia-Pacific 2025, DOI 10.1109/ITECAsia-Pacific63742.2025.11345003; full five-page author-deposited paper, Sections II-V: https://www.ifte.de/mitarbeiter/lienig/ITEC_AP_2025.pdf; TU Dresden institutional publication record: https://fis.tu-dresden.de/portal/en/publications/efficient-architecture-evaluation-and-generation-of-automotive-wiring-harnesses(724c6c22-aba8-4b64-a244-932c01ab6a71).html. **Sources:** D166-NAEKE-STEIN-ETAL-ZONAL-ILP-ROUTING-ITEC-2025 **Area context:** Emerging optimization formulation for zonal E/E architecture and harness design in a 2025 peer-reviewed conference paper; it is a design-stage research method, not evidence of deployed OEM practice. **Limit:** One five-page study with synthetic workloads on one simplified base-vehicle topology. It omits ZCU-to-ZCU wiring and detailed 3D/circle-packing feasibility; no independent reproduction, production harness, timing/QoS, EMC, power integrity, installation, safety validation or full cost/weight objective was inspected. No head-to-head comparison with ConvIO was conducted. **Relationship:** {'type': 'alternative', 'explanation': "Conditional alternative to ConvIO's clustering and greedy routing for zonal placement/assignment and route design only when topology, constraints, objective and required outputs are made comparable; neither study establishes universal superiority."}

**Mapped cell evidence — Techniques, estimators and algorithms, Future**
- **Claim:** Future-facing technique evidence is limited to standardization and interoperability work for software-defined vehicle services, universal ADS interfaces, sensor input contracts and cross-tool simulation/test exchange; no one future interface method is established as settled practice. **Locator:** ITU-T universal ADS interface work item; ASAM SOVD development/status notes; ISO 23150-20:2026; ASAM OSI 3.8.0 and XIL 3.0.0. **Sources:** D166-ITU-T-UNIVERSAL-ADS-INTERFACES-2025, D166-ASAM-SOVD-1-0-0-CURRENT, D166-ISO-23150-20-SENSOR-INTERFACES-2026, D166-ASAM-OSI-3-8-0, D166-ASAM-XIL-3-0-0 **Area context:** The area can teach learners to track emerging interoperability proposals and assess their potential to reduce custom integration across vendors and test systems. **Limit:** A work item, current standard or future development plan does not prove adoption or future technical success; simulation interfaces do not automatically become production interfaces. **Relationship:** Potentially shared interfaces could enable greater component/test reuse, but any downstream use depends on publication, implementation conformance and system-level validation.
- **Claim:** ConvIO's future-zonal design uses a distinct algorithmic stack: k-d-tree mapping of I/O to chassis connection points, k-means/elbow heuristic for initial zone count, Dijkstra-derived chassis path distances for hierarchical agglomerative refinement, and greedy nearest-neighbor communication-path generation. The paper tests this stack in one modeled BEV case; it does not prove globally optimal zoning or deployed network performance. **Locator:** Mauser et al., IEEE Access 14 (2026), pp. 98616-98632, DOI 10.1109/ACCESS.2026.3707952; full published text Sections V.A-V.E and Algorithms 1-6 (PDF pp. 4-8), with validation and limitations in Sections VI-VIII. Author-uploaded full text: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/408232334_ConvIO_A_Framework_for_Convergence_of_Inputs_and_Outputs_in_Automotive_Zonal_EE_Architectures; TUM institutional record cross-check. **Sources:** D166-MAUSER-CONVIO-ZONAL-EE-ARCH-2026 **Area context:** Future/futuristic algorithm candidate for designing zonal SDV E/E integration; research implementation and one modeled case do not establish deployment or adoption. **Limit:** The paper combines heuristics and a greedy route method; global optimality is not established. One BEV-model scenario, limited cable-length KPI and no independent implementation/reproduction; latency, network load, fault containment, cybersecurity, production routing constraints and cross-platform robustness are not validated. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'MAP085 isolates the computational methods embedded within the broader architecture-design framework mapped in MAP084; it is not an independent replication or a second architecture outcome.'}

Vendor statements are not independent evaluations. Adoption, license/cost, target compatibility, determinism, conformance, test coverage, model validity and safety efficacy are not established. **Relationship:** {'type': 'alternative', 'explanation': 'ASAM XIL is an interface standard; NI VeriStand and Vector CANoe are vendor-specific product examples with overlapping but nonidentical roles. **Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Traditional**
- **Claim:** ADS safety foundations distinguish hazards from malfunctioning E/E behavior (functional safety) and hazards from functional insufficiency or foreseeable misuse (SOTIF); both must be interpreted against the system's intended function and operational context. **Locator:** ISO 26262 official package overview; ISO 21448:2022 abstract/status; UL 4600 Edition 3 scope, inspected 2026-10-23/24. **Sources:** D166-ISO-26262, D166-ISO-21448, D166-UL4600-ED3-AUTONOMOUS-SAFETY-2023 **Area context:** This gives learners the core hazard/process distinction behind safety engineering for automated functions and autonomous products. **Limit:** Standards are paid and only public scope/abstracts were reviewed; ISO 21448 is marked for revision. UL 4600 is goal-based voluntary guidance and none alone demonstrates product safety. **Relationship:** Hazard and intended-function analyses inform safety requirements and risk controls; verification/validation provides evidence against those requirements; residual risks remain explicit in the safety argument.
- **Claim:** A foundational safety-V&V competency is recognizing that rare severe outcomes make direct road-exposure demonstrations statistically demanding: required miles depend on event rate, confidence/precision target and comparator assumptions, while underreporting and a moving human-driver benchmark add uncertainty. RAND's 2016 analysis concludes that driving alone cannot establish fatality/injury safety before release under its studied assumptions; it does not conclude that ADS safety is impossible to assess. **Locator:** Kalra and Paddock, RAND RR-1478-RC (2016), official 15-page report: Executive Summary pp. 1-2; statistical formulations/results pp. 3-6; benchmark and limitation discussion. Full official RAND PDF opened 2026-10-26; TRID bibliographic record cross-checked. **Sources:** D166-RAND-RR1478-RARE-EVENT-ROAD-TEST-2016, D166-ZHAO-STATISTICAL-FOUNDATION-SCENARIO-TESTING-2025, D166-OKELLY-RARE-EVENT-AV-TESTING-2018 **Area context:** Established foundational knowledge for planning ADS safety evidence and interpreting road-test claims; the report is a historical U.S. statistical analysis, not a current universal validation prescription. **Limit:** 2016 policy research, not a standard or regulator acceptance criterion. It does not establish today's crash rates, a universally required mileage threshold, scenario/simulator validity, causal safety improvement, or that simulation/other methods automatically solve residual uncertainty. U.S. rates and legal context do not transfer directly to Nigeria or other jurisdictions. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': "Road exposure contributes operational evidence but, under the report's rare-event assumptions, cannot alone supply timely pre-release statistical proof for severe outcomes; scenario, simulation, component and other evidence may complement it, but the report does not validate any particular substitute or fixed assurance sequence."}

**Mapped cell evidence — Foundations, knowledge and competencies, Current**
- **Claim:** Current ADS safety work treats ODD definition, system safety, OEDR, fallback, cybersecurity and testing as connected but distinct safety elements; NHTSA's U.S. ADS guidance is voluntary, and standards provide separate safety, SOTIF and ODD frameworks. **Locator:** NHTSA current ADS guidance/FAQ; ISO 34503:2023 ODD scope; ISO 26262/21448 official records, inspected 2026-10-24. **Sources:** D166-NHTSA-ADS-VOLUNTARY-GUIDANCE-CURRENT, D166-ISO-34503-ODD-TAXONOMY-2023, D166-ISO-26262, D166-ISO-21448 **Area context:** This contextualizes safety practice as a system-level argument tied to operating domain, perception/response, fallback and test evidence rather than a single controller metric. **Limit:** NHTSA is U.S. voluntary guidance, not certification; ISO records are abstract-limited and ODD taxonomy does not itself establish monitoring or test coverage. **Relationship:** Define system function and ODD; identify hazards and safety constraints; verify component behavior and validate scenarios; connect evidence and residual risk to deployment decisions under applicable jurisdiction.
- **Claim:** ISO 26262 and ISO 21448 address different risk causes: E/E malfunctions versus hazards from intended-function insufficiency/performance limits and reasonably foreseeable misuse; 21448 excludes 26262 faults and cybersecurity. **Locator:** ISO 21448:2022 official scope/abstract (edition published June 2022; status to be revised as of 2025-10-14); ISO 26262 series source-index record. **Sources:** D166-ISO-26262, D166-ISO-21448-2022-STATUS-SCOPE **Area context:** Component/system functional safety and SOTIF are related but non-identical safety workstreams. **Limit:** Standards are paid beyond preview and 21448 revision is underway; confirm edition/status and applicability before compliance decisions. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'The standards address distinct hazard sources and can complement one another; neither alone is an ADS-wide safety case.'}

ISO says external AI-element development and AI-based software tools are outside scope. Not a testing-threshold catalogue, standalone certificate or proof of safety. **Relationship:** {'type': 'complement', 'explanation': 'AI safety properties complement functional-safety, SOTIF, ADS scenario evaluation and system-level V&V; the PAS abstract does not replace these or establish a complete safety case.'}

NIST describes ongoing work on combinatorial input-space measurement; 2026 review work identifies simulation-heavy evidence, inconsistent metrics and limited uncertainty validation as gaps. **Locator:** NIST Autonomous Systems Assurance project page, updated 2025-03; 2026 safety-MPC review publisher-indexed abstract; NVIDIA SAFE vendor framework as a bounded example, inspected 2026-10-26. **Sources:** D166-NIST-AUTONOMOUS-SYSTEMS-ASSURANCE, D166-SAFETY-MPC-AV-SYSTEMATIC-REVIEW-2026, D166-NVIDIA-HALOS-SAFE-TECHNICAL-BRIEF **Area context:** Students can learn to ask whether a validation claim covers the input space and deployment context, not only whether a test suite ran or a benchmark score improved. **Limit:** NIST describes ongoing research rather than a completed universal method; review is abstract-limited; NVIDIA is vendor-authored and commercially interested. ODD/model adequacy and complementary empirical testing remain unresolved. **Relationship:** {'type': 'prerequisite', 'explanation': "These formal foundations are prerequisites used by MAP081's CoCoSaFe controller-code verification technique; defining them does not perform verification or establish system-level assurance."}
